![Image 1: 🏜️ Where the Red Rocks Tell a Story Colorado National Monument in Grand Junction, Colorado, is one of those places that makes you stop and realize how powerful nature can be. These incredible red-rock canyons, towering monoliths, and cliffs were shaped over millions of years by uplift, wind, water, freezing, and erosion. The result is a landscape that almost looks impossible. � National Park Service +1 But this land has a story that goes far beyond the rocks. People have lived in and around these canyons for more than 10,000 years. Indigenous peoples, including the Archaic and Fremont peoples and later the Ute, used this land for hunting, gathering plants, farming, traveling, and living with the seasons. Evidence such as rock art, tools, hearths, and ancient travel routes tells us that these canyons were important long before Colorado National Monument was established. � National Park Service The monument was officially established by President William Howard Taft on May 24, 1911, thanks in large part to John Otto, who explored the canyons, built trails, and believed this place deserved protection. � National Park Service Today, there are miles of beautiful trails to explore, from short walks like Window Rock to challenging adventures through Ute Canyon, Monument Canyon, and other rugged routes. The monument has about 46 miles of trails and 14 trailheads. � National Park Service +1 And while the views are breathtaking, they demand respect. Watch every step, especially near canyon edges and steep sections. One careless step can turn a beautiful adventure into something much worse. Bring water, take your time, and enjoy the beauty—but respect the power of this incredible place. #ColoradoNationalMonument #GrandJunction #ColoradoHiking #NationalPark #ExploreColorado ](https://p19-common-sign.tiktokcdn-us.com/tos-useast8-p-0068-tx2/ocHbQQAXsgefEGKA9aRUV2gfwcfHM8hFUtBq1p~tplv-tiktokx-origin.image?dr=9636&x-expires=1791363600&x-signature=iojcRP1jNyAkZ8xkFotULnJCmKw%3D&t=4d5b0474&ps=13740610&shp=81f88b70&shcp=43f4a2f9&idc=useast5)

🏜️ Where the Red Rocks Tell a Story  
Colorado National Monument in Grand Junction, Colorado, is one of those places that makes you stop and realize how powerful nature can be. These incredible red-rock canyons, towering monoliths, and cliffs were shaped over millions of years by uplift, wind, water, freezing, and erosion. The result is a landscape that almost looks impossible. �  
National Park Service +1  
But this land has a story that goes far beyond the rocks. People have lived in and around these canyons for more than 10,000 years. Indigenous peoples, including the Archaic and Fremont peoples and later the Ute, used this land for hunting, gathering plants, farming, traveling, and living with the seasons. Evidence such as rock art, tools, hearths, and ancient travel routes tells us that these canyons were important long before Colorado National Monument was established. �  
National Park Service  
The monument was officially established by President William Howard Taft on May 24, 1911, thanks in large part to John Otto, who explored the canyons, built trails, and believed this place deserved protection. �  
National Park Service  
Today, there are miles of beautiful trails to explore, from short walks like Window Rock to challenging adventures through Ute Canyon, Monument Canyon, and other rugged routes. The monument has about 46 miles of trails and 14 trailheads. �  
National Park Service +1  
And while the views are breathtaking, they demand respect. Watch every step, especially near canyon edges and steep sections. One careless step can turn a beautiful adventure into something much worse. Bring water, take your time, and enjoy the beauty—but respect the power of this incredible place.

## A short but steep hike to a magnificent cliff dwelling called Moon House in Bears Ears National Monument

* * *

### Moon House, a multi-room cliff dwelling named for its celestial pictograph, is an exceptional archaeological site in McCloyd Canyon on Cedar Mesa, Utah.

The Bureau of Land Management [requires a day use permit](https://www.blm.gov/programs/recreation/permits-and-passes/lotteries-and-permit-systems/utah/cedarmesa "BLM Permit information") to visit Moon House and limits access to 20 people per day. Remember, it is illegal to remove any artifacts or damage sites in any way. Fines or jail time can result for those who break the law. Leave all artifacts where you find them, don’t lean on walls or enter interior rooms, avoid touching rock art, and don’t add modern graffiti.

#### Hike to Moon House

From the BLM kiosk at the trailhead, hike north along the dirt road for 1.25 miles. The Abajo Mountains poke above the rolling hills of sagebrush and piñon and juniper trees, and cryptobiotic soil covers the sandy benches on both sides of the road. You cross a wash around 1 mile, and the road ends at a sandstone patio. Foot trails seem to leave from every side of the parking area, but look for two No Motor Vehicle posts separated by a line of rocks on the north side of the 4WD parking area. The wide bedrock trail continues north from here and is marked with large cairns.

#### **Descend into McCloyd Canyon**

The trail starts an immediate descent towards McCloyd Canyon that steepens when you reach the rim. Follow the cairns down a precipitous, rocky route, curve around to the right side of a slickrock amphitheater, and slide down the lip of an overhung ledge. A pile of rocks below aids your descent.

The trail swings back to the left, making a large switchback across the amphitheater. A little ways down the trail, you can see Moon House hidden on a ledge on the opposite canyon wall.

Directly across from the site, the trail drops down to the bottom of the canyon. After a few broad switchbacks, the trail descends a steep scree slope and spits you onto the canyon floor at 1.6 miles.

#### **Climbing up to Moon House**

Turn right, crossing to the other side and proceeding downcanyon a short distance along the slickrock floor. Stay left of a pouroff, and you soon reach a route that ascends the left canyon wall. Climb to the next tier of slickrock, where several cairns lead you higher. The final push involves climbing up a crack to the base of an overhung ledge around 1.7 miles. From here, you can access Moon House.

##### **Visit Moon House with respect**

Look for an ammo can, whose contents include cultural interpretation and visitation information for the site. Archaeologists estimate that migrating Puebloan people built the dwellings around A.D. 1264.

You may enter the main portion through the small doorway in the long rock wall; just be careful not to pull yourself in using the sides or top of the entryway. A hidden hallway and string of rooms stretch behind the fortified wall. Since you can’t enter the rooms, bring a flashlight or headlamp to see inside. Corncobs lie on the floors of the rooms, and pictographs decorate the outside and inside.

The room that gave Moon House its name is the one with a painted white band around it, with pictographs of half moon and full moon figures on opposite walls. Like the other rooms, don’t enter it. You can clearly see the pictograph by shining light into the room. The BLM put sterile sand on the floor to absorb moisture from people’s breath that can break down the ancient pigment on the walls.

With thousands of people visiting this fragile place, please follow all guidelines to help preserve the site. Return the way you came.

* * *

### Directions to the Moon House trailhead

From the junction of UT 95 and UT 261, drive south on UT 261 for about 4 miles. Stop at the Kane Gulch Ranger Station on the left side of the road to pick up your required hiking permit (March 1 – June 15 and Sept 1 – Oct 31). [For other dates, see the BLM’s permit information›](https://www.blm.gov/sites/blm.gov/files/Recreation_Monticello_Moon%20House%20Day%20Use%20Permits.pdf)

Continue heading south on UT 261 for another 6 miles until you reach Snow Flat Road. Turn left, pass a BLM map, and veer left at a small sign marked “Trail.” This road can become impassable when wet, so check the weather before beginning your trip.

In about 3.5 miles, the dirt road deteriorates. Even with high clearance vehicles, some road construction may be necessary to help ease you down bedrock drops. The road improves again, and around 8 miles you reach the trailhead marked by a kiosk. You can park in the dirt lot on the right side of the road.

## A short hike to White House Ruin, a cliff dwelling in the bottom of Canyon De Chelly.

* * *

### _This is the only self-guided trail in Canyon De Chelly; visitors must have a guide to hike beyond White House Ruin._

#### Hike to White House Ruin

Leaving the trailhead behind, follow the canyon rim along a broad flat bench of De Chelly Sandstone, which was deposited as windblown sand dunes 250 million years ago. The trail continues to drop at a steady rate, and at 0.4 mile, it cuts through dark-colored Shinarump Conglomerate, composed of different sediments deposited by streams about 200 million years ago.

The trail continues to switchback down the De Chelly Sandstone into the large amphitheater, carved by the stream when it meandered along the bottom of the cliffs where residents now grow crops. At 0.75 mile, you reach a sandy bench. When the trail drops to the canyon floor, you’ll see a traditional Navajo home called a hogan.

Canyon De Chelly is still home to many Navajo residents; please respect the sign that prohibits taking photographs of the hogan.

#### Continue to White House Ruin

After hooking sharply left, the trail crosses a deeply eroded sandy bench and goes downstream to a bridge. You can either cross the bridge or simply walk downstream (if there is no water) until you see White House Ruin on the right at the base of the cliff. Navajo venders selling arts and crafts are frequently sitting quietly in the shade of the trees beside the stream.

The light-colored plaster on some of the rooms led to the Navajo name for the site — Kinii’ ni gai — which means White House. Archaeologists believe the rooms on the canyon floor used to be high enough to provide access to the upper rooms in the alcove.

Although people have lived in Canyon de Chelly for more than 5,000 years, it was Ancestral Puebloans who built White House around 1060 AD. More rooms were added during the next 200 years, and archaeologists estimate there may have been up to 80 rooms and four kivas when it was most heavily used.

After enjoying the view of White House and the tapestry wall above it, return the way you came.

* * *

### Directions to the White House Ruin trailhead

From the park visitor center, drive 5 miles on the South Rim road and turn left on the paved road to White House Overlook. Drive 0.75 mile to the overlook parking lot. The trail begins on the path to the overlook.

# Colorado  National Monument • Colorado

[![Image 5: sandstone spire hundreds of feet tall stands above sparsely vegetated canyon bottom and cliffs](https://share.google/common/uploads/structured_data/9DAD9E70-FE9C-A507-CCD4F5B8E14B26E4.jpg?width=990&height=742&mode=crop&quality=90)](https://share.google/common/uploads/structured_data/9DAD9E70-FE9C-A507-CCD4F5B8E14B26E4.jpg)

Colorado National Monument preserves one of the grand landscapes of the American West. But this treasure is much more than a monument. Towering monoliths exist within a vast plateau and canyon panorama. You can experience sheer-walled, red rock canyons along the twists and turns of Rim Rock Drive, where you may spy bighorn sheep and soaring eagles.

Blake McCord

# Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument

Protecting canyons, fossils, cultural history, rare species, and precious waters in southern Utah

## Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument’s geology, archaeology, and history span millennia.

### Its sculpted canyons, hidden arches, and colorful cliffs hold stories of our planet’s past, while deep human history traces its contours.

Today Grand Staircase-Escalante remains a living cultural landscape for many tribes, a place of scientific study for researchers, and a refuge for plants and animals.

![Image 3: A man in a blue shirt stands on yellow rock overlooking a valley in Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument](blob:http://localhost/03edef78a65430c163cdfe0e09d59fbf)

Blake McCord

## About Grand Staircase-Escalante national monument

## The science monument

Since its designation in 1996, Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument has served as an outdoor laboratory with a unique mission of conducting science, research, and education to protect, conserve, and restore these vast landscapes.

Scientists have unearthed new dinosaur species, inventoried hundreds of bees and rare plants, and surveyed archaeological sites and rock writings. Even more scientific findings await.

## What does Grand Staircase-Escalante protect?

![Image 5: Two women and a man lean in to examine cones on a pinyon pine tree](blob:http://localhost/c5930cd8f0eb111448873d4446f8deec)

Bureau of Land Management

### [Fossils](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/blog/dinosaur-finds-grand-staircase-escalante)

Grand Staircase-Escalante’s library of fossils includes turtles, crocodiles, lizards, dinosaurs, and more.

![Image 7: Two women and a man lean in to examine cones on a pinyon pine tree](blob:http://localhost/c5930cd8f0eb111448873d4446f8deec)

Marie Read

### [Birds](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/blog/creature-feature-rare-birds-grand-staircase)

Over 200 bird species call the Grand Staircase-Escalante region home. See some of the rare birds.

![Image 9: Two women and a man lean in to examine cones on a pinyon pine tree](blob:http://localhost/c5930cd8f0eb111448873d4446f8deec)

Blake McCord

### [Geology](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/blog/geology-rocks-steps-grand-staircase-escalante-cpe)

Learn about the stepped rock layers that make up the namesake Grand Staircase.

![Image 11: Two women and a man lean in to examine cones on a pinyon pine tree](blob:http://localhost/c5930cd8f0eb111448873d4446f8deec)

Blake McCord

### [Wildflowers](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/blog/grand-staircase-escalante-wildflowers)

There are over 1,000+ plant species in the monument, and most are wildflowers.

![Image 13: Two women and a man lean in to examine cones on a pinyon pine tree](blob:http://localhost/c5930cd8f0eb111448873d4446f8deec)

Blake McCord

### [Canyons](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/blog/cows-escalante-when-win-win-becomes-lose-lose/)

The Escalante river and its tributaries have carved a labyrinth of sandstone canyons.

![Image 15: Two women and a man lean in to examine cones on a pinyon pine tree](blob:http://localhost/c5930cd8f0eb111448873d4446f8deec)

Ellen Morris Bishop

### [Bees](https://vimeo.com/453148842)

Grand Staircase is a hotspot for bee diversity. There are over 660 species buzzing around the monument.

![Image 17: Two women and a man lean in to examine cones on a pinyon pine tree](blob:http://localhost/c5930cd8f0eb111448873d4446f8deec)

Blake McCord

### [Soil crusts](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/blog/biocrusts-protecting-light-and-dark)

Living skins of lichen, moss, and cyanobacteria grow slowly and help prevent erosion.

![Image 19: Two women and a man lean in to examine cones on a pinyon pine tree](blob:http://localhost/c5930cd8f0eb111448873d4446f8deec)

Blake McCord

### [Old-growth](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/pinyon-and-juniper-forests/)

Pinyon and juniper forests in the monument contain trees as old as 1,400 years.

## Americans love national monuments and their public lands

When it comes to national monuments, voters are united. Americans want these lands protected for future generations.

[See the poll results](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/blog/utah-voters-want-bears-ears-grand-staircase-escalante-restored-poll-shows/)

Utah voters support restoring protections to Grand Staircase-Escalante

0%

Utah voters support a president's ability to designate national monuments 

0%

Utah voters oppose the sale of Utah public lands to private interests

0%

## On July 13, 2026, President Trump cut Grand Staircase-Escalante by 91%

[Contact Congress](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/act/national-monuments-petition/)

## Our work

## 30 years of stewardship and advocacy in Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument

![Image 21: Two women and a man lean in to examine cones on a pinyon pine tree](blob:http://localhost/c5930cd8f0eb111448873d4446f8deec)

Blake McCord

### We protect old-growth forests

Large swaths of pinyon and juniper trees in the monument are at risk of being uprooted, toppled, clear-cut, and shredded. We work to stop destructive pinyon and juniper removal projects.

![Image 23: Two women and a man lean in to examine cones on a pinyon pine tree](blob:http://localhost/c5930cd8f0eb111448873d4446f8deec)

Blake McCord

### We advocate for less grazing

Cattle roam across 96% of the monument, with big impacts on the land. We advocate for better management of livestock grazing and have worked to retire grazing permits along the Escalante River.

![Image 25: Two women and a man lean in to examine cones on a pinyon pine tree](blob:http://localhost/c5930cd8f0eb111448873d4446f8deec)

Blake McCord

### We restore habitats

From spring surveys, to pinyon jay monitoring, we bring volunteers out to Grand Staircase-Escalante to study its plants, animals, and habitats, and advocate for their protection.

![Image 27: A woman watches through binoculars, searching for pinyon jays](blob:http://localhost/787b11c48ace34b4d3b83d60f62d64ff)

Blake McCord

## [Grab your binoculars](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/collections/74eb57bc1aad4b0bb9a60b88a2ba4acc?item=1 "Volunteer on your own time")

We need volunteers to gather information about pinyon jays in Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument and beyond. Complete the online training and head out on your own.

[Start learning](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/collections/74eb57bc1aad4b0bb9a60b88a2ba4acc?item=2 "Pinyon jay project online training hub")

## National monument designations are permanent

Nevertheless, unlawful attempts to shrink the boundaries of national monuments continue.

Here’s how this has played out in Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.

Sept 1996

President Clinton designates Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument

President Clinton protects 1.7 million acres of public lands in southern Utah as Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.

Dec 2017

President Trump cuts Grand Staircase-Escalante

President Trump unlawfully slashes the boundaries of Grand Staircase-Escalante by 47%, cutting it into three smaller pieces.

Oct 2021

President Biden restores the boundaries of Grand Staircase-Escalante

President Biden signs a new proclamation restoring the original boundaries of Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.

JULY 2026

President Trump cuts Grand Staircase-Escalante, again

President Trump unlawfully slashes the boundaries of Grand Staircase-Escalante again, this time cutting the monument by [90%](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/resources/maps-2026-bears-ears-grand-staircase-cuts/).

![Image 29: A hiker in a red hat crawls through a slot canyon whose walls are reddish with white stripes](blob:http://localhost/1e84f0104e340a9ead6b45f911618925)

Ed Moss

## Experience Grand Staircase-Escalante

Whether you squeeze through narrow slot canyons, traverse across slickrock, or float down the Escalante River, you’ll quickly see why Grand Staircase-Escalante deserves protection.

[Experience the monument on foot](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/hikes?destination=224&activity=All&managed_as=All)

[Get the latest national monument news](https://www.grandcanyontrust.org/blog/?_categories=national-monuments)

## A short hike to White House Ruin, a cliff dwelling in the bottom of Canyon De Chelly.

* * *

### _This is the only self-guided trail in Canyon De Chelly; visitors must have a guide to hike beyond White House Ruin._

#### Hike to White House Ruin

Leaving the trailhead behind, follow the canyon rim along a broad flat bench of De Chelly Sandstone, which was deposited as windblown sand dunes 250 million years ago. The trail continues to drop at a steady rate, and at 0.4 mile, it cuts through dark-colored Shinarump Conglomerate, composed of different sediments deposited by streams about 200 million years ago.

The trail continues to switchback down the De Chelly Sandstone into the large amphitheater, carved by the stream when it meandered along the bottom of the cliffs where residents now grow crops. At 0.75 mile, you reach a sandy bench. When the trail drops to the canyon floor, you’ll see a traditional Navajo home called a hogan.

Canyon De Chelly is still home to many Navajo residents; please respect the sign that prohibits taking photographs of the hogan.

#### Continue to White House Ruin

After hooking sharply left, the trail crosses a deeply eroded sandy bench and goes downstream to a bridge. You can either cross the bridge or simply walk downstream (if there is no water) until you see White House Ruin on the right at the base of the cliff. Navajo venders selling arts and crafts are frequently sitting quietly in the shade of the trees beside the stream.

The light-colored plaster on some of the rooms led to the Navajo name for the site — Kinii’ ni gai — which means White House. Archaeologists believe the rooms on the canyon floor used to be high enough to provide access to the upper rooms in the alcove.

Although people have lived in Canyon de Chelly for more than 5,000 years, it was Ancestral Puebloans who built White House around 1060 AD. More rooms were added during the next 200 years, and archaeologists estimate there may have been up to 80 rooms and four kivas when it was most heavily used.

After enjoying the view of White House and the tapestry wall above it, return the way you came.

* * *

### Directions to the White House Ruin trailhead

From the park visitor center, drive 5 miles on the South Rim road and turn left on the paved road to White House Overlook. Drive 0.75 mile to the overlook parking lot. The trail begins on the path to the overlook.

Crash landing on the Moon… 🌕🌋 📍 Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve, Idaho 🚀 This surreal volcanic landscape in southern Idaho is so otherworldly that NASA astronauts trained here before the Apollo 14 Moon Landing. With lava fields, towering cinder cones, volcanic craters, and underground lava tubes, it feels like you’ve left Earth behind. 🧡 SAVE this one-day itinerary for visiting Craters of the Moon and SEND it to someone who’d love exploring this area! ⤵️ 1️⃣ Start at the Visitor Center and grab a park map before driving the scenic 7-mile loop through the monument. 2️⃣ Hike the North Crater Flow Trail (0.4 miles), an easy boardwalk walk where you’ll learn about the different lava formations that shaped this incredible landscape. 3️⃣ Tackle the North Crater Trail (3.7 miles) to see massive volcanic craters, ancient lava flows, and the park’s incredible spatter cones, one of the rarest volcanic features on Earth. 4️⃣ Climb Inferno Cone (0.4 miles) for one of the best panoramic views in the park. The short but steep hike rewards you with 360-degree views across the lava fields. 5️⃣ Finish your day exploring the Caves Area, where you can walk through fascinating underground lava tubes carved by flowing lava thousands of years ago. 💧 Pro tip: Bring plenty of water, sunscreen, and sturdy shoes. The black lava rock absorbs heat, making this one of the hottest and sunniest places to explore in Idaho. #cratersofthemoon #idaho #visitidaho #nationalpark | Craters of the Moon itinerary | things to do at Craters of the Moon | Idaho road trip | best national park sites in Idaho

## A short but steep hike to a magnificent cliff dwelling called Moon House in Bears Ears National Monument

* * *

### Moon House, a multi-room cliff dwelling named for its celestial pictograph, is an exceptional archaeological site in McCloyd Canyon on Cedar Mesa, Utah.

The Bureau of Land Management [requires a day use permit](https://www.blm.gov/programs/recreation/permits-and-passes/lotteries-and-permit-systems/utah/cedarmesa "BLM Permit information") to visit Moon House and limits access to 20 people per day. Remember, it is illegal to remove any artifacts or damage sites in any way. Fines or jail time can result for those who break the law. Leave all artifacts where you find them, don’t lean on walls or enter interior rooms, avoid touching rock art, and don’t add modern graffiti.

#### Hike to Moon House

From the BLM kiosk at the trailhead, hike north along the dirt road for 1.25 miles. The Abajo Mountains poke above the rolling hills of sagebrush and piñon and juniper trees, and cryptobiotic soil covers the sandy benches on both sides of the road. You cross a wash around 1 mile, and the road ends at a sandstone patio. Foot trails seem to leave from every side of the parking area, but look for two No Motor Vehicle posts separated by a line of rocks on the north side of the 4WD parking area. The wide bedrock trail continues north from here and is marked with large cairns.

#### **Descend into McCloyd Canyon**

The trail starts an immediate descent towards McCloyd Canyon that steepens when you reach the rim. Follow the cairns down a precipitous, rocky route, curve around to the right side of a slickrock amphitheater, and slide down the lip of an overhung ledge. A pile of rocks below aids your descent.

The trail swings back to the left, making a large switchback across the amphitheater. A little ways down the trail, you can see Moon House hidden on a ledge on the opposite canyon wall.

Directly across from the site, the trail drops down to the bottom of the canyon. After a few broad switchbacks, the trail descends a steep scree slope and spits you onto the canyon floor at 1.6 miles.

#### **Climbing up to Moon House**

Turn right, crossing to the other side and proceeding downcanyon a short distance along the slickrock floor. Stay left of a pouroff, and you soon reach a route that ascends the left canyon wall. Climb to the next tier of slickrock, where several cairns lead you higher. The final push involves climbing up a crack to the base of an overhung ledge around 1.7 miles. From here, you can access Moon House.

##### **Visit Moon House with respect**

Look for an ammo can, whose contents include cultural interpretation and visitation information for the site. Archaeologists estimate that migrating Puebloan people built the dwellings around A.D. 1264.

You may enter the main portion through the small doorway in the long rock wall; just be careful not to pull yourself in using the sides or top of the entryway. A hidden hallway and string of rooms stretch behind the fortified wall. Since you can’t enter the rooms, bring a flashlight or headlamp to see inside. Corncobs lie on the floors of the rooms, and pictographs decorate the outside and inside.

The room that gave Moon House its name is the one with a painted white band around it, with pictographs of half moon and full moon figures on opposite walls. Like the other rooms, don’t enter it. You can clearly see the pictograph by shining light into the room. The BLM put sterile sand on the floor to absorb moisture from people’s breath that can break down the ancient pigment on the walls.

With thousands of people visiting this fragile place, please follow all guidelines to help preserve the site. Return the way you came.

* * *

### Directions to the Moon House trailhead

From the junction of UT 95 and UT 261, drive south on UT 261 for about 4 miles. Stop at the Kane Gulch Ranger Station on the left side of the road to pick up your required hiking permit (March 1 – June 15 and Sept 1 – Oct 31). [For other dates, see the BLM’s permit information›](https://www.blm.gov/sites/blm.gov/files/Recreation_Monticello_Moon%20House%20Day%20Use%20Permits.pdf)

Continue heading south on UT 261 for another 6 miles until you reach Snow Flat Road. Turn left, pass a BLM map, and veer left at a small sign marked “Trail.” This road can become impassable when wet, so check the weather before beginning your trip.

In about 3.5 miles, the dirt road deteriorates. Even with high clearance vehicles, some road construction may be necessary to help ease you down bedrock drops. The road improves again, and around 8 miles you reach the trailhead marked by a kiosk. You can park in the dirt lot on the right side of the road.

What’s Cool?

Cultural Continuity…
Today, many American Indians regard this place as
their ancestral homeland. Contrary to the concept of
abandonment, all ancestral places are considered a
living part of culture. Modern Tribal people maintain
close ties to the spirits of ancestors who are buried
on this landscape. Sites are visited and blessings
made on a regular basis to “keep these places
warm.” Centuries-old oral traditions tell stories of
migration, feast, famine, conflict and comedy on this
landscape…and shrines, traditional plant gathering
areas, sacred springs, and ponds of cattails are still
regarded with great respect.

funding. After almost 25 years of plan-

[![Image 21: 🏜️ Where the Red Rocks Tell a Story Colorado National Monument in Grand Junction, Colorado, is one of those places that makes you stop and realize how powerful nature can be. The result is a landscape that almost looks impossible. � National Park Service +1 But this land has a story that goes far beyond the rocks. People have lived in and around these canyons for more than 10,000 years. Indigenous peoples, including the Archaic and Fremont peoples and later the Ute, used this land for hunting, gathering plants, farming, traveling, and living with the seasons. Evidence such as rock art, tools, hearths, and ancient travel routes tells us that these canyons were important long before Colorado National Monument was established. � National Park Service The monument was officially established by President William Howard Taft on May 24, 1911, thanks in large part to John Otto, who explored the canyons, built trails, and believed this place deserved protection. � National Park Service Today, there are miles of beautiful trails to explore, from short walks like Window Rock to challenging adventures through Ute Canyon, Monument Canyon, and other rugged routes. The monument has about 46 miles of trails and 14 trailheads. � National Park Service +1 And while the views are breathtaking, they demand respect. Watch every step, especially near canyon edges and steep sections. One careless step can turn a beautiful adventure into something much worse. [![Image 71: One of the only national parks that protects man-made places! ➡️ Share this with someone who loves Southwest history and 📌 save this for planning your next trip to Colorado! Welcome to Cliff Palace in Mesa Verde National Park — a 700+ year old dwelling built directly into the cliffs by the Ancestral Pueblo people. With around 150 rooms and 20+ kivas, it’s the largest cliff dwelling in North America and one of the most impressive archaeological sites in the entire country 🤯 To actually go inside Cliff Palace, and many of the other large dwellings in the park, you’ll need to book a ranger-guided tour in advance through Recreation.gov or at the visitor center 🎟️ Tours are seasonal (typically May–October), involve lots of uneven stone steps, ladders, and sometimes tunnels, and can sell out quickly in summer, so plan ahead! Mesa Verde National Park protects over 600 cliff dwellings and thousands of ancestral sites, making it one of the most unique national parks in the US! You can also explore overlooks and additional dwelling and ceremonial sites along the Mesa Top Loop Road without a tour. Need to know before you go: 💰 Park entrance fee: $20–$30 per vehicle depending on season (or America the Beautiful pass accepted) 🎟️Cliff dwelling tours require separate tickets (small fee) 🚙 Expect lots of driving inside the park. Cliff Palace and other dwellings are ~1 hour from the entrance 🥵 Summer days can get HOT and the elevation is over 7,000 feet so drink lots of water ⏰ Start early for cooler temps and fewer crowds 🐶 No dogs allowed in dwellings or on tours or trails but there are dog boarding services available in the park So full of history and culture, Mesa Verde is a national park unlike any other! ✨ Have you been here?? _____________________________________________________ Hi 👋🏼 We are Carson and Melissa McCraw of McCraws on the Map! This summer, Mesa Verde National Park will receive a $4 million Federal Land Highways project
to chip seal all roads in the park. This includes the entire 20 mile (32 km) long main park road,
Mesa Top Loop Road, Cliff  Palace/B alcony House Loop Road, Wetherill Mesa Road, and

construction vehicles on the road hauling materials; wet oil and lane closures in construction
areas; and a pilot car leading traffic through construction sites. Some campground sites will also
be closed while roads are chip sealed.
All trails and overlooks along the Mesa Top Loop Road will also be receiving upgrades and
asphalt replacement. This will include the use of  an asphalt recycler with trucks on the road.
There may be some short-term closures of  individual sites and construction traffic on the roads
throughout the project.

 
  
  
 The Sand Canyon trail is located in the Canyons of the Ancients National Monument east of Cortez, Colorado. Two trailheads provide access to the canyon. The upper trailhead can be found near the [Sand Canyon Pueblo](link_12) on top of the mesa off of N Road. The lower trailhead, where this post begins, is off of G Road along McElmo Creek about 12 miles west of the town of Cortez. This post begins at the lower trailhead and follows the Sand Canyon trail up the canyon where it passes at least 8 significant cliff dwellings and pueblos within just the first 4 miles of the canyon.  
[](https://www.gjhikes.com/2014/12/sand-canyon-trail.html)  

[![Image 15](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg7K-BnKf57Tpf905XHSb2NQ3_WHT8n09wG07WE-xP6CKB6QZhfvOBXAe5TB84doFs5O2ub7GknUMaa3lHBnHQnuJksKgri2peU375HYYHskoRNCBn_1aakdlsQbyBN0_2o5wsuo8nfLmU/s1600/Sand+Canyon+II+004.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg7K-BnKf57Tpf905XHSb2NQ3_WHT8n09wG07WE-xP6CKB6QZhfvOBXAe5TB84doFs5O2ub7GknUMaa3lHBnHQnuJksKgri2peU375HYYHskoRNCBn_1aakdlsQbyBN0_2o5wsuo8nfLmU/s1600/Sand+Canyon+II+004.JPG)

  
 Sand Canyon is the major 1 of 3 trails that leave from the lower trailhead at a spot called Castle Rock. The other two trails are the Rock Creek trail and the East Rock Creek trail. Currently the parking area is a very rough expanse of slickrock. The Park Service has purchased land just to the east of this point, which includes a historic home, and is working on plans to relocate the trailhead to that spot.  
  

[![Image 16](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgibEcAzaohjCiW62wASvAhcZs5YW2pm1uWDWPzmZhgA0unnjPYww_HkJn3Pb9etK78F7UGZaB3Y5ehUJhjBU_WfPW8sgyt3cmes3VjG0yhrGymxKCkXa_rZ9Xtk7A87joP1C5-6IB4eTY/s1600/Sand+Canyon+II+029.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgibEcAzaohjCiW62wASvAhcZs5YW2pm1uWDWPzmZhgA0unnjPYww_HkJn3Pb9etK78F7UGZaB3Y5ehUJhjBU_WfPW8sgyt3cmes3VjG0yhrGymxKCkXa_rZ9Xtk7A87joP1C5-6IB4eTY/s1600/Sand+Canyon+II+029.JPG)

  
 The trail is well marked and easy to follow. Each of the trails junctions have a sign showing the current map location. The trail varies from slickrock to sand with some areas of loose rock.  
  

[![Image 17](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhPJV3_pYufT-1Lhrx4NeIVDM6i5sGdHpmTybuwyNUxEZ2ESzR7hB275br-NyaHAPSMGswx3fsVpQnZYcpcWTLXB3CfKdSPe0yGul1OYWH8hoPrjBFuhv-_ZiYGHvZ-7GZQ8k2UF6eZv4o/s1600/Sand+Canyon+II+040.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhPJV3_pYufT-1Lhrx4NeIVDM6i5sGdHpmTybuwyNUxEZ2ESzR7hB275br-NyaHAPSMGswx3fsVpQnZYcpcWTLXB3CfKdSPe0yGul1OYWH8hoPrjBFuhv-_ZiYGHvZ-7GZQ8k2UF6eZv4o/s1600/Sand+Canyon+II+040.JPG)

  
 Sand Canyon is best known for its numerous archaeological sites that vary from pueblos and towers to cliff dwellings. The remains of the first pueblo is right near the trailhead at Castle Rock. The location in this picture is along the trail a short distance past that.  
  

[![Image 18](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiQko90ToS9GOYgTUYgb_mTxplf743ui4zVm9qqTROJEItCHfufqunrvJeChUhuZOqKf3d1BPGWkRvflGu6tLKTHZ1m7TNH5ZT0jYTzQSg69-r88LoUECdAMkE0QtSAU-gBkWBBtp8ndNk/s1600/Sand+Canyon+II+086.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiQko90ToS9GOYgTUYgb_mTxplf743ui4zVm9qqTROJEItCHfufqunrvJeChUhuZOqKf3d1BPGWkRvflGu6tLKTHZ1m7TNH5ZT0jYTzQSg69-r88LoUECdAMkE0QtSAU-gBkWBBtp8ndNk/s1600/Sand+Canyon+II+086.JPG)

  
 As you continue up the canyon there are trail markers that point out spur trails that lead to closeby ruins.  
  

[![Image 19](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiwGQafX4t_0E1BILOGxgRXBPFFO57UsUUQwpvRXyrV5kK7T3pyuqi4mO3cnuYTmuJPMMS0-m8OorKIGopXuqo4pOyxT_iN347pmfFak4pSWZHvIhN-HDi6Q9WxdvlTMu5je19avOhY0gk/s1600/Sand+Canyon+II+101.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiwGQafX4t_0E1BILOGxgRXBPFFO57UsUUQwpvRXyrV5kK7T3pyuqi4mO3cnuYTmuJPMMS0-m8OorKIGopXuqo4pOyxT_iN347pmfFak4pSWZHvIhN-HDi6Q9WxdvlTMu5je19avOhY0gk/s1600/Sand+Canyon+II+101.JPG)

  
 Little 'museums' of pottery can be spotted on rocks and stumps at some of the sites. Be sure to leave all specimens for others to enjoy and remember that it is illegal to collect, dig, vandalize or disturb any archaeological site. The fine for doing so is $250,000 plu

# Canyons of the Ancient National Monument - Sand Canyon Trail

![Image 5: Writer: Jessica](link_44)

[Jessica](link_45)

Nov 15, 2019

4 min read

Updated: Jul 6, 2021

**October 12th, 2019**

![Image 6: Canyons of the Ancients National Monument view of Ute Peak](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_b90eb2e0d6494953b6643405ea4c6006~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_740,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_b90eb2e0d6494953b6643405ea4c6006~mv2.jpg)

View from southern end of Sand Canyon Trail at Canyons of the Ancients National Monument

Stacia and I are always searching out scenic weekend adventures. From our current location in Albuquerque, New Mexico, there are a multitude of destinations for some fun weekend adventures. For an overnight stay, I like to keep our one-way travel time to 4 1/2 hours or under, that way we’re not spending more time in the car than on the trail!

  

In October, we made a trip up to Cortez, Colorado, which is a little more than a 4 hour drive from Albuquerque. That southwestern corner of Colorado is saturated with remnants of ancient puebloan cultures. We’d been up in this area during a previous summer to visit Mesa Verde National Park, but the summer months are too hot to be hiking in areas with little shade, especially with dogs. October, on the other hand, seems ideal: no snowfall yet, cooler nights and mornings, but the days still warm up into the 50s and 60s. Also of note--dogs are not allowed on most trails in Mesa Verde, but that’s not the case at Canyons of the Ancients National Monument!

  

### **Sand Canyon Trail - North End**

The Sand Canyon Trail is 6 miles in length and runs from Country Road G at its southern terminus to Country Road N at its northern terminus.

  

This is a point-to-point trail, and as much as I would have loved to explore the entire trail, that’s just not possible for me, even on a good day. The day we explored the Sand Canyon Trail was a relatively good day for me, which likely had more to do with my excitement and motivation than it did restfulness. The 4 hour drive on Friday night was enough irritate my lower back, and I only managed to get 5 hours of sleep at the hotel, which typically portends a day of moderate fatigue and joint pain.

  

Instead of tackling the entire trail--a nearly impossible feat anyway--we decided to do two shorter hikes on each end of the trail, therefore book-ending it!

![Image 7: Stone wall at Sand Canyon Pueblo ruins in Canyons of the Ancients National Monument](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_b3b1fc3e89244e7bbf546dbfe0d0a530~mv2.jpeg/v1/fill/w_350,h_467,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_b3b1fc3e89244e7bbf546dbfe0d0a530~mv2.jpeg)

Remnants of stone wall at Sand Canyon Pueblo ruins

The northern end of Sand Canyon Trail has considerably less traffic than the southern end, which is immediately evident by the smaller parking lot. The parking lot itself is off a dirt road and there are no signs leading up to it. Instead, I relied on Google Maps to find my way there! We did not see anyone on the north end of the trail, but did notice one other vehicle in the parking lot.

  

Though this end of the trail sees less traffic, it's still well worth the visit. Very close to the parking lot is the site of Sand Canyon Pueblo, a 13th century village. There’s an interpretive trail to follow with signs pointing out significant features of the pueblo ruins, but most of these features were re-buried after excavation and therefore hard to identify. Regardless, the pueblo looks like it was enormous. Stacia and I had fun trying to identify a wall here or part of a structure there. What can still be identified is the outer wall of the pueblo, along with some remnants of walls for inner structures. What's more, there’s a spectacular view of the McElmo Canyon beyond, and Ute Peak in the distance!

![Image 8: View of McElmo Canyon from Sand Canyon Pueblo ruins](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_7cff0b5de06d4fba84f119f9fbfb44fd~mv2_d_2982_1813_s_2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_450,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_7cff0b5de06d4fba84f119f9fbfb44fd~mv2_d_2982_1813_s_2.jpg)

View looking south from Sand Canyon Pueblo ruins

![Image 9](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_9a78e558f416499fbb361cb2267db572~mv2.jpeg/v1/fill/w_350,h_467,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_9a78e558f416499fbb361cb2267db572~mv2.jpeg)

![Image 10](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_43e1e04cda644670be5fea0d6300a23a~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_555,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_43e1e04cda644670be5fea0d6300a23a~mv2.jpg)

  

We wandered around this area for a while exploring, but not racking up many exercise minutes on my Apple watch. In the meantime, Texie, our 85 lb American Bulldog mix, provided some entertainment! At one point, she took a nap on a trail incline, head pointed down-slope (pictured above). On another occasion, Texie managed to get a piece of a cactus stuck to her face, which is becoming a more frequent occurrence lately! We dared not let her close the the cliff overlooking the canyon--she's a clumsy girl and no one wants to take that chance. We've concluded that she's not well-suited to life in the southwest, at least not with cacti all about!

  

### **Sand Canyon Trail - South End**

I can see why the southern end of the Sand Canyon Trail is more popular. The red rock cliffs lead into the canyon and the appearance of the mountains just south is breathtaking. On top of that, there are more archeological sites to explore on this end of the trail.

  

There are two parking lots at this end of the trail now, and in mid-October both lots were close to full. The beginning of the trail follows rock trail markers set on the sandstone floor. There are remnants of the Castle Rock Pueblo up by the first sandstone butte, but the trail does not travel that way so the site may remain preserved. Instead, there’s an offshoot of the trail just behind the butte that leads to two walls of an ancient stone building.

![Image 11: Canyons of the Ancients National Monument southern trailhead](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_e4e59a7cc2784f0b9e891a8794800ddd~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_555,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_e4e59a7cc2784f0b9e891a8794800ddd~mv2.jpg)

Butte above Castle Rock Pueblo ruins at the southern trailhead

These walls were enough to spark my interest! I imagine the Castle Rock Pueblo contains more walls and remnants partway up the butte, where as [Willa Cather says](link_46), a “village sat looking down into the canyon with the calmness of eternity.”

  

![Image 12](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_c776cb1c56ee472dae6f825839215a68~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_350,h_422,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_c776cb1c56ee472dae6f825839215a68~mv2.jpg)

The trail continues across a sandy floor (another reason why summer hikes are ill-advised with dogs), along the edge of the red and yellow canyon walls. We followed this trail for a little over a mile, since the [Sand Canyon and Rock Creek Trails guide](https://www.blm.gov/sites/blm.gov/files/SC%20Newspaper%202018.pdf) indicates the Saddlehorn Pueblo cliff-dwelling ruins is located about a mile from the southern parking lot.

  

Unfortunately, we had to turn around before reaching the next ruin site, since we had already hiked nearly 3 miles that day and it was another mile back to the parking lot. I was already experiencing some significant pain in my feet and back, and was wearing my knee brace for support. I knew the further we hiked, the more likely I was to trigger a flare (the PA at my rheumatology clinic was mildly shocked when I suggested my flares are sometimes triggered by increased physical activity, but those of us with rheumatic diseases know all too well how true that is!).

  

![Image 13: Sand Canyon trail image of red sandstone canyon walls](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_736bdd684f194daa93ff3af9adb1c162~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_1063,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_736bdd684f194daa93ff3af9adb1c162~mv2.jpg)

Red rock canyon walls about one mile north of the Sand Canyon southern trailhead

With that said, the Canyons of the Ancients trail guide shows several other ‘self-discovery’ sites further along the Sand Canyon Trail. If we had decided to skip the northern end of the trail, we may have made it to some of these other sites. There’s always next time!

  

-Jessica

# Hike Through Cliff Dwellings at Canyons of the Ancients National Monument

This is your guide to visit the wonder-inducing, secret monument in southwestern Colorado.

3

Share

Save[Search](link_3)

![Image 1: Canyons of the Ancients National Monument, Colorado](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/CO-CanyonoftheAncients-night_BLM-Colorado-Flickr_2400-e1750963292842.jpg?auto=webp&width=3840&quality=75&fit=cover)
Canyons of the Ancients National Monument, Colorado (Photo: Colorado BLM/Flickr)

[![Image 2: Mikaela Ruland](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/MikaelaRuland-corn_courtesy_800v.jpg?auto=webp&width=96&quality=75&fit=cover) Mikaela Ruland](https://www.mycoloradoparks.com/byline/mikaela-ruland [link_4])Follow

Updated June 12, 2025 01:38PM

As you drive through the desert surrounding [Cortez](link_5), it’s easy to assume there isn’t much out there besides crumbling hills and scrubby vegetation. It sends a shivery thrill up my spine as I drive Road G into the canyons, thinking of all that’s hidden just out of sight. Past the incongruently green fields to the north, filled with frolicking spring calves, lies Canyons of the Ancients National Monument. This unassuming spot is home to the highest concentration of archeological sites in the United States, from 40-room pueblos to cliff dwellings perched in alcoves high above the canyon floor. These thousand-year-old remains tell the story of the Ancestral Puebloan people who lived in this rugged and beautiful landscape around 1,100 AD.

![Image 3](https://cdn.outsideonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/mail.svg)

### Subscribe to National Parks

*   Inspirational stories
*   Practical planning info
*   Straight to your inbox

[Sign Up Now](link_6)![Image 4](https://cdn.outsideonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/mail.svg)

Wandering trails past ancient stone structures, taking in the watchful view of Sleeping Ute Mountain and listening to coyotes howl from camp, the sense that you’re treading through antiquity is palpable. This place feels special, sacred. “We believe the spirits are still here,” says Ernest Vallo, Sr., of the Eagle Clan, Pueblo of Acoma. It’s the kind of spot that you can’t visit without feeling a subtle shift in your own being. Ready to explore? Here’s everything you need to know to plan your visit to Canyons of the Ancients National Monument.

## Getting to Canyons of the Ancients

![Image 5](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/CO-Cortez-CountyRdG_MobilusInMobili-Flickr_1500.jpg?width=3840&auto=webp&quality=75&fit=cover)

Heading to Canyons of the Ancients via County Road G from Cortez, Colorado (Photo courtesy Mobilus In Mobili/Flickr)

The landscape isn’t the only unassuming thing about this national monument. Unlike nearby [Mesa Verde National Park](link_7), this swath of public lands is relatively undeveloped. Managed by the Bureau of Land Management, many roads are rugged, four-wheel drive paths, camping is primitive and boundaries aren’t always well-marked. Visiting is a unique experience, allowing you to interact with the landscape more independently. Plus, the monument sees few crowds, giving you a chance to experience this piece of our country’s heritage in relative solitude.

Canyons of the Ancients is located in the southwestern corner of Colorado. The closest town is Cortez, which is also the gateway to Mesa Verde National Park. Canyons of the Ancients straddles the Utah border, and sits up against Hovenweep National Monument, making it the perfect addition to a southwestern archeological site tour. Cortez has an airport with regional connector flights, otherwise Albuquerque, Santa Fe and Grand Junction are the closest cities with air service from big name carriers. A car is a must to visit the monument, so road trip or rent one when you fly in.

ADVERTISEMENT

You won’t find fee booths when you enter the monument. Visiting Canyons of the Ancients is free. In fact, it may be hard to tell where exactly private land ends and the monument begins. Your first stop should be [Canyons of the Ancients Visitor Center and Museum](link_8) just north of Cortez, Colorado. Here, you’ll find maps to navigate trails and dispersed camping. Rangers can help you find routes that suit your vehicle and abilities. Planning information is free, but if you want to explore the museum, you’ll need to pay a small fee or show your America the Beautiful or other interagency annual pass. The museum is a great primer on the history of the region from the Ancestral Puebloan people who built many of the structures you’ll see, to the archeologists who excavated these sites. [Dominguez and Escalante pueblos](link_9) are located a short walk from the visitor center and worth exploring. From the pueblos, you can also look out across the McPhee Reservoir which flooded many archeological sites in the Dolores River Valley. The museum houses artifacts that were saved from destruction.

The monument doesn’t have any designated campgrounds, but if you’re prepared to dispersed camp along rough, four-wheel-drive roads, overnighting is allowed at certain spots in the monument. Pick up a brochure at the visitor center and ask a ranger about current conditions. Otherwise, plan to stay in[Cortez or the surrounding area](link_10).

## How long does it take to see Canyons of the Ancients?

Plan to spend at least two days exploring Canyons of the Ancients National Monument, with more time added on if you want to see nearby Mesa Verde National Park and Hovenweep National Monument. These are some of our favorite things to do.

ADVERTISEMENT

### Hike Sand Canyon Trail

![Image 6: Hike Sand Canyon Trail at Canyon of the Ancients National Monument](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/CanyonsoftheAncients_SandCanyon_MikaelaRuland_1500.jpg?width=3840&auto=webp&quality=75&fit=cover)

Hike Sand Canyon Trail at Canyons of the Ancients National Monument (Photo courtesy Mikaela Ruland)

To really walk in the footsteps of the Ancestral Puebloans, you’ll want to get off the roads and into the canyons. A hike or mountain bike ride on the well-marked Sand Canyon Trail is a fantastic way to get a glimpse of this ancient culture. Navigate over slickrock and follow the trail deep into Sand Canyon where you’ll come across many cliff dwellings, tucked away in alcoves high above.

The full trail is 6.5 miles one way, with a parking lot at each end. If you’re on a bike, the trail is rated intermediate/difficult with a steep, switchback section. On foot, the terrain is more manageable and can be done in a day with two cars (one at each trailhead), but if you only have one vehicle, we recommend starting from the South Trailhead on Road G and turning around when you hit the steep switchbacks, approximately 4 miles in. This makes for a long, but manageable day hike (approximately 800 total feet of elevation gain) with plenty of time to ponder the dwellings along the way.

ADVERTISEMENT

Starting from the South Trailhead, you’ll quickly encounter Castle Rock Pueblo, featuring an unusual rectangular kiva–a shape that’s found in more modern Hopi architecture. A mile down the trail is Saddlehorn Pueblo. It sits in an alcove under a rock shaped like a pommel. Next up is Double Cliff House, with two dwellings stacked on ledges above one another. Here, the canyon walls have an odd, dripping effect. Around the corner, Corncob House was where archeologists found ancient corncobs, but the name could easily describe the pattern on the cliff wall.

The cliff dwellings aren’t the only thing to marvel at here. As you make your way down the trail, take the marked side paths leading to viewpoints of the main canyon as it deepens. Twisted ponderosa pines grow from sandy ground that alternates between rosy pink, orange and bone white. The dark, bumpy ground on either side of the trail is healthy, cryptobiotic soil, keeping erosion at bay and protecting this marvelous desert ecosystem. You may spot wildflowers along the way, or raptors riding the thermals. And, of course, the canyon walls rising above tell a geological story even older than the dwellings they house. Take a deep breath and soak it all in.

ADVERTISEMENT

Continue on to a spot where the sun seemingly always shines at Sunny Alcove and there’s a fascinating, two-story dwelling at Tucked Away Two Story House. Wall Curves with Bedrock House, with one nearly intact room still remaining, is the last site along the trail before you reach Sand Canyon Pueblo. This large complex was once three times the size of Mesa Verde’s largest dwelling and is just a short walk from the North Trailhead. If you’re short on time or don’t want to do a longer hike, this spot makes a great place for exploration on its own.

### Take it easy at Sutcliffe Vineyards

![Image 7: Sutcliffe Vineyards in Southwestern Colorado](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/MesaVerdeCountry-SutcliffeVineyards19_EmilySierra_courtesy_1500.jpg?width=3840&auto=webp&quality=75&fit=cover)

Sutcliffe Vineyards in Southwestern Colorado (Photo courtesy Emily Sierra/Mesa Verde Country)

If you return to the South Trailhead, head across the street to Sutcliffe Vineyards for a great post-hike afternoon. The laidback winery is full of cute dogs, casual picnic tables and gorgeous views of the surrounding canyons. Some grapes are grown on-site, while others come from Palisade to the north. Order a glass of wine and a pizza and enjoy the afternoon.

### Visit Lowry Pueblo

![Image 8](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/CO-MesaVerdeCountry-CANM_Lowry-Pueblo-kassiavinsel-photography_courtesy_1500.jpg?width=3840&auto=webp&quality=75&fit=cover)

Lowry Pueblo at Canyon’s of the Ancients National Monument (Photo courtesy Kassia Vinsel Photography/Mesa Verde Country)

While Sand Canyon houses many smaller cliff dwellings, the Ancestral Puebloans also lived in larger pueblos outside of the cliffs. From the little community of Pleasant View, head west on Road CC and you’ll find Lowry Pueblo, a thousand-year-old compound that once comprised 40 rooms. Unlike the sites along Sand Canyon Trail, visitors can walk through the door of Lowry Pueblo and imagine what life would have been like inside this structure in the 1100s. Thanks to stabilization work by archeologists, it’s safe to visit this site, but still be aware of where you put your feet and don’t touch anything unless absolutely necessary. Some of the coolest features of this pueblo are its kivas. The Great Kiva is nearly 50 feet in diameter and probably served as a gathering point for Ancestral Puebloans from hundreds of miles around. The Painted Kiva is a smaller gathering space, with a stair-step painted mural protected by a modern roof.

## What to know before visiting Canyons of the Ancients National Monument

*   **Respect archeological sites and artifacts** – these stalwart sites have existed for 1,000 years. Avoid damaging them by refraining from touching or entering buildings or artifacts and leaving everything as you found it.
*   **Don’t bust the crust** – Canyons of the Ancients is filled with cryptobiotic soil. This cool, living crust creates a mat to help trap water and decrease erosion in the arid landscape. Crypto can live for hundreds of years, but one step or tire track can destroy it. Always stay on trails or designated roads to avoid damaging the landscape. If you need to step off trail, first look for the telltale dark, bumpy ground and be sure not to step there. Rocks and loose sand are the safest bet if you’re unsure.
*   **Dogs are welcome** – The monument allows furry friends to explore too, but keep them on a leash and out of archeological sites. Off-leash dogs can unknowingly damage artifacts or cryptobiotic soil, or get hurt by cactus, rattlesnakes or scorpions.
*   **Pay attention to the forecast** – Intense heat and flash floods are both possibilities in the summer months at Canyons of the Ancients. It’s best to visit in the spring or fall when both risks are limited, but if you do plan a summer trip, be aware of the weather. Hike early on hot days and avoid inner-canyon travel when rain is in the forecast anywhere in the area, as flash floods are a possibility.
*   **Drink up** – Bring plenty of water when you hit the trails. Most of the monument is at more than 5,000 feet in elevation, so not only will you be warding off heat sickness by hydrating, you’ll also be warding off altitude sickness. Each person in your party should bring at least three liters of water when hitting the trails. Don’t forget water for your dog.
*   **Respect the current residents** – The region’s Indigenous residents are not a relic of the past. The Ute, Dine (Navajo) and Pueblo people still live here and you’ll cross their land as you drive through the monument. Visit with respect and take time to learn more about their cultures. The Cortez Cultural Center, which puts on events like Native American dances, is a great place to start.

### Ruins & Rock Art Sites

The following list of Ruins & Rock Art Sites includes places already posted on gjhikes.com as well as ones that are found on our planning lists and maps. All total there are over 1,800 sites. Unless an inadvertent mistake has been made in editing we can vouch for the GPS coordinates for the sites that we have personally visited. For those that we haven't personally visited we are merely passing on either what others have shared or what we have found out by our own means. It is with this information that we set out with when visiting a site for the first time. Among the GPS locations are sites that are found on scanned topo maps. In the past we have found these to be highly reliable. Last of all there are coordinates that are derived from zooming in on Google Maps Satellite View and marking the locations of apparent ruins. We highly recommend doing that for any site that you are planning to visit using the map included on this page. We also suggest downloading the GPX file and saving it on your device. It doesn't take up much space and anytime you are near a site the waypoint will be visible on your GPS map.

[Arizona](link_9) - [California](link_10) - [Colorado](link_11) - [Nevada](link_12) - [New Mexico](link_13) - [Texas](link_14) - [Utah](link_15)

download[GPX](link_16)(last updated 07/26/2026)

  

The list of sites isn't meant to be comprehensive by any means but rather just a drop in the bucket of places that we have at least some information about. In fact, as the process of adding sites to the map and lists is so tedious and time consuming, we decided to stop and make available what we had completed up to this point so that others that are more able can begin using even this small compilation of information. As always, ask permission if the site is on private property or tribal lands and visit with respect. (Some sites on tribal lands might require a guide or special permission.)

  

As many of you know, we have already published one book that, due to all the photos and maps that were included, contained only about 100 sites and was quite expensive in printed format. We had promised to publish a second volume but held back in order to find a way of including more sites for less money. Our plan now is to provide theses lists here on gjhikes.com where they can be freely accessible before making them available in book format. We already don't like the format of these pages so expect changes. Also expect additional sites to be added to the map and lists from time to time.

[![Image 2](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi9DEGAdaJSwIdPRgriGhp3RPlQjBo0Mgdn_bo87ER__zjuX7RS8rBUq-F2IOotZJDNhoTGbNPQIYy334tSgCqI3z244k0Z5wujJgQBwPwhwN17w_WK-tbty_w5Br-Ogu8xrqelpEH4gxE/s200/Sand+Canyon+025.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi9DEGAdaJSwIdPRgriGhp3RPlQjBo0Mgdn_bo87ER__zjuX7RS8rBUq-F2IOotZJDNhoTGbNPQIYy334tSgCqI3z244k0Z5wujJgQBwPwhwN17w_WK-tbty_w5Br-Ogu8xrqelpEH4gxE/s1600/Sand+Canyon+025.JPG)

 Rating:![Image 3](link_9)  
 Round Trip Distance: 0.8 miles  
 Difficulty: Easy  
 Elevation: 6773 - 6830 feet  
 Cellphone: 1-3 bars  
 Time: 45 mins.  
 Trailhead: Upper Sand Canyon  
 Fee: none  
 Attractions: Ancestral Puebloan Ruins  
![Image 4: No Restroom](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEie7BYcUZ3SmMrnESyOF-lYZTM6KiMzT0rhAvnPjS_t-xpKI_mcS4XJBqjEqndx3LggTOpHb5D3oayCOhpY0ixBgqjAB5-96zM3hyphenhyphenNDJPv_zgYc1hWYbYx6ba8MDoRF4JNPVWnYhKRWdUY/s1600/No+Restroom+icon.gif)![Image 5: Dogs allowed](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEja42qMYqjvxlEmAUcEmAqfPGaY1uNlP3u1_ufPfbuBcsiL-JMKSpmx-r6nZkhNryOCepxeL-JvWNWS85Fxl5R0iggDEmZqZEYkMrnzeS_jzWuoOiNGiu8TTPZg1BNsuXveBxNDgfj1xjY/s1600/Dog+Icon.gif)![Image 6: No Camping](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjs7oQb48wH0m9iNh_kdDsJWpyBPzGWHvIKbGYrcNzoPvJodw0WT1Xf7Al31RQp3pQsrWSq_6HSt2zy3aXMhQDH9j5TFsfIRZC06mvGmY1Y6Uf2ENTvgqM7qszEF6dq1mMoPn10bGL85gE/s1600/No+Camping+icon.gif)[![Image 7: Download GPS file](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjk0-w4GoKR7npfO2Hk_3O-WnqpP2Z5XmkkpcB_4wcfn81pQ4LSzZQUgUhyphenhyphenDtXZ_nttFTShMLUzdwujOV5iGw4dMqYEDJXOAdie9L-bXqDRcwGBfUPdpTCqybSMB-BdIlANdLx9HwkiVtI/s1600/GPS3+icon.gif)](https://docs.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1i1MSIezGCpd2xwRMN-rOPUraYYfwDr8y [link_10])  
![Image 8: Hiking](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjmGFhhV3QYbyqzxLwJb8NgMyyXytx5CDNrnfzSQW6OuYORpByPVt53OeidKf7QSmbifG1MnctOX8NfT5CiE7FBJQrT44HfUIx3nSVsstz72ygEkpF-OZ-8i_DNE9_bNreFm8ufmd6_JQM/s200/Hiking+Icon.gif)![Image 9: No Bikes](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEibpOikgDNYhHOKXAF50TvTo9RaeCnxDxGAj9NOYXIprmuohS9AF1QbljGcLfgEUWrFSU_Fz8MxAa2c5wIbHP0CYj-vqS-FnswRofoeOaSDcNU1BnRf4kyaQwRzGWUusUZLuO6-d9M8WYw/s1600/No+Mountain+Bike+Icon.gif)![Image 10: No Horseback Riding](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiTElGUsmaivBTVKzfwmrtsKNbOck5OypvNF3X0M4z5cKbQlRINEdEcZE_QrBZhwgH5hjdaKFRCR_35pWUrQPw26hYS79zLfKnvzA4Cj4IN7khPxx9W4seKvXnqMcNdMXYyNNivkPoeIYg/s1600/No+Horse+Icon.gif)![Image 11: No Motorcycle](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEimRTcfnVkApD8X4mgFn6Nx3mSfBOw9yK61aZleM7pGICbDR26z74JGMxfx9SebHl6Ny2Q3R9jPq_yKeEsmpBI-CDdTs_Yk9hHRrznpHgdsna_PHuB-jXF2YNB_Hm4xSQ0-E83TXXT2IA0/s1600/No+Motorcycle+Icon.gif)![Image 12: No ATV](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhElfRXfjh8SKDrlX1NZAa-EIW0IzId1LH4cX0ov52sxK_7soyOLnNY4ZHK2OZaaELnAS-Bm3Cg0RnT8IRxhqCr0tIgrRGkxM1ynlUHrWdhDf7NXpthLWq5FqHGX1IUiAj5XVQ9XGC_46o/s1600/No+ATV+icon.jpg)![Image 13: No Jeep](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgYWgqGgWltBX4Dnm7AHCtmlHzzZEtN9V1Of_02Nh6h-PN88jvBl8x3-VJhEB1OhAeU_7Z0E7ZeKsZjJyLHupg_bGD7_5FdOnViOKs-6a4WRd-lvRkvCI-DHqCsOaW7RWFfYgKcq9S0MSI/s1600/No+Jeep+icon+3.jpg)  
  
  
 The Sand Canyon Pueblo is located in the Canyons of the Ancients National Monument in southwest Colorado. The village consisting of about 420 rooms, 100 kivas and 14 towers was constructed around AD 1200-1290. The Canyons of the Ancients National Monument comprises over 6,000 excavated sites on over 164,000 acres of land managed by the BLM. The best location to begin exploring the monument is at the [Anasazi Heritage Center](link_11) near Dolores, Colorado. There you will find information about sites you may want to visit as well as maps, brochures and a top notch museum.  
[](http://rexmario.blogspot.com/2012/08/sand-canyon-pueblo.html)  

[![Image 14](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEj6bPhR8M5FTXQhsWQXXCXV5cbt_tOIsd5AUD0YN6QCDfzwJN03o1vfXKCLXag-P7YM5xbyuT6n4uHoBoR9BQhsC1A84hFvbTKvVSm2I61Mo-2D9NmP78BILu2_MFU-bTegnB104tUtl6E/s400/Sand+Canyon+001.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEj6bPhR8M5FTXQhsWQXXCXV5cbt_tOIsd5AUD0YN6QCDfzwJN03o1vfXKCLXag-P7YM5xbyuT6n4uHoBoR9BQhsC1A84hFvbTKvVSm2I61Mo-2D9NmP78BILu2_MFU-bTegnB104tUtl6E/s1600/Sand+Canyon+001.JPG)

  
 There aren't any road signs that point to the Sand Canyon Pueblo and you probably won't find it on a map. The best route to take is to turn west onto Montezuma County Road P from US Highway 491. Follow Road P to Road 18 and turn left. Turn right again onto Road P and continue, past the unmarked trailhead for[Goodman Point](link_12), to Road 16. Turn left on Road 16 and continue to Road N where you turn right. The Sand Canyon trailhead is about a half mile west on Road N. The total distance from US 491 should be around 9.3 miles. The road is all paved although it does have a lot of chuck holes. You will probably want to allow an extra hour to stop and tour the Goodman Point ruins.  
  

[![Image 15](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgi_D1tSpptjJvG1_vnstMB8CZSVlGUBaa1wKuIhiYW2qW7G1X-Bp-ZiaEpvJmY68CwdpMqNpP4H99aql_ovCyLNh56ScuaNbLXL83IpD_Bcf_Xv5b1T9pdMhQL4SHTHvf2otJez_XICm0/s400/Sand+Canyon+002.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgi_D1tSpptjJvG1_vnstMB8CZSVlGUBaa1wKuIhiYW2qW7G1X-Bp-ZiaEpvJmY68CwdpMqNpP4H99aql_ovCyLNh56ScuaNbLXL83IpD_Bcf_Xv5b1T9pdMhQL4SHTHvf2otJez_XICm0/s1600/Sand+Canyon+002.JPG)

  
 The Sand Canyon Pueblo and the Sand Canyon trail share the same trailhead. This is actually the upper trailhead for the Sand Canyon trail. The lower trailhead is about 6.5 miles to the south on Road G in McElmo Canyon.  
  

[![Image 16](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjxIE2NlwEgxEwvAIPGHUHJ59YHyChNM8sIZ3izrei6gPs3OgNBtzqVmU3LDdUAfKl58zZjg0HfMzmrkyQblNYd5GSMlmc2E2l25eQInohnCA07YrWRwl0Cok8Nf0-gqU2pFpAiBrm94mE/s400/Sand+Canyon+006.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjxIE2NlwEgxEwvAIPGHUHJ59YHyChNM8sIZ3izrei6gPs3OgNBtzqVmU3LDdUAfKl58zZjg0HfMzmrkyQblNYd5GSMlmc2E2l25eQInohnCA07YrWRwl0Cok8Nf0-gqU2pFpAiBrm94mE/s1600/Sand+Canyon+006.JPG)

  
 Take the easy trail to the right and follow it as it parallels the county road for a short distance before turning left towards the ruins.  
  

[![Image 17](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEitGY-XWy4koIdroet5aBOHnc-r0XKHnmWJZGUsAy8wlpRLsUvK5ExCwpCSAGDPnq7GeJ6dM7f1FAu7eTCxPNwJLW64N8BeXbTg-tYPHd7d7Uig40E_mByxEjoj_wYYjTNxB4vt5Af6AY4/s400/Sand+Canyon+007-1.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEitGY-XWy4koIdroet5aBOHnc-r0XKHnmWJZGUsAy8wlpRLsUvK5ExCwpCSAGDPnq7GeJ6dM7f1FAu7eTCxPNwJLW64N8BeXbTg-tYPHd7d7Uig40E_mByxEjoj_wYYjTNxB4vt5Af6AY4/s1600/Sand+Canyon+007-1.jpg)

  
 At the 'T' intersection you have the option of exploring the ruins by following the trails in either direction. Both the left and right trails lead to a dead end where you return by the same route. The trail to the right is the longest and has more information to read. This post follows the trail to the right first. The trail to the left is still worth doing as it has a good view of the entire site.  
  

[![Image 18](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhjsvI5d_gT0FPi0DRSRKVlv2AAdZwvHZu7M6T3x_16JyMj6phRUjVEK-_9Ujo54NikcifsrpGWDMrPocDz_WVYScF_BxMpv6j2xmwn-TFL_JQ9HsNZBZj5-xgFbVOpOa0djZj-val4nBw/s400/Sand+Canyon+012.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhjsvI5d_gT0FPi0DRSRKVlv2AAdZwvHZu7M6T3x_16JyMj6phRUjVEK-_9Ujo54NikcifsrpGWDMrPocDz_WVYScF_BxMpv6j2xmwn-TFL_JQ9HsNZBZj5-xgFbVOpOa0djZj-val4nBw/s1600/Sand+Canyon+012.JPG)

  
 Everything above ground is comprised of rubble. The ruins were reburied after being excavated so the walls wouldn't have to be stabilized. It is hard to make out what you are looking at but if you study a map of the ruins it becomes much easier. The trail follows the outside of a wall that enclosed the village so most of what you see is just the wall. There are places where it is possible to see over the wall and into the actual village, which of course, is more piles of rubble.  
  

[![Image 19](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiiGjZZu2OvqIowr-4_cQFuskwBvamzm_3xs0yXmPf_QYE54HN394fNifnKpfdvaqL1O9YztqPfYRcaYLXbANb7H9rDjT9NWB9yKUR_o97AEjs68z4L_lj6GYbsYxMrMEQZ6PZ96zatbr0/s400/Sand+Canyon+018.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiiGjZZu2OvqIowr-4_cQFuskwBvamzm_3xs0yXmPf_QYE54HN394fNifnKpfdvaqL1O9YztqPfYRcaYLXbANb7H9rDjT9NWB9yKUR_o97AEjs68z4L_lj6GYbsYxMrMEQZ6PZ96zatbr0/s1600/Sand+Canyon+018.JPG)

  
 The half dozen or so kiosks go a long way to explain the layout of the ruins. More can be learned from visiting the [Anasazi Heritage Center](link_13) and the [Crow Canyon Archaeological Center](link_14) websites.  
  

[![Image 20](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjfSc4emiKncnu6OrGXVaeAFkwmBSRH8I35yFA3r6tlkQIScDVSqQgZBWmlpnrlZszJX1Tm6-ut4MxHCdlFcyfq1q03AV69GSf9aUlP8qrwzFYve3iYGeWwy87kEm8XsTIzz-Iudm4lpng/s400/Sand+Canyon+039.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjfSc4emiKncnu6OrGXVaeAFkwmBSRH8I35yFA3r6tlkQIScDVSqQgZBWmlpnrlZszJX1Tm6-ut4MxHCdlFcyfq1q03AV69GSf9aUlP8qrwzFYve3iYGeWwy87kEm8XsTIzz-Iudm4lpng/s1600/Sand+Canyon+039.JPG)

  
 The trail ends at a rocky cliff overlooking Sand Canyon. After enjoying the view you can retrace your steps to the 'T' intersection and then explore the short trail to the left.  
  

[![Image 21](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg-pGXET3Y_fXa7fZWn84XCQkrkVcM_TcqMbIcPbpetLhpejPL7TPOym6DQy0AbEU6iZAhZ72ZEoEK2O1yVia4DaibJaCYegM70_4QrVyYJX3njPbIvk8ogpc2jvMerL95s1gA-tWQlJTI/s400/Sand+Canyon+028.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg-pGXET3Y_fXa7fZWn84XCQkrkVcM_TcqMbIcPbpetLhpejPL7TPOym6DQy0AbEU6iZAhZ72ZEoEK2O1yVia4DaibJaCYegM70_4QrVyYJX3njPbIvk8ogpc2jvMerL95s1gA-tWQlJTI/s1600/Sand+Canyon+028.JPG)

  
 If you like looking at potsherds there are a good variety to study. Besides tree ring analysis pottery is another method for dating the age of the ruins. The pottery was made by assembling flattened coils of clay into the desired shape and smoothing them with stones before firing them in an open pit. Some have speculated that the rough texture of some of the pottery, like the above picture, may have come from using a woven basket for a mold.  
  

[![Image 22](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg6gnusVj19h85h8CLf7ABOCmVOYwRclaBap6CTikVcsKofSlz8SkKFUBu73RXhfz4ZyFhEXHWeLZR30c-ULQ-xBsv07cpAUSnc4thrVcI5G17JgyM-gw4q5E3MikFnM4tDAGY4Yv-umng/s400/Sand+Canyon+060.JPG)](

# Living History Surrounding Mesa Verde National Park

See incredible archaeological sites beyond Mesa Verde, sip local wines and learn about Native American culture in southwestern Colorado

1

Share

Save[Search](https://www.mycoloradoparks.com/search)

![Image 4: Mountain biking on the Sand Canyon Trail in Canyons of the Ancients National Monument](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/MesaVerdeCountry-CanyonAncients-bike-SandCanyonTrail3_EmilySierra_courtesy_2400.jpg?auto=webp&width=3840&quality=75&fit=cover)
Mountain biking on the Sand Canyon Trail in Canyons of the Ancients National Monument (Photo: by Emily Sierra courtesy of Mesa Verde Country)

[![Image 5: Mikaela Ruland](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/MikaelaRuland-corn_courtesy_800v.jpg?auto=webp&width=96&quality=75&fit=cover) Mikaela Ruland](https://www.mycoloradoparks.com/byline/mikaela-ruland [link_4])Follow

Updated February 13, 2026 06:57AM

[Mesa Verde National Park’s](link_5) cliff-dwellings might get all the attention, but southwestern Colorado is incredibly full of archeological sites. Spend a few days in the towns of Cortez, Dolores and Mancos to see other historical sites like Canyons of the Ancients and Hovenweep National Monument, an itinerary dubbed “Trail of the Ancients.”

![Image 6](https://cdn.outsideonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/mail.svg)

### Subscribe to National Parks

*   Inspirational stories
