*   Straight to your inbox

[Sign Up Now](link_6)![Image 7](https://cdn.outsideonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/mail.svg)

## Canyons of the Ancients

![Image 8: Lowry Pueblo at Canyons of the Ancients National Monument](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Lowry-Pueblo-CANM-kassia-vinsel-photography-41-Florian-Herrmann-720x480.jpg?width=3840&auto=webp&quality=75&fit=cover)

Lowry Pueblo at Canyons of the Ancients National Monument (Photo: Kassia Vinsel)

Most visitors check out [Canyons of the Ancients](https://www.mycoloradoparks.com/national-parks/colorado-parks/canyons-of-the-ancients/) Visitor Center and Museum near Dolores and don’t venture out to explore the 176,000-acre monument, which contains the highest known archaeological site density in the U.S. The monument is huge and you could spend weeks exploring it, but a great start is to spend the day mountain biking or hiking Sand Canyon Trail in the monument, a difficult, 12-mile roundtrip ride that will take you past tons of ancient dwellings built into the sandstone walls. It’s one of many area trails that make recreating easy.

Phil’s World is another favorite of Colorado mountain bikers, with a variety of world-class trails for all levels of riding. As an added treat, you’ll rarely find the area busy.

![Image 9: Mountain bike in the snow](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/emily-sierra-mesa-verde-country-dolores-boggy-draw-fat-biking-3-Florian-Herrmann-720x480.jpg?width=3840&auto=webp&quality=75&fit=cover)

Mountain bike in the snow (Photo: Emily Sierra)

Mountain biking isn’t limited to the summer months in Cortez. Rent fat bikes, which are mountain bikes equipped with wider tires for the snow, from Kokopelli Bike & Board and explore the Phil’s World Trail System or Chicken Creek Trail when the snow flies.

ADVERTISEMENT

## More Indigenous History

![Image 10: Hovenweep National Monument in Colorado](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/MesaVerdeCountry-HovenweepNP_FlorianHerrmann_courtesy_1500-720x478.jpg?width=1920&auto=webp&quality=75&fit=cover)

Hovenweep National Monument in Colorado (Photo: Mesa Verde Country)

Can’t get enough archaeology? There’s more to explore at several nearby national monuments. Head to Hovenweep National Monument to see incredible stone masonry that’s stood the test of time. Yucca House National Monument was preserved in 1919, leaving a large pueblo unexcavated for future generations. Lowry Pueblo National Historic Landmark houses a 40-room village in Canyons of the Ancients national monument.

![Image 11: Lowry Pueblo National Historic Landmark](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/mesaverde-country-lowry-pueblo_EmilySierra_courtesy_1500-720x480.jpg?width=1920&auto=webp&quality=75&fit=cover)

Lowry Pueblo National Historic Landmark (Photo: Emily Sierra)

The new Montezuma Heritage Museum offers a wide glimpse into the region’s past from pioneer history, to the region’s Hispanic influences to a large exhibit in partnership with the Ute Mountain Ute.

Indigenous history and culture isn’t limited to the past in this part of Colorado. Visit the Cortez Cultural Center to learn more about the Ute Mountain Ute, Pueblo and Navajo through art installations, interpretive exhibits and frequent dances in the summer.

ADVERTISEMENT

## Stargaze Near Mesa Verde

![Image 12: The Milky Way in the skies above Hovenweep National Monument](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/MesaVerdeCountry-Hovenweep-NightSkies_ScottDWSmith_courtesyCortezTourism_1500.jpg?width=3840&auto=webp&quality=75&fit=cover)

The Milky Way in the skies above Hovenweep National Monument (Photo courtesy of Mesa Verde Country)

Mesa Verde National Park and nearby Hovenweep and Canyons of the Ancients national monuments have some of the darkest skies in the country. All three are International Dark Sky Parks, meaning they are revered for their dark skies and dedication to keeping light pollution at bay.

Seeing the Milky Way arching over ancient buildings is perhaps one of the most special ways to experience this corner of the Southwest. For the best skies, visit in the winter and spring months when longer nights give you more time to stargaze and colder air brings less moisture and haziness. To see the most stars, visit around a new moon when the sky will be darkest.

ADVERTISEMENT

After a long evening of stargazing, check-in to the Mesa Verde Motel in Mancos. This boutique spot was saved from demolition by a pair of best friends and their husbands and turned into a fun, hip spot just seven miles from the park entrance. Every room has its own theme (#13 is Twilight Zone) and there’s a morning coffee bar and evening cocktail bar that’s fun for a visit even if you aren’t staying the night.

## Surprising Cuisine

Southwestern Colorado is also home to a burgeoning craft beverage scene. Lush vineyards and orchards dot this part of the state, making it home to wine and hard cider producers. Try both at Fenceline Cider, tucked next to the Mancos River with food trucks and live music. If you want to make a day of wine tasting, add in Sutcliffe Vineyards and Yellow Car Country Wines. Dolores River Brewery is a great spot for those looking for a craft beer. Dolores is located along Highway 145 leading into the mountains, which makes it cooler in the summer than the nearby parks and monuments situated in the desert. They also have excellent pizza.

![Image 13: Sutcliffe Vineyards in Southwestern Colorado](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/MesaVerdeCountry-SutcliffeVineyards19_EmilySierra_courtesy_1500.jpg?width=3840&auto=webp&quality=75&fit=cover)

Sutcliffe Vineyards in Southwestern Colorado (Photo courtesy Emily Sierra/Mesa Verde Country)

When you’re ready for dinner, Dolores, Mancos and Cortez have a surprisingly vibrant dining scene for small towns. You’ll find everything from creative farm-to-table restaurants like The Boathouse, which has a Spanish-inspired menu that changes daily (make a reservation), to Burger Boy Drive In, a retro spot complete with car hops.

Her passion is to introduce people to the outdoors so that they fall in love and help protect the wild places she loves to play in. She spends most of her free time outside hiking, skiing, mountain biking, doing yoga – you name it. When she’s not outside, you can find her researching cheap flights, exploring hipster coffee shops or on the hunt for Denver’s best mac n’ cheese. ## Explore Mesa Verde Country

Uncover the endless activities Mesa Verde has to offer.

![Image 3: 4 corners map](https://mesaverdecountry.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/4-corners-map-2023.jpeg)

*   Getting to Mesa Verde

Located in beautiful Southwest Colorado, Mesa Verde Country is within easy driving distance of several gateway cities, including Denver, Albuquerque, Salt Lake, Phoenix and Las Vegas.

[Learn More](https://mesaverdecountry.com/archaeology-road-trip-10-days-in-the-four-corners-region/)

*   ![Image 4](https://mesaverdecountry.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/white-bed.svg)Places to stay

Discover a wide variety of lodging options and accommodations, from international hotels to historic bed & breakfasts, to guest ranches, cabins, campgrounds and RV parks.

[View Our Lodging Options](https://mesaverdecountry.com/directory_category/places-to-stay/)

*   ![Image 5](https://mesaverdecountry.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/white-signs.svg)Things to do

The call of the wild is answered with bikes, kayaks and fishing lines. The ancient story unfolds at our cultural centers and Native American dances. In the communities of Cortez, Dolores and Mancos, you’ll discover thousands of years of history and endless outdoor adventures.

[View Tours & Itineraries](https://mesaverdecountry.com/things-to-do/)

*   ![Image 6](https://mesaverdecountry.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/white-cmera.svg)Mesa Verde National Park

Mesa Verde National Park offers knowledgeable tours of the cliff dwellings guided by rangers. Balcony House, Cliff Palace, and Long House may only be visited on a ranger-guided tour.

[Book Your Tour Today](https://mesaverdecountry.com/things-to-do/mesa-verde-national-park/)

*   ![Image 7](https://mesaverdecountry.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/white-fork.svg)Where to eat

With so many local foods and regional flavors from our local Mesa Verde restaurants, you’ll be planning your next meal before you’ve finished your first.

[Find Places to Snack](https://mesaverdecountry.com/directory_category/where-to-eat/)

## Mesa Verde National Park

![Image 1: Cliff Palace tour at Mesa Verde National Park](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Mesa-Verde-Cliff-Palace-tour_Ordelheide_1600.jpg)

Mesa Verde Cliff Palace tour Photo: Grant Ordelheide

Described as the pyramids of North America, the ancient ruins at Mesa Verde hold the early stories of our nation. About 1,400 years ago ancestral Puebloans built more than 600 dwellings into the gorgeous sandstone cliffs. Go on a guided tour of cliff dwellings with a ranger. Purchase your tickets in advance because these tours are really popular. Buy them online at recreation.gov or call 1-877-444-6777 starting March 9, 2020.

You can purchase them in person at the Mesa Verde Visitor and Research Center up to two days in advance. Keep in mind there are limited walk-up tickets.

## Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park

![Image 1: Sunset at the Painted Wall in Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park](https://cdn.mycoloradoparks.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Black-Canyon-Gunnison-sunset_Ordelheide_2400.jpg)

Sunset at the Painted Wall in Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park Photo: Grant Ordelheide

At this impossibly sheer, narrow canyon in southwestern Colorado—at its thinnest points, the gorge spans just 40 feet at the Gunnison River and 1,100 feet at the rim—rock walls plunge as deep as 2,722 feet.

Intrepid hikers and rock climbers can venture into the depths on several very steep, unmaintained trails. Other visitors prefer to peer into the chasm from a network of trails lining the north and south rims. Anglers love this place for its gold-medal water for trout fishing.

## Colorado National Monument

This desert park perched at the western edge of Colorado features rock pillars, juniper-cloaked hills and incredible rock formations.

Best known for its vistas from the 23-mile scenic drive (or road bike ride) on Rim Rock Drive, the park also is a great place to hike, watch wildlife (such as desert bighorn sheep, coyotes and golden eagles) and stargaze. You’ll find some of the country’s darkest skies here. It’s also uncrowded, making it a great place to experience solitude.

### Escalante Ruins

[![Image 2](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhS7I5mW40fVLrDePE0-1QKee3FCrX6gDKs0QwQz3JGoZVRdgVTQ6DvmLN-bZoyWot8rjrmqkIu1G4cVdF2qXJPBAP0j4daaOi0H28qgwOanbNfGgmhb2cV5QN1WvTNeqwFmTXsBIaCqJfi/s200/Escalante+Ruins+100.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhS7I5mW40fVLrDePE0-1QKee3FCrX6gDKs0QwQz3JGoZVRdgVTQ6DvmLN-bZoyWot8rjrmqkIu1G4cVdF2qXJPBAP0j4daaOi0H28qgwOanbNfGgmhb2cV5QN1WvTNeqwFmTXsBIaCqJfi/s1600/Escalante+Ruins+100.JPG)

 Rating:![Image 3](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhIFTfTQ9bHx8V-a9L0U-ZRkkzR__1GjI31IxZrU9oue_A2nGluJ_L_srOk0TprV14gHn6wI5hkeCiCI4RiVj8IdnB-qRfam2bAP0VoBvphTmX0lDN9aIblSV3Vss5DJWDO-NAKERtod10/s1600/45stars.bmp)  
 Round Trip Distance: 1.3 miles  
 Difficulty: Easy  
 Elevation: 7086 - 7214 feet  
 Cellphone: 2-4 bars  
 Time: 1 hr.  
 Trailhead: Anasazi Heritage Center  
 Fee: $3/adult Mar-Oct (Free Nov - Feb)  
 Attractions: Ancestral Puebloan Ruins, museum  
![Image 4: Vault toilet](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiW6nSWCAMfwOhUHm85r-m_SHAmQFbbFvnF5O20sjJet97M_7N2izqWQoWNLyPg8dIFl8n5n81S7XvkTfDd-ykWESAdlzeRJxNFP4ewcEbUXBAKFnAcguGz-A9vsLyeDDNK8m73R4QTSsA/s1600/Restroom+icon.gif)![Image 5: Water](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhKjE0o7T5JCtpMkpOUSlMo7LVlii6RAHt0eTiO0i8OIDPb4Z2OR9ceYvVBE-afthucDVal6zKjqYRuPRCcnCkNiLw_stjisYv2UhO2kovMnPrkv8-lOKEo_mX-FXQinjxRf5el10bksmw/s1600/Water+spigot+icon.gif)![Image 6: No Dogs](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhq_Y_RVH827ofk-Lo3IkCvsEnaOHHVih6PBnOMDVwNamgt6pbidM5vlduR-0ozi2g_TB93DtwbhFD5x2JKuufNJvPdqRmpB7pG5xk4LVzstI8fSenpYjEyH_4Z-qwgw0EkMmETGfS-DSI/s1600/No+Dog+Icon.gif)![Image 7: No Camping](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjs7oQb48wH0m9iNh_kdDsJWpyBPzGWHvIKbGYrcNzoPvJodw0WT1Xf7Al31RQp3pQsrWSq_6HSt2zy3aXMhQDH9j5TFsfIRZC06mvGmY1Y6Uf2ENTvgqM7qszEF6dq1mMoPn10bGL85gE/s1600/No+Camping+icon.gif)![Image 8: Wheelchair Accessible](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiSRjAuo0z2t5wb51Dypzt4rQx0vAfRKuAYVgTWlEAFC7vAsdeFHki-hg6nGBgdGkPYGV9cu4J_aqzktgpoQT9g85ZfyE6W-RA2TFxVMV_0OuTOR1bsM4qD-_b71blz2scNM1MhG7ItKOY/s1600/Wheelchair+icon.gif)[![Image 9: Download GPS file](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjk0-w4GoKR7npfO2Hk_3O-WnqpP2Z5XmkkpcB_4wcfn81pQ4LSzZQUgUhyphenhyphenDtXZ_nttFTShMLUzdwujOV5iGw4dMqYEDJXOAdie9L-bXqDRcwGBfUPdpTCqybSMB-BdIlANdLx9HwkiVtI/s1600/GPS3+icon.gif)](https://docs.google.com/uc?export=download&id=0ByQop1XsLUTVRV85Q280RGE3Zm8)  
![Image 10: Hiking](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjmGFhhV3QYbyqzxLwJb8NgMyyXytx5CDNrnfzSQW6OuYORpByPVt53OeidKf7QSmbifG1MnctOX8NfT5CiE7FBJQrT44HfUIx3nSVsstz72ygEkpF-OZ-8i_DNE9_bNreFm8ufmd6_JQM/s200/Hiking+Icon.gif)![Image 11: No Bikes](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEibpOikgDNYhHOKXAF50TvTo9RaeCnxDxGAj9NOYXIprmuohS9AF1QbljGcLfgEUWrFSU_Fz8MxAa2c5wIbHP0CYj-vqS-FnswRofoeOaSDcNU1BnRf4kyaQwRzGWUusUZLuO6-d9M8WYw/s1600/No+Mountain+Bike+Icon.gif)![Image 12: No Horseback Riding](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiTElGUsmaivBTVKzfwmrtsKNbOck5OypvNF3X0M4z5cKbQlRINEdEcZE_QrBZhwgH5hjdaKFRCR_35pWUrQPw26hYS79zLfKnvzA4Cj4IN7khPxx9W4seKvXnqMcNdMXYyNNivkPoeIYg/s1600/No+Horse+Icon.gif)![Image 13: No Motorcycle](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEimRTcfnVkApD8X4mgFn6Nx3mSfBOw9yK61aZleM7pGICbDR26z74JGMxfx9SebHl6Ny2Q3R9jPq_yKeEsmpBI-CDdTs_Yk9hHRrznpHgdsna_PHuB-jXF2YNB_Hm4xSQ0-E83TXXT2IA0/s1600/No+Motorcycle+Icon.gif)![Image 14: No ATV](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhElfRXfjh8SKDrlX1NZAa-EIW0IzId1LH4cX0ov52sxK_7soyOLnNY4ZHK2OZaaELnAS-Bm3Cg0RnT8IRxhqCr0tIgrRGkxM1ynlUHrWdhDf7NXpthLWq5FqHGX1IUiAj5XVQ9XGC_46o/s1600/No+ATV+icon.jpg)![Image 15: No Jeep](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgYWgqGgWltBX4Dnm7AHCtmlHzzZEtN9V1Of_02Nh6h-PN88jvBl8x3-VJhEB1OhAeU_7Z0E7ZeKsZjJyLHupg_bGD7_5FdOnViOKs-6a4WRd-lvRkvCI-DHqCsOaW7RWFfYgKcq9S0MSI/s1600/No+Jeep+icon+3.jpg)  
  
  
 The Escalante Ruins are located in the Canyons of the Ancients National Monument just south of Dolores, Colorado on Highway 184. These Ancestral Puebloan ruins, which were named after Padre Silvestre Velez de Escalante, sit on the high point of a hill that now overlooks the present day McPhee Reservoir. There is no charge for hiking up the hill to the ruins. There is a charge for all adults over the age of 18 to enter the museum at the Anasazi Heritage Center during the months of March through October.  
[](http://rexmario.blogspot.com/2011/10/escalante-ruins.html)  

[![Image 16](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjPOCVa9siYjhruaVAsvNSzVEFC6euy4Aio_GCK3nJ1NT4qTC3p3v8HuqJ_wcIoev0NXo42O9ljiBjuyUU3BekPI4CdWoqLDMBaoZpu-qELoOv4nWjya0-gU-miOhhER-KL9VaQgkKQ7Xe-/s400/IMG00123-20110904-1539.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjPOCVa9siYjhruaVAsvNSzVEFC6euy4Aio_GCK3nJ1NT4qTC3p3v8HuqJ_wcIoev0NXo42O9ljiBjuyUU3BekPI4CdWoqLDMBaoZpu-qELoOv4nWjya0-gU-miOhhER-KL9VaQgkKQ7Xe-/s1600/IMG00123-20110904-1539.jpg)

  
 The Canyons of the Ancients National Monument is located in southwestern Colorado. The area contains the highest known concentration of archaeological sites in the nation. The sites, some of which date back thousands of years, show regular use and habitation of the area from the Archaic period, 10,000 years ago, through the times of the Anasazi, Utes and Navajo.  
  

[![Image 17](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhq1LwhlPJNGP4WBZu6RxjVvY5kenqcXBSLc-WLb7wFDm7e4d4-WZeo9pPoZj5s_YGK6Yaa7hxJEQ4VxvN-2yf7-LAwAyFm82UlDu9HIMD4yfD5pGT6wWVNrvdSZqmNIF3Mu709m5tLzrUi/s400/IMG00122-20110904-1529.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhq1LwhlPJNGP4WBZu6RxjVvY5kenqcXBSLc-WLb7wFDm7e4d4-WZeo9pPoZj5s_YGK6Yaa7hxJEQ4VxvN-2yf7-LAwAyFm82UlDu9HIMD4yfD5pGT6wWVNrvdSZqmNIF3Mu709m5tLzrUi/s1600/IMG00122-20110904-1529.jpg)

  
 The museum at the Anasazi Heritage Center is well worth visiting before hiking up to the ruins. The museum has a large assortment of artifacts and panels providing information on everything from how some of the pieces were made to a little incite into the life of the early inhabitants. There is also a replica of a dwelling that makes it easier for the imagination to grasp what the ruins may have looked like when they were intact.  
  

[![Image 18](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiDlJQ4cWDxRbEGSq_oBq1006EXtBezgCkpLDhMoaFd_1R7aEjAV-L7dyFF_h5yX5wzv6GDb7yhVt88YdYJ4uBhvyGvhMnEceqfkFuqPmZ_-d-PjT9TVXu3a-9y4_DfIwCpV5RoJxF_w_PB/s400/Escalante+Ruins+113.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiDlJQ4cWDxRbEGSq_oBq1006EXtBezgCkpLDhMoaFd_1R7aEjAV-L7dyFF_h5yX5wzv6GDb7yhVt88YdYJ4uBhvyGvhMnEceqfkFuqPmZ_-d-PjT9TVXu3a-9y4_DfIwCpV5RoJxF_w_PB/s1600/Escalante+Ruins+113.JPG)

  
 The trail begins just below the museum at the site of the Dominguez Pueblo.  
  

[![Image 19](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiNVTXAHCK25VRgZbk16hCPos5qKsqiGR2t2JUTxEBe81q0ZHU3Qpkm-WOcj7T2g8XytFXTHBlS55tD389Hbus65KFkJBHeDbgxq-Sd5NFhcCQkT9sCLvdXjixD22T6VNBqci2vvIkny3-f/s400/Escalante+Ruins+116.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiNVTXAHCK25VRgZbk16hCPos5qKsqiGR2t2JUTxEBe81q0ZHU3Qpkm-WOcj7T2g8XytFXTHBlS55tD389Hbus65KFkJBHeDbgxq-Sd5NFhcCQkT9sCLvdXjixD22T6VNBqci2vvIkny3-f/s1600/Escalante+Ruins+116.JPG)

  
 From the Dominguez Pueblo the paved trail passes through a very nice picnic area.  
  

[![Image 20](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjg5eRQqRkFsuhj5rRZ7pkH262pX_KQ8-qLyeVzkbxSYVYQnkOPL_WMphC-exc7Dooo3D44ZmEGRpR9EsdJEOgl8odM09qyTYe8s8xcphNpRitJs-REEbAvBlwfRtGQwpVW9zE2llX3Y7NE/s400/Escalante+Ruins+103.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjg5eRQqRkFsuhj5rRZ7pkH262pX_KQ8-qLyeVzkbxSYVYQnkOPL_WMphC-exc7Dooo3D44ZmEGRpR9EsdJEOgl8odM09qyTYe8s8xcphNpRitJs-REEbAvBlwfRtGQwpVW9zE2llX3Y7NE/s1600/Escalante+Ruins+103.JPG)

  
 Many kiosks along the way point out interesting things to learn about such as the vegetation or surrounding area.  
  

[![Image 21](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhyM2IUpFMhMobXg49E33qBjwZWN5D0prDTwOWMSSKRvvTIsA94oJxDHKiw8j_h_o_fpx7bJUl6xgufhPYbVnkynYHMJj3yZSCko2rXnHZBcvM0mAu0nVK0G2qhEwYtWuxfXfzOEf6wyE2O/s400/Escalante+Ruins+037.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhyM2IUpFMhMobXg49E33qBjwZWN5D0prDTwOWMSSKRvvTIsA94oJxDHKiw8j_h_o_fpx7bJUl6xgufhPYbVnkynYHMJj3yZSCko2rXnHZBcvM0mAu0nVK0G2qhEwYtWuxfXfzOEf6wyE2O/s1600/Escalante+Ruins+037.JPG)

  
 Since the trail does gradually climb a hill there are many benches providing a place to rest. There are also pull outs for wheelchairs so they don't need to block the trail. I thought that was a very nice tough.  
  

[![Image 22](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjGiHNps5Fp4S6VhWWUn_9DhMGGNFq4r9S4cF7TMMwQm7IV7OrgAwXYjA5r8Iu08e6Yq9eJ4yPFtS7jQx02kpQ-FOaGWmigaBZr_K4iZdrs9rVrykEwbx45xHy2TlF-G-i37dQWa6zZTV-D/s400/Escalante+Ruins+041.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjGiHNps5Fp4S6VhWWUn_9DhMGGNFq4r9S4cF7TMMwQm7IV7OrgAwXYjA5r8Iu08e6Yq9eJ4yPFtS7jQx02kpQ-FOaGWmigaBZr_K4iZdrs9rVrykEwbx45xHy2TlF-G-i37dQWa6zZTV-D/s1600/Escalante+Ruins+041.JPG)

  
 One kiosk points out the making of the mountain across the valley. This mountain is call the Sleeping Ute Mountain.  
  

[![Image 23](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhlrD412z4EjGgnMo_cFMbOFljXnKPeonAxxhpOwhYqm6bWdpSGfRjUDJM8HpbaEf_BTHNJ1xNaD9xN4aENTVNEwS8BkARtALFLJvfu1Gc3KA71nbvVjxgSH-ogcE_Df4j8Qi-L_4xehMr_/s400/Escalante+Ruins+084.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhlrD412z4EjGgnMo_cFMbOFljXnKPeonAxxhpOwhYqm6bWdpSGfRjUDJM8HpbaEf_BTHNJ1xNaD9xN4aENTVNEwS8BkARtALFLJvfu1Gc3KA71nbvVjxgSH-ogcE_Df4j8Qi-L_4xehMr_/s1600/Escalante+Ruins+084.JPG)

  
 There is a fork in the trail near the top of the hill where you can stroll over to a lookout point with great views of McPhee Reservoir.

# Hike to Interlaken Historic Resort

![Image 5: Writer: Jessica](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/a-/AAuE7mBIRKQAxoVGoBN_WbNeVQakUzDwKt-DhPWtllgc3Q%3Ds96-c)

[Jessica](https://www.backcountrychronic.com/profile/gamajlyn22/profile)

Oct 16, 2021

3 min read

Updated: Nov 7, 2021

October 16, 2021

![Image 6: A close-up of the historic hotel at Inter-Laken Resort in Twin Lakes](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_7caf9c1758a24e978d48b3f0b8b618bf~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_514,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_7caf9c1758a24e978d48b3f0b8b618bf~mv2.jpg)

The hotel building from Historic Inter-Laken Resort

There are few areas more scenic in the state of Colorado than the area around the Collegiate Peaks, with majestic views of some of the tallest peaks in the state. But if you’re like me and don’t see yourself bagging these 14k footers, don’t worry. There are plenty of beautiful and unique trails to explore in the area!

  

Among these is the Interlaken Trail, which follows close to the southern shore of Twin Lakes. This is one of my favorite trails in Colorado so far, with stunning views, lots of explorable lakeshore, little elevation change, and a neat destination at the end of the trail. In my opinion, this hike is a must!

  

![Image 7: Dexter's house surrounded by yellow trees in autumn](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_cf0521d2562a4ee6bd0510d0154703c7~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_522,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_cf0521d2562a4ee6bd0510d0154703c7~mv2.jpg)

A view of Dexter's house from the shore of Twin Lakes

### **Interlaken, Twin Lakes...Where’s That?**

I recently recounted my Interlaken Trail adventures to a native Coloradan who spends a fair amount of time outdoors hiking and fishing. His response: where is Twin Lakes?

  

A small, unincorporated town, [Twin Lakes](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Twin+Lakes,+CO+81251/@39.1048647,-106.3539928,28469m/data=!3m1!1e3!4m5!3m4!1s0x876aa30b84ae8a71:0x31a5382fd8cb6b8e!8m2!3d39.0820396!4d-106.382246) (the original mining town here was Dayton) sits at about 9,600 feet above sea level in the heart of the Rocky Mountains. At the base of Mount Elbert, Twin Lakes is approximately 21 miles south of Leadville and 25 miles north of Buena Vista. Route 82 through Independence Pass starts in this tiny mountain town**.**

  

The town itself was founded during the silver mining days as a go between Leadville and Aspen, sitting at the base of the route through Independence Pass. The Historic Interlaken Resort was a [popular destination during the 1880s](https://www.visittwinlakes.com/history/), though it’s success was short-lived. Check out [this cool photograph](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/45537) taken by the famed landscape photographer William Henry Jackson in 1875.

  

![Image 8: A view of Mount Elbert from Interlaken trail in autumn](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_ee77df35519b4287b3cc4692c7e5deac~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_539,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_ee77df35519b4287b3cc4692c7e5deac~mv2.jpg)

Mount Elbert through aspens with the moon atop

### **The Interlaken Trail**

Stacia and I hiked the Interlaken Trail one Saturday morning in late September. We hit the trailhead around 9am and had the trail mostly to ourselves for the first hour. There are multiple short side trails branching off the first half-mile of the trail, many leading down to a rocky lakeshore, others leading to backcountry camp sites.

  

*   ![Image 9](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_94f369153f56401b975ea3dbbb9dbc7e~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_1920,h_2723,al_c,q_90,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_auto/06b282_94f369153f56401b975ea3dbbb9dbc7e~mv2.jpg)
*   ![Image 10](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_c443320e21be41d688f305cba08bd0bf~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_1920,h_2731,al_c,q_90,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_auto/06b282_c443320e21be41d688f305cba08bd0bf~mv2.jpg)
*   ![Image 11](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_5f709dc8438a4799884ecd8c6fea0cf3~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_1920,h_2601,al_c,q_90,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_auto/06b282_5f709dc8438a4799884ecd8c6fea0cf3~mv2.jpg)

  

At one point, the Interlaken Trail joins with both the Colorado Trail and the Continental Divide Trail, and these lakeside campsites offer an ideal spot to stop for the night before heading on to conquer Mount Elbert (if trekking north). But Stacia and I are hardly that ambitious. Instead, we enjoyed a stunning autumn stroll through the pine and aspen forest, here and there peaking out at Mount Elbert awash in ochres and umbers.

  

![Image 12: Mount Elbert in Autumn from Twin Lakes shoreline](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_fad7453aa8cd4ad09712ac76d24ee9b7~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_532,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_fad7453aa8cd4ad09712ac76d24ee9b7~mv2.jpg)

A view of Mount Elbert from the shore of Twin Lakes

The trail itself is relatively flat, with an overall elevation change of 213 feet according to [AllTrails](https://www.alltrails.com/explore/trail/us/colorado/interlaken-trail). At one point, the trail crosses a bridge over a small creek and then enters into a grove of quaking aspens that were nearly at the height of their fall foliage show in late September!

  

Then, after a pleasant stroll of about 2.25 miles, suddenly the trail opens up to a sandy, sage-covered opening with what’s left of the Interlaken Historic Resort.

  

![Image 13: Dexter's House in Twin Lakes from trail](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_29d9eebe9a3946098db69c627340ddc3~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_540,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_29d9eebe9a3946098db69c627340ddc3~mv2.jpg)

Dexter's House at Inter-Laken Historic Resort

### **Exploring Inter-Laken Historic Resort**

I love trails with a clear destination at the end (waterfalls, scenic overlooks, waterfalls, historic ruins, oh and did I mention waterfalls?). In terms of destinations, this trail takes the cake! There’s literally an old, well-maintained ghost town (ghost resort?) at the end, and the best part is it’s only accessible by trail or by boat.

  

Traveling west on Interlaken Trail, the first building you see (and the most iconic) is Dexter’s house. James V. Dexter was a wealthy miner who [purchased the resort in 1883](https://coloradocentralmagazine.com/twin-lakes-the-interlaken-resort/#more-21524), built it out, and turned it into a popular travel destination until his death in 1899. The resort finally [closed in 1950](https://www.leadvilletwinlakes.com/things-to-do-detail/interlaken-resort/).

  

![Image 14: View of the top of Dexter's house at Twin Lakes in Autumn](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_60255f87b22c43c8ae1b2140127101af~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_1043,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_60255f87b22c43c8ae1b2140127101af~mv2.jpg)

The cupola of Dexter's house in Autumn

Dexter’s house is the only building that’s been restored and maintained enough for visitors to enter and explore--you can even walk up into the 3rd floor cupola for 360-degree views of the lake and surrounding mountains.

  

*   ![Image 15](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_cf0521d2562a4ee6bd0510d0154703c7~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_1920,h_1353,al_c,q_90,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_auto/06b282_cf0521d2562a4ee6bd0510d0154703c7~mv2.jpg)
*   ![Image 16](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_f1357d7727f04ea0adc9584f0f23cb06~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_1920,h_1331,al_c,q_90,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_auto/06b282_f1357d7727f04ea0adc9584f0f23cb06~mv2.jpg)
*   ![Image 17](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_d2a061b788494283ad772c3cf47d7b52~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_1920,h_1280,al_c,q_90,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_auto/06b282_d2a061b788494283ad772c3cf47d7b52~mv2.jpg)

  

But the current perspective from the cupola is a slightly different from the original view, since several of the [buildings were relocated](https://www.visittwinlakes.com/history/) (moved back from the lakeshore) when a dam was built. Some buildings were finally stabilized and repaired in [1979 by the Bureau of Reclamation](https://www.usbr.gov/gp/multimedia/archive/glimpse/interlaken.html).

  

Other buildings still remaining include the hotel building, two granaries, a hexagon-shaped privy (which contained leather toilet seats!), a stable, laundry, and cow barn.

  

Needless to say, the hike to Inter-Laken Historic Resort is a unique experience. I recommend visiting in autumn so you can see the resort framed by golden yellow aspens. With that said, be sure to arrive at the trailhead early, as traffic picked up considerably toward mid-day.

  

-Jessica

# 6 Great Easy Hikes Near Colorado Springs

![Image 5: Writer: Jessica](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/a-/AAuE7mBIRKQAxoVGoBN_WbNeVQakUzDwKt-DhPWtllgc3Q%3Ds96-c)

[Jessica](https://www.backcountrychronic.com/profile/gamajlyn22/profile)

Mar 27, 2022

4 min read

March 27, 2022

![Image 6: Field of sunflowers with a view of Cheyenne Mountain in the background](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_22623ec3e5294671a672a6684695fb13~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_535,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_22623ec3e5294671a672a6684695fb13~mv2.jpg)

Late Summer sunflowers in front of Cheyenne Mountain in Colorado Springs

[Colorado Springs](https://www.visitcos.com/) sits at the foot of the southern portion of Colorado’s Front Range mountains. Pikes Peak, one of the tallest peaks in the range, looms large over the area and, on a clear day, is visible for miles and miles away.

  

Since the city basically begins in the foothills of the mountains, it’s not difficult to find a variety of hiking trails to suit your needs and skill level. For this post, I’ve chosen six hikes that are either in Colorado Springs or only a short drive away.

  

The hikes below are typically rated as ‘easy’ on [trail rating apps](https://www.alltrails.com/), but I think rating systems that simply describe trails on the easy-moderate-difficult scale are subjective and rated from the perspective of someone who is athletic and able-bodied. I use ‘easy’ here for lack of a better word.

  

The fact of the matter is that ‘easy’ trails are not easy for everyone. Instead, the trails I selected are ‘easy’ because of the length and change in elevation. All trails outlined here have little elevation gain.

  

![Image 7: Snowy trail at Garden of the Gods Park leading to a giant red rock formation](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_f01d9c334eb645a58bf6dc23158bd84b~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_535,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_f01d9c334eb645a58bf6dc23158bd84b~mv2.jpg)

View of the Garden of the Gods rock formations from the Scotsman Trail

### **1. Garden of the Gods - Scotsman Trail Loop**

If you haven’t visited [Garden of the Gods Park](https://www.gardenofgods.com/) while in Colorado Springs, it’s a must! The park offers 21 miles of trails, a visitor’s center and a trading post, and is free entry to the general public.

  

[Scotsman Trail Loop](https://gardenofgods.com/images/GoG-Park-Map-Detail-2016.pdf) is a 1 mile trail that begins at the Scotsman Picnic Area and opens up to some spectacular views of the fiery red sandstone and limestone formations. This trail is a wide trail, open to horses and dogs as well as foot traffic, and offers access to the central garden trails as well as the longer Palmer and Buckskin Charlie Trails. There are several steps on the north end of this loop so this trail isn’t fully accessible.

  

![Image 8: Creek and hiking trail side-by-side winding through the forest](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_0f498de9dfbf46189cca5b88e982931c~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_1077,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_0f498de9dfbf46189cca5b88e982931c~mv2.jpg)

Mule Creek Trail following the creek in Pike National Forest

### **2. Pike National Forest - Mule Creek Trail**

[Mule Creek Trail](https://www.alltrails.com/explore/trail/us/colorado/mule-creek-trail) is one of my favorite trails around Colorado Springs during the warm summer months. This trail is mostly shaded and follows the meandering Troutman and Mule Creeks with little elevation gain. There are several creek-side spots along the way that would be ideal for a summer picnic or just to rest and splash your feet in the water.

  

I especially like this trail because it meets the needs of the [two arthritic hikers](https://www.backcountrychronic.com/post/9-things-to-consider-before-hiking-with-a-chronic-illness) in my family: myself and [my american bulldog](https://www.backcountrychronic.com/post/hiking-with-dogs). Both my dog Texie and I need relatively ‘easy’ trails and Texie is always a fan of some cool, flowing water to soothe her achy wrist joints. While I highly recommend this trail, it is far from a secret spot. The small parking lot at the trailhead can fill up quickly in the summer, so plan ahead and arrive early!

  

![Image 9: Sun shining on golden grass and Cheyenne Mountain at Cheyenne Mountain State Park](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_1f775a3a3f964e819d68efd71921822b~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_514,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_1f775a3a3f964e819d68efd71921822b~mv2.jpg)

Autumn at Cheyenne Mountain State Park on the Blackmer Trail

### **3. Cheyenne Mountain State Park - Blackmer Loop**

[Cheyenne Mountain State Park](https://cpw.state.co.us/placestogo/parks/CheyenneMountain/Documents/CMSPTrailMap.pdf) is a great option for hikers looking for more of a wilderness feel while remaining close to the city. This state park is located on the southwestern edge of town right in the foothills below Cheyenne Mountain.

  

While there are lots of trails at this park, and one that stretches nearly to the peak of Cheyenne Mountain, my favorite is Blackmer Loop. This trail has slightly more elevation change than the previous trails and can be narrow in spots, but opens up to some great views of the mountain and the city sprawl below. We have encountered many deer along this trail and one giant black bear right before winter hibernation, so [be prepared and be safe](https://www.nps.gov/articles/hiking-in-bear-country.htm)!

  

![Image 10: Red rock walls of an old quarry at Red Rock Canyon Open Space](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_368a6e007b96449786b0b03f22eac825~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_1016,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_368a6e007b96449786b0b03f22eac825~mv2.jpg)

The quarry at Red Rock Canyon Open Space in Colorado Springs

  

### **4. Red Rock Canyon Open Space - Greenlee & Quarry Pass Trails**

To me, Red Rock Canyon Open Space is a sister park to Garden of the Gods. The open space is located directly south of the more popular park and features a strand of red rock formations that are only slightly less spectacular than those found at Garden of the Gods Park.

  

This large open space offers numerous trails (and an enormous fenced in dog park), but I recommend exploring the quarry area–remnants of an old sandstone and gypsum quarry from the late 1800s. If starting south on the [Quarry Pass Trail](https://coloradosprings.gov/sites/default/files/inline-images/rrc_brochuremap_6_12_2018_2.pdf), hikers enter the quarry by a cool stairway cut into the rock. There are some rock steps on this path both to enter the quarry and to explore within the quarry, but the short climbs are well worth it!

  

![Image 11: Winter trail shot of Mount Cutler in North Cheyenne Canyon Park](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_e0149078912040e5ba7e0417557f54ae~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_575,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_e0149078912040e5ba7e0417557f54ae~mv2.jpg)

Moon above Mount Cutler in North Cheyenne Canyon Park

### **5. North Cheyenne Canyon Park - Lower Columbine Trail**

One great thing about a city that stretches along the edge of a mountain range is the sheer number of outdoor recreation opportunities. Another great park to visit is [North Cheyenne Canyon Park](https://coloradosprings.gov/page/north-cheyenne-canon) in southern Colorado Springs. This park features a narrow road that winds up the canyon with several trailheads along the way, some more difficult than others, and eventually arrives at the parking lot for Helen Hunt Falls.

  

The Columbine Trail is split into three sections: Upper, Middle and Lower. The entire trail stretches nearly 8 miles all the way up the canyon for a total elevation gain of around 1,600 feet. But the Lower Columbine Trail is just over 2 miles and follows North Cheyenne Creek for minimal elevation gain. The trail is wide, with no stairs and several picnic tables scattered along the way.

  

![Image 12: Blue skies and blue water at Rampart Reservoir in Colorado](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_6e859116b6674a5d9f6a95b8aa213c32~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_520,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_6e859116b6674a5d9f6a95b8aa213c32~mv2.jpg)

Summer at Rampart Reservoir in Pike National Forest

### **6. Rampart Reservoir Recreation Area - Rainbow Gulch Trail**

Rampart Reservoir, within the Pike National Forest, is located close to the town of Woodland Park. While at a high elevation (approximately 9,000 feet above sea level), the Rainbow Gulch Trail itself features a flat, even terrain. The trail itself stretches about 1.75 miles from parking lot to the reservoir, and follows a creek for much of the way.

  

[Rampart Reservoir Recreation Area](https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/psicc/recarea/?recid=16852) makes for a great day trip from Colorado Springs. The Reservoir is a popular spot in the summer for fishing, kayaking, paddle boarding, camping and picnicking. The longer Rampart Reservoir Trail follows the entire length of the reservoir’s shoreline for a total of nearly 11 miles and mostly shaded. The shorter [Rainbow Gulch Trail](https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/colorado/rampart-reservoir-via-rainbow-gulch-trail) is beautiful in the summer with wildflowers sprouting all around, therefore the trail is popular and the parking lot fills quickly.

  

-Jessica

# Climbing into the Past - Bandelier National Monument

![Image 5: Writer: Jessica](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/a-/AAuE7mBIRKQAxoVGoBN_WbNeVQakUzDwKt-DhPWtllgc3Q%3Ds96-c)

[Jessica](https://www.backcountrychronic.com/profile/gamajlyn22/profile)

Mar 14, 2021

4 min read

Updated: Jul 5, 2021

March 14, 2021

![Image 6: The Park Store entrance at Bandelier National Monument](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_4fc0ec8d1a2b49698eb14a4d8874ec9b~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_513,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_4fc0ec8d1a2b49698eb14a4d8874ec9b~mv2.jpg)

  

The road into Frijoles canyon snakes along the top of the north side of the canyon, then turns sharply west, opening up to expansive views of the canyon below. The road is somewhat narrow, having been built in the 1930s, and the only thing standing between the edge of the road and the canyon below is a knee-high stone wall.

  

But the views are breathtaking. It’s easy to see why Ancestral Puebloan peoples made home in this canyon, carving rooms--called cavates--in the volcanic tuft canyon walls and constructing buildings with bricks carved from that same tuft.

  

![Image 7: Big Kiva and frijoles canyon at Bandelier National Monument](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_a00f8666f9354d6b9b5c8a60c20059b7~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_572,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_a00f8666f9354d6b9b5c8a60c20059b7~mv2.jpg)

The remaining walls of the Tyuonyi and the cliff walls beyond

  

Bandelier National Monument was on my list to visit ever since we moved to New Mexico in 2017, but for some reason it took us three years to get there. Stacia and I headed to Bandelier in the Fall of 2020, right around my birthday. We new better than to visit during the summer, since temperatures can get pretty hot and make hiking in desert environments somewhat unbearable. Early Fall was still warm, so we arrived at the National Monument entrance early to both beat the heat and the traffic.

  

While Bandelier boasts over 70 miles of hiking trails, we decided to stick with the tourist routes that take visitors through the ruins Ancestral Puebloans left behind several hundred years ago. From the visitor’s center, we headed out onto the Main Loop trail.

  

![Image 8: Talus House at Bandelier National Monument](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_e4fde0b6560a42f583ea2dfe1ce84be6~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_493,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_e4fde0b6560a42f583ea2dfe1ce84be6~mv2.jpg)

Looking through a window at Talus House

  

[The Main Loop](https://www.nps.gov/band/planyourvisit/the-main-loop-trail.htm) is paved and heads straight through the Tyuonyi and Big Kiva r uins before turning toward the north canyon wall and up into some of the carved dwellings. The cliff walls themselves were interesting to see, shaped by erosion and chalked-full of holes made or made home by birds and perhaps other small creatures. But the real fun came when we reached the first ladder leading into one of the cavates.

  

![Image 9: Big Kiva view at Bandelier National Monument](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_78cee84938f844b98a91a75178231176~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_1033,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_78cee84938f844b98a91a75178231176~mv2.jpg)

Looking out at the Tyuonyi from a cavate

  

Bandelier National Monument is one National Monument that was created and functions mostly in accordance with the original language of [the American Antiquities Act of 1906](https://www.nps.gov/history/local-law/anti1906.htm); that is, to preserve and protect “historic landmarks, historic and prehistoric structures, and other objects of historic or scientific interest that are situated upon the lands owned or controlled by the Government of the United States.” The Antiquities Act came about somewhat in part because of gathering pressure to preserve similar ruins and ancient sites across the southwest (from looting and other destructive behaviors), but mainly in the area that is now [Mesa Verde National Park.](https://www.nps.gov/meve/learn/historyculture/stories.htm)

  

Interestingly, Mesa Verde was never declared a National Monument, but was designated a National Park the same year that Congress signed the Antiquities Act into law. [Bandelier National Monument was enacted in 1916](https://www.nps.gov/band/learn/historyculture/index.htm), only ten years after the signing of the Antiquities Act.

  

![Image 10: Alcove House view at Bandelier National Monument](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_f3e6285d9a6f47ba8b9b53bbe31a664c~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_968,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_f3e6285d9a6f47ba8b9b53bbe31a664c~mv2.jpg)

Looking up at Alcove House from halfway up the ladders

  

Stacia and I walked along the trail, poking our heads into Talus House, climbing wooden ladders into the few cavetes the NPS allows visitors access to, and inspecting the gardens and artwork still intact at Long House. What strikes me about these ruins is how creative it’s builders were, to look at this landscape of volcanic tuft cliffs, stream running through, and build dwellings suitable for a presumably large community. Their imaginativeness to carve a home out of what was available to them.

  

As we passed the intersection of [Frey Trail](https://www.nps.gov/band/planyourvisit/frey-trail.htm), we ran into a park ranger sitting on a bench beneath a tree. He was an older man and lean, and was out on a leisurely stroll around the developed trails. We greeted one another and started a casual conversation about the area. He informed us of some of the monument’s history, explaining how Frey Trail was the only route in and out of the canyon for years before the canyon road was built. Inhabitants and visitors to the monument in its early days had to carry everything down the 1.5 mile trail riddled with switchbacks as it descends 550+ feet into the canyon (and up the canyon too).

  

![Image 11: Cavates at Bandelier National Monument](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_a0e5769fa1f84260ad5d8aa012b322e7~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_870,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_a0e5769fa1f84260ad5d8aa012b322e7~mv2.jpg)

Stacia peaking out one of the cavates along the Main Loop Trail

  

We did not head up Frey Trail since we were concerned with the mid-day heat and since I was testing out a new pair of hiking boots, which I ended up returning because their thin soles hurt my feet. Instead, we headed toward [Alcove House](https://www.nps.gov/band/planyourvisit/alcove-house.htm).

  

![Image 12: Alcove House, wooden ladders, and the canyon wall](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_f9eea6ff141c460fa80e2cf0ceadbd9d~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_773,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_f9eea6ff141c460fa80e2cf0ceadbd9d~mv2.jpg)

A view up at Alcove House from the canyon floor below

  

At Alcove House, four ladders allow visitors access to an alcove 140 feet up the canyon wall. Standing on the ground beneath he wooden ladders, Stacia considered sitting this one out. But she quickly overcame her hesitation, fueled by a fear of heights, and led the way up the ladders that replicated how original inhabitants reached this dwelling. We spent around fifteen minutes observing the ruins in this cave, then headed back down to allow others access. As with most climbs, the descent was a bit more shaky than the climb up, and a bit harder on my knees.

  

![Image 13: A view of the Kiva within Alcove House and a view of the canyon](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_bb3b48884edf419899c7c34d54b9210b~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_538,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_bb3b48884edf419899c7c34d54b9210b~mv2.jpg)

The reconstructed Kiva at Alcove House

  

We stopped at the park store on the way out, purchasing some souvenirs and supporting the upkeep of this magical place. We had intentions of hiking the 1.5 miles to Upper Falls, in addition to completing the Mail Loop Trail and Alcove House, but temperatures were rising and my joints were hurting.

  

![Image 14: Climbing to Alcove House in Bandelier National Monument](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_8a0dc41e33774c30bdbcdfe440a9fa5a~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_596,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_8a0dc41e33774c30bdbcdfe440a9fa5a~mv2.jpg)

Me climbing one of the wooden ladders leading to Alcove House

  

Though we didn’t make it outside of the commonly traversed trails, it’s worth noting that Bandelier offers a variety of different hiking and backpacking opportunities for the outdoor enthusiasts with more time on their hands and a greater level of mobility.I recommend checking the temperature when planning a trip to this National Monument, since the summer heat may make hiking more difficult and even dangerous if hikers are unacquainted with desert hiking. All in all, Bandelier is definitely worth the trip for hikers and tourists alike!

  

-Jessica

# Exploring Eleven Mile Canyon Recreation Area in Colorado

![Image 5: Writer: Jessica](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/a-/AAuE7mBIRKQAxoVGoBN_WbNeVQakUzDwKt-DhPWtllgc3Q%3Ds96-c)

[Jessica](https://www.backcountrychronic.com/profile/gamajlyn22/profile)

Jul 15, 2021

4 min read

Updated: Jul 17, 2022

July 15th, 2021

![Image 6: View of Eleven Mile Reservoir and mountains in the distance](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_3fced91633444fd5812d65075f2313cc~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_559,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_3fced91633444fd5812d65075f2313cc~mv2.jpg)

View of Eleven Mile Reservoir from the Overlook Trail at Spillway Campground

  

I’m just in the early stages of exploring all that Colorado has to offer for outdoor adventures (or at least all that I can explore). I discovered [Eleven Mile Canyon Recreation Area](https://www.fs.usda.gov/wps/portal/fsinternet/cs/recarea?ss=110312&navtype=BROWSEBYSUBJECT&navid=110240000000000&pnavid=null&position=BROWSEBYSUBJECT&recid=41667&ttype=recarea&pname=Eleven+Mile+Canyon+Recreation+Area) in part by accident, after searching a 100-mile radius on the map for last-minute campground reservations. After many fails on [recreation.gov](https://www.recreation.gov/), I finally secured one campsite at Spillway Campground within the Recreation Area and off we went!

  

One Friday afternoon in June, I cut off work a little early, Stacia and I loaded up the car with gear and dogs, and we hit the road. From Colorado Springs, it took about an hour to reach the entrance to Eleven Mile Canyon Recreation Area.

  

There’s a small booth at the entrance to the Rec Area used to collect a fee and hand out tags. Since we had camping reservations, we were not charged an additional fee. The Day Use fee, however, is $7.

  

![Image 7: Dirt road to the right, South Platte River to the left running through the canyon](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_2f622a8a1be441728855f11c99c62ad9~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_536,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_2f622a8a1be441728855f11c99c62ad9~mv2.jpg)

Dirt road through Eleven Mile Canyon Recreation Area along the South Platte River

  

Once through the entrance point, the road becomes narrow as it follows the old Colorado Midland Railroad bed, always remaining in sight of the South Platte River. Just a drive on this road is pretty cool, as it overlooks some river rapids, offers scenic views of the winding South Platte and canyon walls, and traverses several old railroad tunnels cut through the granite.

  

![Image 8: A dirt road and two old railroad tunnels through granite rock](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_3a9d9a23d3ef4d33ad42f5a554166167~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_955,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_3a9d9a23d3ef4d33ad42f5a554166167~mv2.jpg)

Two of three old railroad tunnels through the granite rock of Eleven Mile Canyon

  

### **Why Visit Eleven Mile Canyon Recreation Area?**

  

**1. Proximity to Denver and Colorado Springs**

Did I say that Eleven Mile Canyon is a short drive from Colorado Springs? Well that also means the drive is short-ish from Denver too! In fact, one can leave Denver and arrive at the Recreation Area entrance in just over 2 hours, depending on the route.

  

In theory, the quickest route from Denver takes you south on Interstate 25 to Colorado Springs, then west through Woodland Park and Divide. The alternate, scenic route follows route 285 partway to 126 through Deckers. This route adds on about fifteen minutes but offers more views of the South Platte River, where it runs through Deckers a bit north of the recreation area.

  

![Image 9: A view of rapids and lots of boulders in the South Platte River](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_6cdb0355daf2420ca98360937ea31582~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_536,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_6cdb0355daf2420ca98360937ea31582~mv2.jpg)

The raging South Platte River

  

**2. The Fishing**

I’ll admit, my limited fishing skills are a bit rusty. But if I were to take up fishing again, I would head over the Eleven Mile Canyon to fish the South Platte. There’s over 8 miles of fishing spots right off the dirt road, with some areas more accessible than others. Judging by the abundance of fishermen and fisherwomen (and fisherchildren...is that a word?) lining this canyon during our June weekend, I’d say the fish are abundant!

  

In fact, our camp neighbor (a ten-year-old boy who frequently popped over to pet the dogs) excitedly reported numerous fish caught and released (this is a strict catch-and-release area) throughout our 48-hour camp stay.

![Image 10](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_2a21fe492d064060a2aa71f95196149d~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_605,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_2a21fe492d064060a2aa71f95196149d~mv2.jpg)

The western half of Spillway Campground one evening in June

  

**3. Camping Opportunities**

As I said previously, one last-minute camp site opening drew us to Eleven Mile Canyon Recreation Area, but I think most people visit for the fishing or the river. With that said, this Recreation Area contains four separate campgrounds, all of which require reservations during the peak season - aka the summer months.

  

Stacia and I [camped](https://www.backcountrychronic.com/camping) at [Spillway Campground](https://www.recreation.gov/camping/campgrounds/233721), located at the very end of the road through the canyon. It was a nice spot with plenty of shade and a view of the Eleven Mile Dam, though there are several campsites that trade off shade for direct access to the river. At 8,500 feet in elevation, I’d choose shade over direct river access in the summer, but that’s just me!

  

![Image 11](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_19efe83de2cf4ca98edc4e02bb462ccc~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_581,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_19efe83de2cf4ca98edc4e02bb462ccc~mv2.jpg)

The South Platte River widening in spots as it weaves through the canyon

  

**4. Picnicking by the River**

In addition to four campgrounds, there are also four picnic areas dotted along the South Platte River. The most popular of the four is Eleven Mile Picnic Area, where the canyon opens up and the river widens and slows, leaving a large grassy area along the west bank. Here, picnic tables are spread out along the canyon walls with plenty of pines for shade, and little sandy river beaches line the river’s edge.

  

![Image 12](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_5e107eb646db4beea2ad9358edad817b~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_1027,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_5e107eb646db4beea2ad9358edad817b~mv2.jpg)

Stone stairs up through the rock on the Overlook Trail

  

**5. Rock Climbing**

I am no rock climber, though I do enjoy it as a spectator sport! Judging by the looks of the giant granite domes in and around Eleven Mile Canyon, along with the various websites with climbing route information, this area looks like an excellent and relatively unknown gem for rock climbing enthusiasts. While I did not see any climbers during our weekend in the canyon, [SummitPost](https://www.summitpost.org/elevenmile-canyon/195711) boasts 21 climbing routes within the canyon.

  

![Image 13](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_90a26695dd304cf2970350f45cbd3ed4~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_579,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_90a26695dd304cf2970350f45cbd3ed4~mv2.jpg)

Me standing at the end of the Overlook Trail, looking out over Eleven Mile Reservoir

  

**6. Hiking the Overlook Trail**

Okay as you can tell from this blog, I’m usually in it for [the hiking](https://www.backcountrychronic.com/getting-outdoors). Unfortunately for me, the main activity within this recreation area is not hiking, but fishing. Actually, there’s only one hiking trail along this 8 mile road - [the Overlook Trail](https://www.alltrails.com/explore/trail/us/colorado/eleven-mile-canyon-overlook-trail) at the Spillway Campground. This trail is not long by any means (0.8 miles out-and-back), but it does climb nearly 400 feet in elevation to one stunning view of Eleven Mile Reservoir and the peaks of the Sawatch Range in the distance.

  

Whether you’re looking to camp, fish, or just spend the day by the river, I highly recommend this recreation area just south of Lake George, Colorado!

  

-Jessica

# Best Albuquerque Area Day Hikes

![Image 5: Writer: Jessica](https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/a-/AAuE7mBIRKQAxoVGoBN_WbNeVQakUzDwKt-DhPWtllgc3Q%3Ds96-c)

[Jessica](https://www.backcountrychronic.com/profile/gamajlyn22/profile)

Jan 15, 2020

6 min read

Updated: Jul 6, 2021

January 15th, 2020

![Image 6](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_aed28348a5bf4a3ba81b2025aa7625a1~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_579,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_aed28348a5bf4a3ba81b2025aa7625a1~mv2.jpg)

View of the Sandia Mountains from the Placitas Open Space

Albuquerque is a growing city, but in a way it still carries on the legacy left behind by the author and environmentalist Aldo Leopold. When Leopold served as the Secretary of Albuquerque’s Chamber of Commerce in 1918, the city boasted barely fifteen thousand residents, so you can imagine the small city engulfed by a high desert wilderness.

  

New Mexico itself in the early 1900s abounded in wilderness, with five different ecosystems displaying the state’s wide variations of geology and habitation. Leopold was closely connected to the state’s wild spaces through his work with the U.S. Forest Service. During his time in New Mexico, he worked hard to enact protections for wild spaces throughout the state, undoubtedly anticipating not only population growth, but also the need to protect these wild spaces and their inhabitants from outside forces. Leopold succeeded by being instrumental in making the Gila Wilderness the country’s first designated Wilderness Area, while also petitioning to protect the area surrounding the Rio Grande in Albuquerque, now the Rio Grande Valley State Park.

  

![Image 7](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_03b756e60b664369856b90cab0f435cd~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_350,h_350,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_03b756e60b664369856b90cab0f435cd~mv2.jpg)

Bosque Trails along the Rio Grande in Albuquerque

Albuquerque today contains 29,000 acres of Open Space within the city limits, and though the population inches closer to six hundred thousand people, there’s still a sense of those wild spaces both within the city and at close reach. In fact, [NerdWallet](https://www.nerdwallet.com/blog/travel/4-urban-destinations-nature-lovers/) recently ranked Albuquerque as the number one urban destination for nature lovers!

  

Though I certainly haven’t compared every city in the country, I have to agree that Albuquerque and the surrounding area has a wealth of choices for outdoor enthusiasts like me. To prove it, I’ve made a list of some of the area’s best hiking trails, most within a one-hour driving distance.

  

The below list is sorted by season, since some areas have little cover during hot summer months, while the high elevation of others areas make them less ideal for hiking in the winter months (especially for those of us with arthritis and joint pain). Please note my list is also geared toward those of us who cannot take on a 10-mile hike or a 6 thousand foot elevation gain, such as my fellow chronic illness warriors.

  

### **Winter**

**1.**[**Petroglyphs National Monument - Piedras Marcadas Canyon**](https://www.nps.gov/petr/planyourvisit/pmc.htm)

![Image 8](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_463586a607674dc6a6b37d81c3ea1021~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_350,h_340,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_463586a607674dc6a6b37d81c3ea1021~mv2.jpg)

Piedras Marcadas Canyon within Petroglyphs National Monument

This national monument sits on the western edge of the city and many of the canyon entrances plug directly into a residential neighborhood. While there are several trails at the [Petroglyphs National Monument](https://www.nps.gov/petr/index.htm), I chose Piedras Marcadas Canyon because it’s hiking trail is a decent length (1.5 miles round-trip) and it allows dogs. The monument itself is beautifully shaped by volcanic rock formations, where you’ll find hundreds of petroglyphs etched onto the black basalt that still look as if they just tumbled from the mesa-top.

  

**2.**[**Placitas Open Space**](https://www.cabq.gov/parksandrecreation/open-space/lands/sandoval-county-open-space)

One of the city’s many Open Spaces, the Placitas Open Space covers a large area of land at the northwestern foot of the Sandia Mountains. There are many intertwining trails here at the base of the mountain which makes it a popular space for mountain bikers. I love the Placitas Open Space because the area is fairly flat, but offers a beautiful silhouette of the mountain nearby as well as a scenic overlook of the mesas to the northwest.

  

### **Spring**

There’s little rainfall in Albuquerque at any point of the year, and definitely not in the spring where wind is the main force of nature. Wind in the desert kicks up the sand and dirt, is unpleasant, and can even affect visibility. Temperatures can be unpredictable too, with late spring temperatures often getting up into the 80s. Even if you’re not checking the weather here for precipitation, it’s important to check for wind warnings and temperature fluctuations!

  

**3.**[**Elena Gallegos Open Space**](https://www.cabq.gov/parksandrecreation/open-space/lands/elena-gallegos-open-space)

I have to admit that this is one of two areas on my list that I have yet to visit. Much of the city’s open spaces exist in the foothills area at the base of the Sandia Mountains. The Elena Gallegos Open Space is one of the larger parks with little change in elevation, encompassing 640 acres and sitting at an elevation of 6,500 feet.

  

**4.**[**Kasha-Katuwe Tent Rocks National Monument**](https://www.blm.gov/visit/kktr)

![Image 9](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_6d65a60c9988439b9a2332108fb4fea8~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_905,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_6d65a60c9988439b9a2332108fb4fea8~mv2.jpg)

View from the top of the Canyon Trail at Kasha-Katuwe Tent Rocks National Monument

This is a must! The Kasha-Katuwe Tent Rocks National Monument is about an hour’s drive almost directly north of Albuquerque. The monument’s draw are the unique rock formations -- tall “tapered hoodoos” formed from a volcanic eruption which deposited over 1,000 feet of “pumice, ash, and tuft.” The Canyon Trail will take you through a slot canyon and to the top of the rock formations for an elevation gain of 630 feet. The trail itself is a heavily-trafficked, 1.5 mile trek from trailhead to peak. If you decide to visit in mid-to-late Spring (or summer for that matter), be sure to bring plenty of water!

  

### **Summer**

Even though, due to its elevation, Albuquerque is technically the ‘high desert’ - this is still a desert landscape that experiences some pretty extreme and dry weather. In the summer months the temperature consistently rises into the high 90s and often hits 100 degrees fahrenheit. That’s why, during the summer months, it’s important to either find trails with lots of cover (head for the mountains) or plan early morning hikes to avoid the scorching daytime sun.

  

**5.**[**Travertine Falls Trail**](https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/cibola/recarea/?recid=64194)

This trail is about a twenty-minute drive east of Albuquerque heading toward the mountains. You’ll find Travertine Falls about 1.1 miles from the trailhead engulfed in a juniper scrub landscape, but don’t be fooled--this is still the desert so water won’t always be flowing here! Early or mid summer after a rainstorm may be your best chance of seeing some water trickling down the falls, but water or not this is a beautiful and shady hike! Oh, and for those of you wanting a more rigorous hike, this trail connects directly to the South Crest Trail, which then leads into a network of trails within the Cibola National Forest on the eastern side of the Sandia Mountains.

  

**6.**[**Rio Grande Valley State Park - Bosque Trails**](https://www.cabq.gov/parksandrecreation/open-space/lands/rio-grande-valley-state-park)

![Image 10](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_d4c4effa0b63488db314bcf35cfdf541~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_350,h_355,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_d4c4effa0b63488db314bcf35cfdf541~mv2.jpg)

Texie splashing in the Rio Grande in Albuquerque

This is my go-to most of the year when the dogs and I need a dose of nature on a weekday evening. The Bosque Trails run along the Rio Grande as it weaves its way through the city. These trails run under the shade of the cottonwood trees, many of them leading to small sandy beaches along the river. My dog Texie normally leads the way to her favorite beach and plunges directly into the water! Be careful if you’re on these trails on hot days with dogs--there are a few sandy spots that may burn their paws.

  

  

### **Fall**

Most years, I’d consider fall in Albuquerque the best season. Typically the temperatures begin to drop in late August or early September, and by October the mornings are cool but the afternoons still get up into the 60s and 70s. Perfect hiking weather, if you ask me!

  

**7.**[**Fourth of July Trail**](https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/cibola/recarea/?recid=64174)[](https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/cibola/recarea/?recid=64174)

I confess, I have not been to the Fourth of July Trail in the Manzano Mountains. Though this trail is actually closer to Albuquerque than Kasha-Katuwe Tent Rocks National Monument as the crow flies, there’s no easy way to get there. Even though it takes nearly an hour and a half to arrive at the trailhead, the drive scenically winds its way south from Tijeras through a hilly, pine-covered landscape until you finally get a view of the Manzano Mountains ahead. I’ve heard this trail is a top choice in the fall because of its reds, oranges and yellows--a suggestion of deciduous fall foliage. Of course, it won’t compete with a trip to Vermont in October, but for the Southwest it puts on a pretty good display!

  

**8.**[**Ojito Wilderness Area**](https://www.blm.gov/visit/ojito-wilderness)

By far one of my favorite places to visit, the Ojito Wilderness Area was made famous-ish by the late [20th century discovery](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/whatever-happened-to-seismosaurus-78770907/) (by hikers!) of a Seismosaurus skeleton, deemed the largest of the sauropod dinosaurs. More recently, a group of hikers discovered a [jurassic crocodile skull](https://www.krqe.com/news/new-mexico/hikers-discover-new-mexicos-first-jurassic-crocodile-fossil/) while hiking in the Ojito Wilderness. This area covers a spectacular landscape of mesas and badlands with colorful hoodoos all around. I have [trekked the Seismosaurus Trail](https://www.backcountrychronic.com/post/finding-the-seismosaurus-trail) that leads to the dig site, though there’s little there now but a large sandy area where the dig took place. Even with few man-made signs of the dig site, the trail still offers a beautiful mesa view and some petroglyphs just beyond the dig site! This is a true backcountry area with no marked trails, which makes it a great place to explore. Plan ahead for this trip, since there’s little cover and no facilities--you’ll need cooler weather and lots of water.

![Image 11](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/06b282_34c28a402603405d9e686c152bd001b5~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_740,h_810,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/06b282_34c28a402603405d9e686c152bd001b5~mv2.jpg)

Trail leading into the Ojito Wilderness Area

Narrowing this list down to eight recommendations wasn’t easy, but if anything that statement confirms NerdWallet’s assertion that Albuquerque is a unique destination for nature lovers and those seeking a variety of outdoor adventures. Really, New Mexico as a whole has an abundance of [government-owned lands](https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2019/10/29/how-much-land-government-owns-in-every-state/40453833/) open for recreation, ranking 10th in states with the largest percentage of public lands, and 9th by total federally-owned acreage!

  

-Jessica

![Image 8: Hiking](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjmGFhhV3QYbyqzxLwJb8NgMyyXytx5CDNrnfzSQW6OuYORpByPVt53OeidKf7QSmbifG1MnctOX8NfT5CiE7FBJQrT44HfUIx3nSVsstz72ygEkpF-OZ-8i_DNE9_bNreFm8ufmd6_JQM/s200/Hiking+Icon.gif)![Image 9: No Bikes](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEibpOikgDNYhHOKXAF50TvTo9RaeCnxDxGAj9NOYXIprmuohS9AF1QbljGcLfgEUWrFSU_Fz8MxAa2c5wIbHP0CYj-vqS-FnswRofoeOaSDcNU1BnRf4kyaQwRzGWUusUZLuO6-d9M8WYw/s1600/No+Mountain+Bike+Icon.gif)![Image 10: No Horseback Riding](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiTElGUsmaivBTVKzfwmrtsKNbOck5OypvNF3X0M4z5cKbQlRINEdEcZE_QrBZhwgH5hjdaKFRCR_35pWUrQPw26hYS79zLfKnvzA4Cj4IN7khPxx9W4seKvXnqMcNdMXYyNNivkPoeIYg/s1600/No+Horse+Icon.gif)![Image 11: No Motorcycle](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEimRTcfnVkApD8X4mgFn6Nx3mSfBOw9yK61aZleM7pGICbDR26z74JGMxfx9SebHl6Ny2Q3R9jPq_yKeEsmpBI-CDdTs_Yk9hHRrznpHgdsna_PHuB-jXF2YNB_Hm4xSQ0-E83TXXT2IA0/s1600/No+Motorcycle+Icon.gif)![Image 12: No ATV](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhElfRXfjh8SKDrlX1NZAa-EIW0IzId1LH4cX0ov52sxK_7soyOLnNY4ZHK2OZaaELnAS-Bm3Cg0RnT8IRxhqCr0tIgrRGkxM1ynlUHrWdhDf7NXpthLWq5FqHGX1IUiAj5XVQ9XGC_46o/s1600/No+ATV+icon.jpg)![Image 13: No Jeep](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgYWgqGgWltBX4Dnm7AHCtmlHzzZEtN9V1Of_02Nh6h-PN88jvBl8x3-VJhEB1OhAeU_7Z0E7ZeKsZjJyLHupg_bGD7_5FdOnViOKs-6a4WRd-lvRkvCI-DHqCsOaW7RWFfYgKcq9S0MSI/s1600/No+Jeep+icon+3.jpg)  
  
  
 Goodman Point is located in the Hovenweep National Monument in southwestern Colorado. Goodman Point was the first archaeological site in the country to receive protection from the federal government. Hovenweep National Monument is comprised of 6 discontiguous acreages that protect groups of ancestral Puebloan ruins. Goodman Point is the eastern most unit of Hovenweep National Monument. The remarkable masonry skills that are seen at the other Hovenweep sites are completely missing at Goodman Point as all of the ruins have been reduced to piles of ruble. Hovenweep is a Ute word that means 'deserted valley' which aptly describes the surrounding area with all the villages of ghostly ruins.  
[](http://rexmario.blogspot.com/2012/07/hovenweep-goodman-point.html)  

[![Image 14](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhWbMSn02_VzJovKRgNPmhQa_jIcjwpzd7dUvG_cto8CIXsBcGgcpiC0vePJnqTtFGS1kBLXXb03oCYP90BvAEa1pHJUAmbo3vuh2qSg7Yw03iQ3bTAjc1Grw49gegyXjHP79AExilS2c4/s400/Goodman+001.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhWbMSn02_VzJovKRgNPmhQa_jIcjwpzd7dUvG_cto8CIXsBcGgcpiC0vePJnqTtFGS1kBLXXb03oCYP90BvAEa1pHJUAmbo3vuh2qSg7Yw03iQ3bTAjc1Grw49gegyXjHP79AExilS2c4/s1600/Goodman+001.JPG)

  
 The Goodman Point trailhead is unmarked and there are no road signs indicating where to find it. Your best bet is to use the Google Map and choose 'Get directions'. The last leg of the drive is to turn west off of Highway 491 onto Road P and follow it for 5.8 miles to the unmarked parking area. Road P has a funny little kink in it where it bends to the right at about a 45 degree angle for about 8 tenths of a mile then straightens up again for a half mile where you make a left turn onto 18 road for another half mile and then turn right onto Road P again. As you continue west on Road P you will notice a fence on the left side of the road after about 7 tenths of a mile that has the metal NPS signs on it. The parking area is on the left within a quarter mile.  
  

[![Image 15](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjcAr_Jn8P0VbeKjnv8diwLQH3__UaP-9lFajn0NOCkgEYb7TtY5SAkIxNnW4n8rL9d5G3o7F6Pf3qbI8y4TkGsLAuYD-hO45Hf4-w9a_5s6rhpluPuPcmeVgwQq6H_lhcFLb5YY3B4nQk/s400/Goodman+005.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjcAr_Jn8P0VbeKjnv8diwLQH3__UaP-9lFajn0NOCkgEYb7TtY5SAkIxNnW4n8rL9d5G3o7F6Pf3qbI8y4TkGsLAuYD-hO45Hf4-w9a_5s6rhpluPuPcmeVgwQq6H_lhcFLb5YY3B4nQk/s1600/Goodman+005.JPG)

  
 The trail register and Hovenweep sign are about a tenth of a mile from the parking area. Be sure and check the trail register for a brochure. The brochure is very important for making any sense of the piles of rubble that make up the site. Without the brochure the site is very anticlimactic.  
  

[![Image 16](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEj-5yDUjMEw840bmcPf5SK1uVaXi-yGd6yW-bEbZ_rSkfRm83oaovZOe_vWmuG-K2L1Ht1aMpChe1Cz8DK0PHq7gFuYVUlHyhFsdH7w4kmGARd89V4A1JomG_5kRX7746u9aCVUgh1wl_Q/s400/Goodman+012.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEj-5yDUjMEw840bmcPf5SK1uVaXi-yGd6yW-bEbZ_rSkfRm83oaovZOe_vWmuG-K2L1Ht1aMpChe1Cz8DK0PHq7gFuYVUlHyhFsdH7w4kmGARd89V4A1JomG_5kRX7746u9aCVUgh1wl_Q/s1600/Goodman+012.JPG)

  
 There is a trail that leads to the left just over a hundred yards from the trail register. This marker is the last of the improvements made on the trail. For being the first protected archaeological site in the country and part of Hovenweep National Monument since 1951 it is very surprising to find no more improvements.  
  
  

[![Image 17](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjyq-cUo1y_f-iRXJn1eZA3tOk0lSKdNTlHt3hJqaKgbIceROiurh_fOKv0xBL7IfcQV7Ile5FWU3Sxule9JLLwH1vzcuy6i9Qsifef8M8uoDPNpuAaI1qf3GdHQPDVKnrINhlxBdi9kuY/s400/Goodman+013.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjyq-cUo1y_f-iRXJn1eZA3tOk0lSKdNTlHt3hJqaKgbIceROiurh_fOKv0xBL7IfcQV7Ile5FWU3Sxule9JLLwH1vzcuy6i9Qsifef8M8uoDPNpuAaI1qf3GdHQPDVKnrINhlxBdi9kuY/s1600/Goodman+013.JPG)

  
 There are continuous piles of rubble that once formed the pueblo with its numerous kivas, towers and enclosing walls. From a cursory investigation one component of the ruins that is so obviously missing is any sign of mortar. The mud mortar has all been dissolved and returned to the ground. It would be interesting to know what was different about mortar at this site and similar ruins, like Sand Canyon Pueblo, that they are nothing more than piles of rubble while others like Lowry Pueblo are still standing.  
  

[![Image 18](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjYv_WTSngBdfnU8Pl23oCig93bHzO-SANk4kvCovZLZjqB-Lgtmupmjibx3yA8NHuK3U1GLHTr1-L5z5Nq29p2PQuWsEj-CPrbDiYcA77ht8OF8N2n6jOWhpkxx8zFgXkiij-9vQcVruo/s400/Goodman+040.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjYv_WTSngBdfnU8Pl23oCig93bHzO-SANk4kvCovZLZjqB-Lgtmupmjibx3yA8NHuK3U1GLHTr1-L5z5Nq29p2PQuWsEj-CPrbDiYcA77ht8OF8N2n6jOWhpkxx8zFgXkiij-9vQcVruo/s1600/Goodman+040.JPG)

  
 It doesn't take much effort to spot sherds of pottery. There are many samples displayed on rocks where it is easy to compare the different styles of pottery and the variety of designs they were painted with. The sherds might be the most redeeming aspect of Goodman Point for the layman visitor to enjoy. And, to be enjoyed by everyone that visits they need to be left where they are.  
  

[![Image 19](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhWZrst9zvnAwLGKDpixZ1tB5PTHRz69reCMXAQBEoIROBtqUbq_wEPDxGhgnuEEzISPpWq9y2v1Uqd9AB5R-yM44tgxHq3278_3V9QgrepGq4gJaTarMJ_L2-305gKtYO9-MLQiTIdPEg/s400/Goodman+043.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhWZrst9zvnAwLGKDpixZ1tB5PTHRz69reCMXAQBEoIROBtqUbq_wEPDxGhgnuEEzISPpWq9y2v1Uqd9AB5R-yM44tgxHq3278_3V9QgrepGq4gJaTarMJ_L2-305gKtYO9-MLQiTIdPEg/s1600/Goodman+043.JPG)

  
 If you look at this picture carefully you can make out a square depression in the ground that is several inches deep. This could possibly be the remnants of a 'waffle garden'. The farming technique of making a depression in the ground divided with small interior walls, which resembles a waffle, was used to contain moisture around the plants.  
  

[![Image 20](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhIzozT6oo_lVF2Wz8HE7bU7-7hOs4hMk-Hc66FYffZxbsFoWWLprjQdCTeicS7XlzLJtq_EkyBOTYJwZAlGaV_znO4VoeKTq9oID1_qL-HsBbYOqJuAy-vXafclyC41F0nck6Rk8mEiAg/s400/Goodman+050.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhIzozT6oo_lVF2Wz8HE7bU7-7hOs4hMk-Hc66FYffZxbsFoWWLprjQdCTeicS7XlzLJtq_EkyBOTYJwZAlGaV_znO4VoeKTq9oID1_qL-HsBbYOqJuAy-vXafclyC41F0nck6Rk8mEiAg/s1600/Goodman+050.JPG)

  
 As long as you aren't expecting to see standing walls and the remarkable masonry and skilled construction that are seen at the other Hovenweep sites you won't be disappointed with Goodman Point. This location is only a short distance from the Sand Canyon Pueblo which is a little further to the west. The two sites are similar enough that they tend to compliment each other. If you would like to see it for yourself then all you have to do is 'Take a hike'.  
  

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CMMhtU6ugRc)
