![Image 6: Basket Makers](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/BasketMaker-300x297.jpg)
Basket Makers.

Later, Basketmaker III people added beans, an essential protein source, to their crops, began making pottery, and hunted with the bow and arrow. Clusters of small family farms formed the first settled communities across the landscape. About 1,300 years ago, warmer, drier weather during the Pueblo I period prompted many families to relocate to higher elevations such as the Dolores River Valley. These people built many villages, and cultural practices shifted over time from hunting and gathering to farming.

By about 750 AD, the[Ancestral Puebloans](link_93) occupied a widespread region that encompassed the Canyons of the Ancients and much of southwestern Colorado.Their year-round villages began as clustered pit houses. Over time, these ancestors of the modern-day [Pueblo Indians](link_94) developed larger masonry homes with connecting walls above ground. Some of these homes were built at canyon heads where a spring supplied water. Other homes were cliff dwellings.

At the end of this period, severe drought drove many people from the region. However, farmers resettled the area during the more favorable climate of the Pueblo II period beginning about 920 AD. As the wild game became depleted, families depended on their crops, and around 1100 AD, domesticated turkeys became an important food source. Soon, communities dotted the landscape in greater numbers than ever before, and during the early Pueblo III period, the population increased substantially around 1170.

In time, factors such as population growth, soil exhaustion, and changing weather compromised the area’s natural resources. In about 1276 AD, a severe, long-term drought began, resulting in poor or failed corn crops. As elk and deer became scarce, the people hunted rabbits, rodents, birds, and even carnivores. Some villagers migrated shortly after the drought began; others remained, attempting to endure the harsh conditions. Sometime after 1277 AD, Sand Canyon Pueblo suffered a devastating attack, possibly by other Pueblo people competing for the meager resources. Many residents were killed, and soon after, the survivors migrated away from the region. By about 1300 AD, these Pueblo ancestors had migrated to[New Mexico’s](link_95)Rio Grande Valley or farther west to where the[Acoma](link_96),[Laguna](link_97),[Zuni](link_98), and[Hopi](link_99) peoples live today.

![Image 7: Ancestral Puebloans](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/AncientPuebloans.jpg)
Ancestral Puebloans

Soon after the Ancestral Puebloans left the monument area, the nomadic [Ute](link_100) and [Navajo](link_101) exploited the natural diversity of the variable topography by moving to lower areas, including the monument’s mesas and canyons, during the cooler seasons. A small number of forked stick hogans, brush shelters, and wickiups are the most obvious remnants of this period of occupation.

Spanish Conquistadors reached northern New Mexico, where they settled in the 16th century. They introduced items for trade, such as guns and horses; new, deadly diseases; and cultural influences in the form of religion, language, and forms of government.

Ute communities were well established in western Colorado when the Spanish first explored the region in the late 1700s. Archaeological evidence indicates that the Ute ancestors arrived in western Colorado centuries earlier. Both Ute and Hopi oral histories say that Ute and Ancestral Pueblo people lived in the region at the same time. Historically, the Navajo people were based on the south side of the San Juan River, and the Ute groups on the north side. Scholars debate the exact timing of the Navajo’s arrival in the American Southwest, but they were likely in southwestern Colorado by the early 1500s. The Ute and Navajo people also used the Monument’s mesas and canyons for hunting and gathering. Remains of hogan, brush shelters, and wickiups tell their story. Today, many descendant peoples still live in or near their ancestors’ homelands.

[![Image 8: Spanish Conquistadors](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/Spanishconquistador-249x300.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/Spanishconquistador.jpg)
Spanish Conquistadors

In July 1776, a party of Spanish explorers — [Father Silvestre Velez de Escalante](link_102) with his superior Francisco Dominguez and eight others — set out from Santa Fe, New Mexico, to find a safe route to California and avoid the Mohave Desert and the Grand Canyon. After several weeks, they camped by a river called El Rio de Nuestra Señora de Los Dolores (The River of Our Lady of Sorrows). Father Escalante found the remains of a village overlooking the river and remarked in his journal that it resembled the living Pueblo villages of New Mexico. As the first archaeological site record in present-day Colorado, it was later named Escalante Pueblo. The Dominguez Pueblo was excavated and named 200 years later.

# The Treacherous Raton Pass on the Santa Fe Trail

[![Image 2: Raton Pass between Colorado and New Mexico](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/RatonPassPostcard.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/RatonPassPostcard.jpg)
Raton Pass between Colorado and New Mexico.

At the border of present-day [New Mexico](link_91) and [Colorado](link_92), Raton Pass was one of the most important yet treacherous segments of the [Mountain](link_100)[Branch](link_100) of the [Santa Fe Trail](link_93). The pass cut through the snow-capped Sangre de Cristo Mountains, allowing wagons access to the vast western territory.

When Spain controlled the southwestern United States, the Spanish officially banned international trade of all kinds. After Mexico gained its independence from Spain in 1821, the Mexicans lifted the ban and opened the area to commercial and cultural exchange. The Santa Fe Trail, which spanned 1,200 miles from[Franklin](link_94),[Missouri,](link_95)to[Santa Fe](link_96), New Mexico, passing through deserts, mountains, and forests, became the primary means of transportation to and from the area.

Shorter routes were eventually developed, but Raton Pass, which crossed safer terrain, remained in use. The pass was critical in [General Stephen Watts Kearny’s](link_97) conquest of Santa Fe and the eventual American annexation of New Mexico in 1846.

As the first significant passage West through the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, the Raton Pass National Historic Landmark celebrates the development of American trade, cultural interaction, and westward expansion.

[![Image 3: Sangre de Cristo Range, courtesy Wikipedia](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Sangre-de-Cristo-RangeWiki-300x201.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Sangre-de-Cristo-RangeWiki.jpg)
Sangre de Cristo Range, courtesy Wikipedia.

When Mexico opened its borders to trade with the United States in 1821, a great commercial, military, and emigrant trail was born. However, the Sangre de Cristo Mountains loomed huge and daunting between the western edge of the United States in Missouri and the bustling Mexican center of commerce, Santa Fe. Early [explorers, trappers](link_23), and [American Indian](link_32) peoples had previously discovered various paths through the treacherous mountains, but before 1821, no covered wagons had made the journey.

In June 1821, [William Becknell](link_98), a horse and mule trader, traveled west from Franklin, Missouri, with a wagon and four companions. History has written for years that Becknell would be the first of many to travel via wagon through the narrow, torturous Raton Pass. However, that portion of his journey has been called into question after the discovery of the diary of Pedro Ignacio Gallego in 1993. Mexican Captain Gallego and his 400 men met Becknell on his first journey to Santa Fe. His writings and Becknell’s journal describing the landscape show more evidence that he and his men probably misidentified the Canadian River and instead crossed another river or stream. Researchers now say evidence points to a location between the Arkansas River and Puertocito Piedra Lumbre in Kearny Gap, south of present-day [Las Vegas](link_99), New Mexico.

[![Image 4: Santa Fe Trail near "The Caches" in Ford County, Kansas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/FordCountySoulesDitchSantaFeTrail-300x200.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/FordCountySoulesDitchSantaFeTrail.jpg)
Santa Fe Trail near “The Caches” in Ford County, Kansas

Soon, however, a new branch of the Santa Fe Trail developed. The so-called “[Cimarron Route](link_100)” was not only 100 miles shorter but cut across the relatively flat grasslands and deserts of present-day [Kansas](link_101) and [Oklahoma](link_102) instead of through the mountains. Although the openness of the Cimarron Route led to frequent raids from American Indian tribes and provided far less water, the dangers of the shorter path were still preferable to travel. Between the 1820s and early 1840s, most wagon traffic along the Santa Fe Trail opted to take the Cimarron Route.

In 1846, the pass again played a significant role in history. Tensions were running high between the United States and Mexico over land disputes in [Texas](link_103), which included what is now the State of New Mexico. Both countries laid claim to the land, and Mexico disputed the United States’ decision to annex Texas in 1845. President James Polk declared war on Mexico in 1846 and sent American forces into the territory. [General Stephen Watts Kearny](link_97) set out with his famed 1,600-man “Army of the West” along the [Santa Fe Trail](link_104).

[![Image 5: The Army of the West Travels into New Mexico](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/ArmyoftheWest-300x171.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/ArmyoftheWest.jpg)
The Army of the West Travels into New Mexico.

Although the Mountain Branch and the Raton Pass were dangerous, Kearny chose to head west through the mountains rather than take the Cimarron Route. The steep, narrow Raton Pass afforded better protection from invading forces and an ample water supply, unlike the dry desert along much of the Cimarron Route. Before Kearny and his men arrived, a team of workers set out along the trail to make passage more accessible, including clearing rocks and debris from the notorious Raton Pass. Despite their efforts, Kearny’s journey was still fraught with difficulty. Many wagons were destroyed, and supplies had to be left behind.

Weakened, the men emerged from the Raton Pass and expected to meet resistance from Mexican forces that the provincial governor Manuel Armijo sent. They instead found the valley abandoned. Kearny’s takeover of Santa Fe thus was swift. Without a struggle, the United States laid claim to the territory.

The Mountain Branch was again mostly abandoned after Kearny’s army used it because traders and travelers still preferred the shorter, easier route. However, the Raton Pass was used once again after the outbreak of the [Civil War](link_61) in 1860. The vulnerability of the Cimarron Branch was recognized as concerns heightened around [Confederate](link_105) raids. The Santa Fe Trail saw heavy use as a [Union](link_106) Army supply route west, and the narrow, protected Raton Pass was easy to guard. The pass continued to serve Union troops through 1865.

[![Image 6: Ox team in Raton Mountains between Trinidad and Raton](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Ox-team-in-Raton-Mountains-between-Trinidad-and-RatonAbt1915-300-300x204.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Ox-team-in-Raton-Mountains-between-Trinidad-and-RatonAbt1915-300.jpg)
Ox team in Raton Mountains between Trinidad and Raton.

Raton Pass became part of a toll road that entrepreneur[Richens L. Wootton](link_107) built and managed for several years after the war. Beginning in 1866, the most treacherous part of the Santa Fe Trail was heavily altered by grading, blasting, bridge building, and clearing. The formerly difficult Raton Pass was made passable in all seasons for horses, wagons, and stagecoaches alike. # The Treacherous Raton Pass on the Santa Fe Trail

[![Image 2: Raton Pass between Colorado and New Mexico](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/RatonPassPostcard.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/RatonPassPostcard.jpg)
Raton Pass between Colorado and New Mexico.

At the border of present-day [New Mexico](link_91) and [Colorado](link_92), Raton Pass was one of the most important yet treacherous segments of the [Mountain](link_100)[Branch](link_100) of the [Santa Fe Trail](link_93). The pass cut through the snow-capped Sangre de Cristo Mountains, allowing wagons access to the vast western territory.

When Spain controlled the southwestern United States, the Spanish officially banned international trade of all kinds. After Mexico gained its independence from Spain in 1821, the Mexicans lifted the ban and opened the area to commercial and cultural exchange. The Santa Fe Trail, which spanned 1,200 miles from[Franklin](link_94),[Missouri,](link_95)to[Santa Fe](link_96), New Mexico, passing through deserts, mountains, and forests, became the primary means of transportation to and from the area.

Shorter routes were eventually developed, but Raton Pass, which crossed safer terrain, remained in use. The pass was critical in [General Stephen Watts Kearny’s](link_97) conquest of Santa Fe and the eventual American annexation of New Mexico in 1846.

As the first significant passage West through the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, the Raton Pass National Historic Landmark celebrates the development of American trade, cultural interaction, and westward expansion.

[![Image 3: Sangre de Cristo Range, courtesy Wikipedia](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Sangre-de-Cristo-RangeWiki-300x201.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Sangre-de-Cristo-RangeWiki.jpg)
Sangre de Cristo Range, courtesy Wikipedia.

When Mexico opened its borders to trade with the United States in 1821, a great commercial, military, and emigrant trail was born. However, the Sangre de Cristo Mountains loomed huge and daunting between the western edge of the United States in Missouri and the bustling Mexican center of commerce, Santa Fe. Early [explorers, trappers](link_23), and [American Indian](link_32) peoples had previously discovered various paths through the treacherous mountains, but before 1821, no covered wagons had made the journey.

In June 1821, [William Becknell](link_98), a horse and mule trader, traveled west from Franklin, Missouri, with a wagon and four companions. History has written for years that Becknell would be the first of many to travel via wagon through the narrow, torturous Raton Pass. However, that portion of his journey has been called into question after the discovery of the diary of Pedro Ignacio Gallego in 1993. Mexican Captain Gallego and his 400 men met Becknell on his first journey to Santa Fe. His writings and Becknell’s journal describing the landscape show more evidence that he and his men probably misidentified the Canadian River and instead crossed another river or stream. Researchers now say evidence points to a location between the Arkansas River and Puertocito Piedra Lumbre in Kearny Gap, south of present-day [Las Vegas](link_99), New Mexico.

[![Image 4: Santa Fe Trail near "The Caches" in Ford County, Kansas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/FordCountySoulesDitchSantaFeTrail-300x200.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/FordCountySoulesDitchSantaFeTrail.jpg)
Santa Fe Trail near “The Caches” in Ford County, Kansas

Soon, however, a new branch of the Santa Fe Trail developed. The so-called “[Cimarron Route](link_100)” was not only 100 miles shorter but cut across the relatively flat grasslands and deserts of present-day [Kansas](link_101) and [Oklahoma](link_102) instead of through the mountains. Although the openness of the Cimarron Route led to frequent raids from American Indian tribes and provided far less water, the dangers of the shorter path were still preferable to travel. Between the 1820s and early 1840s, most wagon traffic along the Santa Fe Trail opted to take the Cimarron Route.

In 1846, the pass again played a significant role in history. Tensions were running high between the United States and Mexico over land disputes in [Texas](link_103), which included what is now the State of New Mexico. Both countries laid claim to the land, and Mexico disputed the United States’ decision to annex Texas in 1845. President James Polk declared war on Mexico in 1846 and sent American forces into the territory. [General Stephen Watts Kearny](link_97) set out with his famed 1,600-man “Army of the West” along the [Santa Fe Trail](link_104).

[![Image 5: The Army of the West Travels into New Mexico](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/ArmyoftheWest-300x171.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/ArmyoftheWest.jpg)
The Army of the West Travels into New Mexico.

Although the Mountain Branch and the Raton Pass were dangerous, Kearny chose to head west through the mountains rather than take the Cimarron Route. The steep, narrow Raton Pass afforded better protection from invading forces and an ample water supply, unlike the dry desert along much of the Cimarron Route. Before Kearny and his men arrived, a team of workers set out along the trail to make passage more accessible, including clearing rocks and debris from the notorious Raton Pass. Despite their efforts, Kearny’s journey was still fraught with difficulty. Many wagons were destroyed, and supplies had to be left behind.

Weakened, the men emerged from the Raton Pass and expected to meet resistance from Mexican forces that the provincial governor Manuel Armijo sent. They instead found the valley abandoned. Kearny’s takeover of Santa Fe thus was swift. Without a struggle, the United States laid claim to the territory.

The Mountain Branch was again mostly abandoned after Kearny’s army used it because traders and travelers still preferred the shorter, easier route. However, the Raton Pass was used once again after the outbreak of the [Civil War](link_61) in 1860. The vulnerability of the Cimarron Branch was recognized as concerns heightened around [Confederate](link_105) raids. The Santa Fe Trail saw heavy use as a [Union](link_106) Army supply route west, and the narrow, protected Raton Pass was easy to guard. The pass continued to serve Union troops through 1865.

[![Image 6: Ox team in Raton Mountains between Trinidad and Raton](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Ox-team-in-Raton-Mountains-between-Trinidad-and-RatonAbt1915-300-300x204.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Ox-team-in-Raton-Mountains-between-Trinidad-and-RatonAbt1915-300.jpg)
Ox team in Raton Mountains between Trinidad and Raton.

Raton Pass became part of a toll road that entrepreneur[Richens L. Wootton](link_107) built and managed for several years after the war. Beginning in 1866, the most treacherous part of the Santa Fe Trail was heavily altered by grading, blasting, bridge building, and clearing. The formerly difficult Raton Pass was made passable in all seasons for horses, wagons, and stagecoaches alike. # Muse, AI that gets it done for you Muse[Video 1](https://l.facebook.com/videos/avatars/hatch_connecting.mp4)[Video 2](https://l.facebook.com/videos/avatars/hatch_working.mp4), AI that gets it done for you sorts your email books reservations shops for you saves you money manages calendars builds fitness plans gets it done for you sorts your email![Image 2](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/icon-envelope.webp)books reservations![Image 3](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/icon-airplane.webp)shops for you![Image 4](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/icon-cart.webp)saves you money![Image 5](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/icon-piggybank.webp)manages calendars![Image 6](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/icon-calendar.webp)builds fitness plans![Image 7](https://l.facebook.com/images/landing/icons/b-01.webp)gets it done for you

## Built around your whole life

Give Muse a goal or task and it handles the rest, from saving money and improving your health to smart shopping and helping you strengthen your relationships.

[Video 3](https://scontent.xx.fbcdn.net/o1/v/t6/f2/m421/AQPvdntV2G814fVexG62mHy9MLAFz-IUx2_276pwlTOScjlG7403bT1NxrxgW2yToPZR5BOsHoRWgC3EQGGX.mp4?_nc_sid=9c7e41&_nc_ht=scontent.xx.fbcdn.net&ccb=17-1&_nc_gid=fs7UBOzWuLyIUXtQ26sofw&edm=AIlawRcEAAAA&_nc_zt=28&oh=00_AQMjmzGtnikkw9KAQavJwejMjDN0jQ3unrwWncs0GlDIdg&oe=6AEAC82E#t=1)

### Every Muse user shares their own computer in the cloud with their Muse.

Muse Secure VM is a persistent, isolated Linux computer with a full browser that you and your agent can use to complete tasks, allowing you to intervene at any point. It's your computer and your browser, with the storage, CPU, and memory to handle real work.

### Designed around the way you already communicate

# Byways & Historic Trails – Great Drives in America

[![Image 2: Skyline Drive, Canon City, Colorado by Kathy Alexander.](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/SkylineDrive-4-800.jpg)](https://photos.legendsofamerica.com/centralcolorado/eb6b11d45)
Skyline Drive, Canon City, Colorado, by Kathy Alexander.

There are wonderful drives across America, including National Scenic Byways, Back Country Byways, and State Scenic Byways. The United States Department of Transportation recognizes a National Scenic Byway for one of the six “intrinsic qualities”: archeological, cultural, historical, natural, recreational, and scenic. The most scenic byways are designated All-American Roads, which must meet two of the six intrinsic qualities. Currently, there are 120 National Scenic Byways and 31 All-American Roads. In addition, individual states designate hundreds more, and the Bureau of Land Management designates scenic drives and back-country byways.

# Branches of the Santa Fe Trail

![Image 2: Branches of the Santa Fe Trail](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/santafetrailmapbranches.jpg)

Branches of the Santa Fe Trail.

The historic[Santa Fe Trail](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-santafetrail/)trade route from[Missouri](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/missouri/)through[Kansas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/kansas/)to[Santa Fe](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-santafe/),[New Mexico](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/new-mexico/), had two primary branches:the [Cimarron Route](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-santafetrailroutes/#cimarron) and the [Mountain Route](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-santafetrailroutes/#mountain). During the trail’s heyday, both were well traveled for different reasons.

[![Image 3: William Becknell blazes the Santa Fe Trail.](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/WilliamBecknell_color-300x165.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/WilliamBecknell_color.jpg)
William Becknell blazes the Santa Fe Trail.

When[William Becknell](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-williambecknell/) and his companions first blazed the Santa Fe Trail in 1821, they followed the north bank of the[Arkansas River](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/arkansas-river/), the international boundary between the United States and Mexico. After passing through Kansas and into eastern [Colorado](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/colorado/), they crossed the Arkansas River near its confluence with New Mexico. Historians have recorded that they then traveled over [Raton Pass](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-ratonpass/) before making their way to Santa Fe, New Mexico. This route would become known as the Mountain Route of the Santa Fe Trail. That portion of the journey has been called into question following the discovery of Pedro Ignacio Gallego’s diary in 1993. Mexican Captain Gallego and his 400 men met Becknell on his first journey to Santa Fe. His writings and Becknell’s journal describing the landscape provide further evidence that he and his men likely misidentified the Canadian River and instead crossed another river or stream. Researchers now say evidence points to a location between the Arkansas River and Puertocito Piedra Lumbre in Kearny Gap, south of present-day [Las Vegas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-lasvegas/), New Mexico. Later, wagon trains would take the known Mountain Route.

However, the Becknell party took another route home to Missouri on their return. This path extended into eastern New Mexico,[Oklahoma,](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/oklahoma/)and[Kansas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/kansas/), where it crossed the Arkansas River back into the United States. This route became known as the Cimarron Route or the Cimarron Cutoff.

Raton Pass, New Mexico.

Becknell’s first trip was so successful that he and 22 men made a second trip in 1822. Loading three prairie schooners with goods, they decided to travel the Cimarron Route again, knowing their wagons couldn’t cross the mountains.

Though there were various paths and trails at different times throughout the history of the Santa Fe Trail, the journey was essentially the same until travelers reached western Kansas, in the area of present-day Cimarron, where the trail divided into two alternative routes — the Mountain Branch, following the Arkansas River further west to the site of Bent’s Fort, Colorado, south through Raton Pass into New Mexico; and the Cimarron Cutoff which, made a more direct diagonal route southwest through Oklahoma. The two paths rejoined in present-day Watrous, New Mexico, continuing southward to Santa Fe.

**Cimarron Route**:

[![Image 5: The Plains of Southwest Kansas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/SWKansasAntelope-300-300x199.jpg)](https://photos.legendsofamerica.com/stanton-county/e1e4207a2)
The Plains of Southwest Kansas by Kathy Alexander.

The Cimarron Route, also known as the Cimarron Cutoff and Cimarron Crossing, was the most favored in the earliest days of the Santa Fe Trail, even though the path was known for its water scarcity. This route was shorter by about 100 miles, shortened the traveling time by ten days, and was more suited to wagon travel.

The [Cimarron River](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/cimarron-river/), which gives the route its name, flows through southwestern Kansas and northeastern [Oklahoma](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/oklahoma/). Depending upon where the travelers left the Arkansas River, it was a journey of fifty or more miles to reach the Cimarron River. With poor grass and scant water, the sandy Cimarron River, often dry, defined the landscape as one of the riskiest sections of the entire Trail. This much-dreaded, waterless area was often called the Cimarron Desert, Waterscape, and, by Mexicans, the Jornada del Muerte, or Journey of Death.

[![Image 6: Wagon Bed Spring Box on the Santa Fe Trail in Grant County, Kansas by Kathy Alexander.](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/WagonBedSpringsBox-300.jpg)](https://photos.legendsofamerica.com/ks-grantcounty/e1a388abe)
Wagon Bed Spring Box on the Santa Fe Trail in Grant County, Kansas, by Kathy Alexander.

The trail cut southwest across the Cimarron River valley near [Ulysses](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/ks-ulysses/), Kansas, before finding its first reliable water supply since leaving the Arkansas River. Lower Cimarron Spring, also known as [Lower Springs](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wagon-bed-spring-kansas/) and [Wagon Bed Springs](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wagon-bed-spring-kansas/), is on the north bank of the Cimarron River, approximately 11 miles south and 1.5 miles west of Ulysses, about two miles west of the markers on U.S. Highway 25 south of the Cimarron River bridge. Travelers breathed a sigh of relief upon finding Lower Spring, as it meant they had survived. However, that would not be the case for all travelers, as near here, the famous hunter, trapper, and explorer[Jedediah Strong Smith](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-jedediahsmith/) would lose his life. In 1831, Smith’s well-equipped wagon train became lost in the maze of buffalo trails. Seeking water for the dying animals and suffering men, Smith finally found the Cimarron River but was killed by the [Comanche](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/na-comanche/)[Indians](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/native-americans/) near Wagon Bed Springs. His body was never recovered.

[![Image 7: Cimarron National Grasslands, Kansas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/CimarronNatGrassland-300-300x201.jpg)](https://photos.legendsofamerica.com/moresouthwestkansas/h6cfddf00#h6cfddf00)
Cimarron National Grasslands, Kansas, by Kathy Alexander.

The path then continued into [Morton County](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/ks-santafetrailhsco/#morton-county), past Point of Rocks, and through the Cimarron National Grasslands, which appear very much as they did during the Santa Fe Trail’s heydays. Following the Cimarron River, the trail moved south into present-day Cimarron County, Oklahoma, where it crossed the river at Willowbar Crossing and continued southwest to Cold Springs. There, Autograph Rock (on private land) still displays the names that scores of travelers carved into the ledges at the springs. The trail then passed by [Camp Nichols](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/camp-nichols-oklahoma/), a short-lived military post established by [Christopher “Kit” Carson](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-kitcarson/) in 1865. The trail exited Oklahoma and entered Union County, New Mexico. Subsequently, the trail passed several historic sites and landmarks, including [Rabbit Ears Mountain](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-cimarronroute/#Rabbit%20Ears), [McNee’s Crossing](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-cimarronroute/#McNees%20Crossing), and [Wagon Mound](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-cimarronroute/#Wagon%20Mound), before joining the northern branch

# Durango residents decry Trump cuts to national monuments

U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd makes low-profile trip through Southwest Colorado

[Christian Burney](https://www.durangoherald.com/author/christian-burney/)

Herald Staff Writer

Saturday, Sep 12, 2026 3:11 PM MT

Updated Saturday, Sep 12, 2026 3:26 PM MT

SHARE[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.durangoherald.com%2Farticles%2Fnews%2Fdurango-residents-decry-trump-cuts-to-national-monuments%2F)[](mailto:?subject=Durango%20residents%20decry%20Trump%20cuts%20to%20national%20monuments&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.durangoherald.com%2Farticles%2Fnews%2Fdurango-residents-decry-trump-cuts-to-national-monuments%2F)

SHARE[Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.durangoherald.com%2Farticles%2Fnews%2Fdurango-residents-decry-trump-cuts-to-national-monuments%2F)[Email](mailto:?subject=Durango%20residents%20decry%20Trump%20cuts%20to%20national%20monuments&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.durangoherald.com%2Farticles%2Fnews%2Fdurango-residents-decry-trump-cuts-to-national-monuments%2F)Copy Link

![Image 4: Concerned citizens gather on Camino del Rio in front of the Double Tree Hotel on Friday waving signs advocating for the preservation of national parks; others denounced the Trump administration and U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd over their public lands policies. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)](https://imengine.public.prod.dur.navigacloud.com/?uuid=749ee912-9379-514c-a58a-68b395b02cfc&function=cover&type=preview&source=false&width=2000)

Concerned citizens gather on Camino del Rio in front of the Double Tree Hotel on Friday waving signs advocating for the preservation of national parks; others denounced the Trump administration and U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd over their public lands policies. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)Jerry McBride

Concerns about federal public lands policy drew protesters to the sidewalks along Camino del Rio outside the DoubleTree Hotel by Hilton in Durango on Friday where they demonstrated against the Trump administration and U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Conservation advocates clutched protest signs and waved them at passing drivers, who sometimes honked in support. Some signs displayed messages advocating for the preservation of national parks; others denounced the Trump administration and U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd.

![Image 5: Jacquelyn Kovach with her sign on Camino del Rio in front of the DoubleTree Hotel on Friday with a group of about 50 people waving signs advocating for the preservation of national parks; others denounced the Trump administration and U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)](https://imengine.public.prod.dur.navigacloud.com/?uuid=c4f11c37-77fc-5f73-a515-61a08caebc80&function=cover&type=preview&source=false&width=2000)

Jacquelyn Kovach with her sign on Camino del Rio in front of the DoubleTree Hotel on Friday with a group of about 50 people waving signs advocating for the preservation of national parks; others denounced the Trump administration and U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)Jerry McBride

One issue many protesters raised was the Trump administration’s move in July to [cut national monument protections on nearly 3 million acres, or about 91%, of land](https://www.sltrib.com/news/environment/2026/07/13/president-trump-shrinks-bears-ears/) at Grand Staircase-Escalante and Bears Ears national monuments in Utah, as reported by _The Salt Lake Tribune_.

Protesters also criticized what they described as Hurd’s unwillingness to listen to his constituents.

“We’re here because Rep. Hurd and the (Congressional Western Caucus) is in Mesa Verde today, and they’re having a reception here,” said Debra Meyers of Indivisible Durango.

The Congressional Western Caucus, of which Hurd serves as a vice chair, was scheduled to be in the Durango area Friday and Saturday, [according to a September calendar](https://westerncaucus.house.gov/uploadedfiles/cwc_september_calendar.pdf) obtained by _The Durango_ _Herald_, although the field trip appeared to have a low profile.

![Image 6: Concerned citizens gather on Camino del Rio in front of the Double Tree Hotel on Friday waving signs advocating for the preservation of national parks; others denounced the Trump administration and U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd for their public lands policies. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)](https://imengine.public.prod.dur.navigacloud.com/?uuid=52bc5bef-3e80-51dc-b936-e781096bc76a&function=cover&type=preview&source=false&width=2000)

Concerned citizens gather on Camino del Rio in front of the Double Tree Hotel on Friday waving signs advocating for the preservation of national parks; others denounced the Trump administration and U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd for their public lands policies. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)Jerry McBride

The caucus did not provide much information about the field trip on its September calendar, which simply says “Southern Colorado Field Tour” scheduled for Friday and Saturday in Durango.

A [draft itinerary](https://westerncaucus.house.gov/uploadedfiles/_draft_itinerary_southern_colorado_field_tour_.pdf) obtained by the _Herald_ showed the field trip involved tours of wildfire scars, Mesa Verde National Park and the Southern Ute Reservation; a roundtable with the Southern Ute Growth Fund; a presentation from the Southern Ute Indian Tribe; and receptions Friday and Saturday evenings in Durango and the reservation, respectively.

The _Herald_ attempted to reach Nick Bayer, Hurd’s chief of staff, and the Congressional Western Caucus on Saturday to inquire about the field trip and to allow Hurd to respond to protesters but was unsuccessful.

![Image 7: Concerned citizens gather on Camino del Rio in front of the Double Tree Hotel on Friday waving signs advocating for the preservation of national parks; others denounced the Trump administration and U.S. Rep. # Thousands of sheep fill Buck Highway for Bayfield Heritage Day

Celebrating town’s history helps to keep culture alive with population growth

[Jane Rooney](https://www.durangoherald.com/author/jane-rooney/)

Herald Staff Writer

Sunday, Sep 27, 2026 5:00 AM MT

SHARE[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.durangoherald.com%2Farticles%2Fnews%2Fthousands-of-sheep-fill-buck-highway-for-bayfield-heritage-day%2F)[](mailto:?subject=Thousands%20of%20sheep%20fill%20Buck%20Highway%20for%20Bayfield%20Heritage%20Day&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.durangoherald.com%2Farticles%2Fnews%2Fthousands-of-sheep-fill-buck-highway-for-bayfield-heritage-day%2F)

SHARE[Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.durangoherald.com%2Farticles%2Fnews%2Fthousands-of-sheep-fill-buck-highway-for-bayfield-heritage-day%2F)[Email](mailto:?subject=Thousands%20of%20sheep%20fill%20Buck%20Highway%20for%20Bayfield%20Heritage%20Day&body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.durangoherald.com%2Farticles%2Fnews%2Fthousands-of-sheep-fill-buck-highway-for-bayfield-heritage-day%2F)Copy Link

![Image 4: People line up along Buck Highway (County Road 521) to watch La Plata County rancher and former Rep. J. Paul Brown move his sheep through Bayfield on Saturday during the Bayfield Heritage Day and Sheep Trailing annual event. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)](https://imengine.public.prod.dur.navigacloud.com/?uuid=7bc6f4a4-eeba-5872-8dd6-022e93bf7594&function=cover&type=preview&source=false&width=2000)

People line up along Buck Highway (County Road 521) to watch La Plata County rancher and former Rep. J. Paul Brown move his sheep through Bayfield on Saturday during the Bayfield Heritage Day and Sheep Trailing annual event. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)Jerry McBride

Sheep flowed down Buck Highway (County Road 521) in Bayfield like a raging river, contained by the crowd lining the sidewalks and the steeper side of the highway.

Some sheep still spilled up the hill, only to be wrangled back by herders and their dogs.

For Bayfield Heritage Day, a flock of about 2,000 sheep from former Rep. J. Paul Brown’s herd was brought down from the mountains by Vallecito onto Buck Highway in Bayfield, which will then will move onto winter pastures, said Anne Schrier, a volunteer with the Pine River Valley Heritage Society.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WFh5KAKXlME)

Before the sheep arrived, children stepped into the street, trying to get the first peek of the flock. Volunteers and parents herded the children back to the sidewalk as they eagerly waited for the best view of the woolen creatures.

This year, the Bayfield Heritage Day parade included the town’s homecoming parade, which was delayed because of rainy weather.

As Bayfield grows, organizers said this event celebrates the community’s agricultural roots for longtime residents and helps newcomers understand the town’s culture, said Marian Tone, an organizer for Bayfield Heritage Day.

![Image 5: La Plata County rancher and former Rep. J Paul Brown moves his sheep through Bayfield on Saturday during the annual Bayfield Heritage Day and Sheep Trailing. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)](https://imengine.public.prod.dur.navigacloud.com/?uuid=f130294c-91b2-5fa5-9757-747f06191f57&function=cover&type=preview&source=false&width=2000)

La Plata County rancher and former Rep. J Paul Brown moves his sheep through Bayfield on Saturday during the annual Bayfield Heritage Day and Sheep Trailing. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)Jerry McBride

“It shows the new people what our history is,” Chelsea Rey Ransford, a fifth-generation Bayfield resident said. “It’s a very delicate balance because you either have new people coming in, and sometimes they’ll bring their ideas, but this shows them in a way what Bayfield is all about, what it has always been- the heart of the Pine River Valley.”

The Bayfield Heritage Day celebration has taken place every year since 2000, with the exception of the COVID-19 pandemic, Tone said. For the first time, this year’s event featured a historic walking tour in which volunteers stood outside notable buildings and recounted its history.

The idea for the historic walking tours originated from the Wolverine Wonders Homeschool Co-op curriculum, Ransford said.

![Image 6: La Plata County rancher and former Rep. J. Paul Brown moves his sheep through Bayfield on Saturday during the annual Bayfield Heritage Day and Sheep Trailing. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)](https://imengine.public.prod.dur.navigacloud.com/?uuid=42116811-dd7a-53fd-8ef8-c025dde826e3&function=cover&type=preview&source=false&width=2000)

La Plata County rancher and former Rep. J. Paul Brown moves his sheep through Bayfield on Saturday during the annual Bayfield Heritage Day and Sheep Trailing. (Jerry McBride/Durango Herald)Jerry McBride

Melissa Strand, a volunteer for the historic walking tours, recounted the history of the Presbyterian Church, which is the oldest church in Bayfield. She wore an outfit representing a traditional prairie woman.

The church broke ground in April 1898, with land donated by William Bay, one of the founders of Bayfield, Strand said.

She said she hopes more young people get involved with preserving the town’s history as a farm and ranch community. Events like Heritage Day help provide exposure to the town’s history and pique people’s interest.

The Tawnee family, who moved to Vallecito about six years ago from Southern California, were excited to see the sheep run and said it was their second time attending Bayfield Heritage Day.

Everly, 8, Indira, 10, and Esmehre, 7, said they liked watching the sheep run and listening to the noises they make.

# Three projects to mark Montelores Coalition’s first field season in Dolores, Montezuma counties

Group established in 2024 launches pilot restoration work

[Anna Watson](https://www.durangoherald.com/author/anna-watson/)

Journal Staff Writer

Thursday, Aug 6, 2026 5:00 AM MT

Updated Monday, Aug 10, 2026 4:10 PM MT

![Image 4: Members of Montelores Coalition participate in a cleanup in May co-hosted with the Dolores Watersheds Collaborative and the San Juan Mountains Association for Colorado Public Lands Day. Montelores Coalition is a regional partnership that works to balance conservation and recreation in Montezuma and Dolores counties. (Courtesy of Montelores Coalition)](https://imengine.public.prod.dur.navigacloud.com/?uuid=796d633d-f980-5b27-b953-454e46266cd7&function=cover&type=preview&source=false&width=2000)

Members of Montelores Coalition participate in a cleanup in May co-hosted with the Dolores Watersheds Collaborative and the San Juan Mountains Association for Colorado Public Lands Day. Montelores Coalition is a regional partnership that works to balance conservation and recreation in Montezuma and Dolores counties. (Courtesy of Montelores Coalition)

After roughly two years building partnerships and gathering local input, Montelores Coalition, a sustainable land and recreation coalition, is preparing to initiate field work.

The coalition announced three projects scheduled for mid-September through late October, marking its first season of visible restoration work for Montezuma and Dolores communities.

The projects are cleanup and trail improvements at Hawkins Preserve in Cortez, removing old fencing in Rico and continuing river restoration along the Mancos River in collaboration with Montezuma Land Conservancy.

Montelores Coalition was established in 2024 as part of Colorado Outdoor Regional Partnerships Initiative, a statewide program aiming to balance conservation and growing recreational strain on the land.

“Increased visitation to popular recreation areas, including Colorado state parks, have caused maintenance backlogs and management challenges,” reads Gov. Jared Polis’ 2020 executive order [B 008](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Ic5EWQz55rCQ58GmFeo-IhLT8b3DI3o1/view) establishing the initiative.

“We are at a critical juncture where we must act to ensure that our state remains a world-class outdoor destination while preserving our land, water, wildlife and quality of life,” the order continued.

Cara Gildar, executive director of Montelores Coalition, said the organization and work are valuable opportunities. The potential is two-fold, she added, allowing the group to proactively plan ahead while accounting for local priorities.

Other areas of the state experienced higher rates of tourism, particularly during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, that caused damage in outdoor spaces for which couldn’t sustain the influx of visitors, Gildar said.

“We’re in a really sweet spot where compared to the rest of the state, our visitation and recreation from locals is – and just our population is – a lot lower. So, we can direct how things unfold, which is a great place to be in,” she said.

Funding initially came from grants provided by Colorado Parks and Wildlife and now stems in part from the agency and Great Outdoors Colorado, which is supported through lottery proceeds. Last December, the state [awarded $300,000](https://cpw.state.co.us/news/12152025/governor-polis-colorado-parks-and-wildlife-and-great-outdoors-colorado-award-999) to Montelores Coalition, one of a total of 19 awards equaling $9.99 million awarded this grant cycle to regional partnerships.

Some of that funding supported finalizing the coalition’s [Outdoor Recreation and Conservation Plan](https://montelorescoalition.org/draftplan/), a major focus and process since the coalition has formed.

“It’s interesting doing this work because everyone in this community has really strong opinions about the landscape,” Gildar said. “But one thing that I see we all have in common is wanting to take care of it and wanting to preserve this rural and more wild experience.”

![Image 5: Cara Gildar, executive director of Montelores Coalition, said an executive order allowed communities to “self-select” into regions and then identify their own priorities. “The thing I think is really valuable about this opportunity is this isn’t a top-down state directive – it’s an opportunity.”  (Courtesy of Montelores Coalition)](https://imengine.public.prod.dur.navigacloud.com/?uuid=5a5be868-8ebc-5c13-a484-77249308da0d&function=cover&type=preview&source=false&width=2000)

Cara Gildar, executive director of Montelores Coalition, said an executive order allowed communities to “self-select” into regions and then identify their own priorities. “The thing I think is really valuable about this opportunity is this isn’t a top-down state directive – it’s an opportunity.” (Courtesy of Montelores Coalition)

A larger value identified in the plan is directing visitors to spaces that can accommodate them, such as more infrastructure, parking or restrooms.

# Colorado – The Centennial State

[![Image 2: Rocky Mountain reflection in one of the string of Alta Lakes outside Telluride, Colorado.](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/Alta-Lakes-outside-TellurideHighsmith-800.jpg)](https://photos.legendsofamerica.com/southerncolorado/e9b53eba2)
The Rocky Mountains outside Telluride, Colorado, by Carol Highsmith.

[![Image 3: Greetings from Colorado](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/cs-co102-300x233.jpg)](https://store.legendsofamerica.com/index.php?l=product_detail&p=86)
Greetings from Colorado Postcard. Available at Legends’ General Store.

Majestic peaks, lush valleys, a history rich with mining tales, the life and death of boomtowns, and rags-to-riches stories are the focus of Colorado Legends.

Tumbling down gold mines and virtually intact[ghost towns](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/ghost-towns/) dot the landscape, along with bustling cities filled with events and festivals. Colorado’s four national parks, 13 national forests, and 42 state parks offer ever-boundless adventure opportunities, including camping, fishing, hiking, sightseeing, and horseback riding.

In the Fall, the foliage of the mountains and valleys is absolutely breathtaking, and wildlife viewing opportunities are everywhere. In the winter, bring your skis and snowboards and enjoy the slopes of the beautiful [Rocky Mountains](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/ah-rockymountains/). You’re going to love it here!

Colorado offers much to experience; you won’t be disappointed. Enjoy your travels in Colorado, and welcome to the Centennial State.

Kathy R. Alexander  
 Owner/Editor

![Image 4: Colorado Flag](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Flag-CO.gif)The official state flag of Colorado was adopted on June 5, 1911. Andrew Carlisle Johnson designed it in 1911. The white in the flag symbolizes Colorado’s snow-capped mountains, the blue symbolizes clear blue skies, the red symbolizes the reddish soil, and the golden yellow represents the Sun. Attached to the flag is a cord of gold and silver intertwined with gold and silver tassels.

# Santa Fe Trail – Highway to the Southwest

[![Image 5: Army Train Crossing the Plains by Harper's Weekly, 1858.](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/ArmyTrainCrossingThePlainsApril241858HarpersWeeklyColor-800.jpg)](https://photos.legendsofamerica.com/militarypeople/e67c94d9e)
Army Train Crossing the Plains by _Harper’s Weekly_, 1858.

In 1821, the land beyond [Missouri](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/missouri/) was a vast uncharted region called home to great buffalo herds and unhappy [Indians](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/native-americans/), angered over the continual westward expansion of the white man. Before Mexico gained independence from Spain in 1821, the Spanish banned trade between [Santa Fe](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-santafe/) and the United States. After independence, Mexico encouraged trade. Though numerous dangers awaited him, [Captain William Becknell](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-williambecknell/) was determined to travel through waterless plains and warlike Indians to trade with the distant Mexicans in [New Mexico](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/new-mexico/).

[![Image 6: Santa Fe Trail Map](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/santafetrailmaplarge-300x154.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/santafetrailmaplarge.jpg)

![Image 10: Wagon Train on the Santa Fe Trail](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/SantaFeTrailWagonTrain-dpl-300x221.jpg)
Wagon Train on the Santa Fe Trail.

On September 1, 1821, Willliam Becknell left [Franklin](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/mo-oldfranklin/), Missouri, with four trusted companions. After arriving in Santa Fe on November 16 and making an enormous profit, he made plans to return, thus blazing the path that would become known as the Santa Fe Trail.

On his first trip, Becknell loaded manufactured goods from Missouri onto a mule train to trade for furs, gold, silver, and other goods in New Mexico. However, Becknell found a passable wagon route on his third trip, thus beginning the many wagon trains heading to the [Southwest](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/american-southwest/). Credited as the “Father of the Santa Fe Trail,” Becknell continued to make multiple trips along the trail, profiting enormously on his daring travels. Soon, many [traders](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-santafetrailtraders/), as well as the military, were traveling the route.

[![Image 11: Mule Train by Frederic Remington](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/MuleTrainFrederic-Remington-300x233.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/MuleTrainFrederic-Remington.jpg)
Mule Train by Frederic Remington.

Two routes soon developed along the trail, the [Mountain Route](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-santafetrailroutes/#mountain) and the [Cimarron Route](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-santafetrailroutes/#cimarron), also called the Jornada Route. Skyline Drive, Canon City, Colorado, by Kathy Alexander.

There are wonderful drives across America, including National Scenic Byways, Back Country Byways, and State Scenic Byways. The United States Department of Transportation recognizes a National Scenic Byway for one of the six “intrinsic qualities”: archeological, cultural, historical, natural, recreational, and scenic. The most scenic byways are designated All-American Roads, which must meet two of the six intrinsic qualities. Currently, there are 120 National Scenic Byways and 31 All-American Roads. In addition, individual states designate hundreds more, and the Bureau of Land Management designates scenic drives and back-country byways.

Bent’s Fort, Colorado by Kathy Alexander.

**[Bents Fort](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/co-bentsfort/)**[](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/co-bentsfort/)– Situated on the north bank of the [Arkansas River](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/arkansas-river/)in southeastern[Colorado](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/colorado/), this non-military fort was one of the most significant outposts on the[Santa Fe Trail.](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-santafetrail/) As the principal outpost of American civilization on the southwestern Plains, it was instrumental in shaping the area’s destiny.

[**Canyons of the Ancients National Monument**](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/canyons-of-the-ancients/)—Located in southwestern Colorado, the Saddlehorn Pueblo along the Sand Canyon trail contains a huge number of archaeological sites—more than 6,000 recorded so far, and up to 100 per square mile in some places—representing Ancestral Puebloan and other Native American cultures.

**Escalante Ruin** – The Escalante Pueblo was a compact village on a hilltop overlooking the Dolores River in southwest Colorado. Archaeologists believe it was occupied three different times, based on tree-ring dating of the wood used in its construction. Ancestral Pueblo people built the central complex in 1129 AD and lived there for at least nine years. The Spanish explorers, Atanasio Domínguez and Silvestre Vélez de Escalant, made note of this site in 1776 during their trek across the Southwest.

The architecture and masonry indicate that Escalante Pueblo was one of the northernmost settlements influenced by the culture of [Chaco Canyon](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-chacocanyon/), [New Mexico](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/new-mexico/), about 100 miles south. Some archaeologists speculate that such villages were part of an interdependent system spread across the Four Corners area. Escalante may have been a gathering place for religious or social activities in the smaller surrounding villages.

The pueblo is a rectangular block of about 28 rooms surrounding a kiva (a round subterranean room probably used for religious purposes). Other rooms were used as work areas, sleeping quarters, and storage. These rooms are larger than those typically found in the local region, and their walls were made of parallel faces enclosing a rubble-fill core—both features typical of Chacoan construction. Lowry Pueblo is another nearby Chaco-style site.

After a short abandonment, Escalante Pueblo was briefly reoccupied by people from the local Northern San Juan branch of the[Ancient Puebloan](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/na-ancientpuebloans/) tradition about 1150 AD. A final occupation, also by the Northern San Juan people, was very short and occurred sometime around 1200 AD.

Escalante Pueblo is on the Anasazi Heritage Center grounds at the end of a half-mile trail. The center is located in Delores, Colorado.

**[Fort Lyon](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/co-fortlyon/)** – Fort Wise, established just west of [Bent’s New Fort](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/co-forts.html#Bents%20New%20Fort), was built in 1860 and named for Henry Wise, governor of [Virginia](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/virginia/). That same year, the U.S. Army leased from [William Bent](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/bent-brothers/) his fortification, which consisted of 12 rooms surrounding a central courtyard. Bent’s New Fort buildings were used as a commissary for the fort and as housing for the Upper Arkansas [Indian](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/native-americans/) Agency. The post served as an essential military link on the Santa Fe Trail between [Fort Leavenworth](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/ks-fortleavenworth/), [Kansas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/kansas/), and [Fort Union](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-fortunion/), [New Mexico](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/new-mexico/).

[![Image 3: Hovenweep National Monument](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/Hovenweep-300x225.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/Hovenweep.jpg)
Hovenweep National Monument.

**[Hovenweep National Monument](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/co-hovenweep/)** – Protecting six prehistoric [pueblo](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/na-pueblos/) villages in a twenty-mile expanse of mesa tops along the [Colorado](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/colorado/)–[Utah](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/utah/) border, Hovenweep National Monument is noted for its solitude and undeveloped, natural character. The name Hovenweep was bestowed on the region by explorer and photographer [William Jackson](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-williamjackson/) in 1874. It is a Ute word meaning “deserted valley,” referring to numerous small river valleys that feed into lower McElmo Creek and the San Juan River.

**[Mesa Verde National Park](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/co-mesaverde/)** – Mesa Verde, Spanish for “green table,” rises high above the surrounding country of southwest Colorado, providing a spectacular look into the lives of the [Ancient Puebloan](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/na-ancientpuebloans/) people who made it their home for over 700 years, from 600 A.D. to 1300 A.D. The [National Park](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/national-parks/), containing 52,073 acres, protects over 600 cliff dwellings and 4,000 known archeological sites, only a few of which have been excavated.

**[Old Spanish National Historic Trail](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-oldspanishtrail/)** – Not nearly as well known as the [Oregon](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-oregontrail/) or Santa Fe Trails, the [Old Spanish Trail](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-oldspanishtrail/) was a contemporary of these two more famous trails but was primarily a trade route rather than an emigrant trail, as the path was too rough for wagons. Put together with pieces of previous routes utilized by the [Indians](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/native-americans/) and explorers, this extension of the Santa Fe Trail from [Missouri](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/missouri/) to New Mexico connected [Santa Fe](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-santafe/) with [California](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/california/), playing a significant role in the development of the southern part of the state.

[![Image 4: Raton Pass, New Mexico postcard.](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/RatonPassPostard-300x181.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/RatonPassPostard.jpg)
Raton Pass, New Mexico postcard.

**[Raton Pass](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-ratonpass/)** – Raton Pass, at the border of present-day New Mexico and Colorado, was one of the most essential, yet treacherous, segments of the [Mountain Branch](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-mountainbranch/) of the Santa Fe Trail. The pass cut through the snow-capped Sangre de Cristo Mountains, allowing wagons access to the vast western territory. Shorter routes were eventually developed, but Raton Pass, which crossed safer terrain, remained in use. The pass played a critical role in General Stephen Watts Kearny’s conquest of [Santa Fe](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-santafe/) and the eventual American annexation of New Mexico in 1846.

**[Santa Fe National Historic Trail](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/co-santafetrail/)**– The Santa Fe Trail is significant to the history of what became the State of Colorado. When legal trade began in 1821, over half of the land now comprising Colorado was under Mexican ownership; the other half was unorganized territory. Southeastern Colorado’s dramatic landscape inspired the name for one of the main routes of the trail; the Mountain Route became especially important as the railroads moved into the state. Both the Mountain and [Cimarron Routes](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-cimarronroute/) of the Santa Fe Trail crossed the southeastern corner of Colorado, though the Cimarron Route traversed approximately only 14 miles of Baca County. In contrast, the Colorado segment of the Mountain Route was much longer, totaling 181 miles. This route crossed present Prowers, Bent, Otero, and Las Animas counties before entering New Mexico.

**Trujillo Homesteads** – The Trujillo Homestead is a historic ranch site in Alamosa County, Colorado, not far from the Great Sand Dunes National Park. The area was first settled in the 1860s by Teofilo Trujillo, a Mexican sheep farmer. His son, Pedro, built a log cabin house beginning in 1879, along with other ranch outbuildings and structures. In 1902, the elder Trujillo’s home was destroyed by fire during conflicts between English-speaking cattle ranchers and the Spanish Trujillos, who were by then major landowners in the area. The Trujillos sold their holdings, which became part of the Medano Zapata Ranch, now owned by the Nature Conservancy. The homestead area, including the surviving homestead and the ruins of the destroyed one, was declared a National Historic Landmark District in February 2012.

# The Treacherous Raton Pass on the Santa Fe Trail

[![Image 2: Raton Pass between Colorado and New Mexico](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/RatonPassPostcard.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/RatonPassPostcard.jpg)
Raton Pass between Colorado and New Mexico.

At the border of present-day [New Mexico](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/new-mexico/) and [Colorado](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/colorado/), Raton Pass was one of the most important yet treacherous segments of the [Mountain](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-santafetrailroutes/#mountain)[Branch](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-santafetrailroutes/#mountain) of the [Santa Fe Trail](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-santafetrail/). The pass cut through the snow-capped Sangre de Cristo Mountains, allowing wagons access to the vast western territory.

When Spain controlled the southwestern United States, the Spanish officially banned international trade of all kinds. After Mexico gained its independence from Spain in 1821, the Mexicans lifted the ban and opened the area to commercial and cultural exchange. The Santa Fe Trail, which spanned 1,200 miles from[Franklin](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/mo-oldfranklin/),[Missouri,](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/missouri/)to[Santa Fe](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-santafe/), New Mexico, passing through deserts, mountains, and forests, became the primary means of transportation to and from the area.

Shorter routes were eventually developed, but Raton Pass, which crossed safer terrain, remained in use. The pass was critical in [General Stephen Watts Kearny’s](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/stephen-kearney/) conquest of Santa Fe and the eventual American annexation of New Mexico in 1846.

As the first significant passage West through the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, the Raton Pass National Historic Landmark celebrates the development of American trade, cultural interaction, and westward expansion.

[![Image 3: Sangre de Cristo Range, courtesy Wikipedia](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Sangre-de-Cristo-RangeWiki-300x201.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/Sangre-de-Cristo-RangeWiki.jpg)
Sangre de Cristo Range, courtesy Wikipedia.

When Mexico opened its borders to trade with the United States in 1821, a great commercial, military, and emigrant trail was born. However, the Sangre de Cristo Mountains loomed huge and daunting between the western edge of the United States in Missouri and the bustling Mexican center of commerce, Santa Fe. Early [explorers, trappers](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/explorer-list/), and [American Indian](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/native-americans/) peoples had previously discovered various paths through the treacherous mountains, but before 1821, no covered wagons had made the journey.

In June 1821, [William Becknell](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-williambecknell/), a horse and mule trader, traveled west from Franklin, Missouri, with a wagon and four companions. History has written for years that Becknell would be the first of many to travel via wagon through the narrow, torturous Raton Pass. However, that portion of his journey has been called into question after the discovery of the diary of Pedro Ignacio Gallego in 1993. Mexican Captain Gallego and his 400 men met Becknell on his first journey to Santa Fe. His writings and Becknell’s journal describing the landscape show more evidence that he and his men probably misidentified the Canadian River and instead crossed another river or stream. Researchers now say evidence points to a location between the Arkansas River and Puertocito Piedra Lumbre in Kearny Gap, south of present-day [Las Vegas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-lasvegas/), New Mexico.

[![Image 4: Santa Fe Trail near "The Caches" in Ford County, Kansas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/FordCountySoulesDitchSantaFeTrail-300x200.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/FordCountySoulesDitchSantaFeTrail.jpg)
Santa Fe Trail near “The Caches” in Ford County, Kansas

Soon, however, a new branch of the Santa Fe Trail developed. The so-called “[Cimarron Route](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-santafetrailroutes/#cimarron)” was not only 100 miles shorter but cut across the relatively flat grasslands and deserts of present-day [Kansas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/kansas/) and [Oklahoma](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/oklahoma/) instead of through the mountains. Although the openness of the Cimarron Route led to frequent raids from American Indian tribes and provided far less water, the dangers of the shorter path were still preferable to travel. Between the 1820s and early 1840s, most wagon traffic along the Santa Fe Trail opted to take the Cimarron Route.

In 1846, the pass again played a significant role in history. Tensions were running high between the United States and Mexico over land disputes in [Texas](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/texas/), which included what is now the State of New Mexico. Both countries laid claim to the land, and Mexico disputed the United States’ decision to annex Texas in 1845. President James Polk declared war on Mexico in 1846 and sent American forces into the territory. [General Stephen Watts Kearny](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/stephen-kearney/) set out with his famed 1,600-man “Army of the West” along the [Santa Fe Trail](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-santafetrail/).

[![Image 5: The Army of the West Travels into New Mexico](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/ArmyoftheWest-300x171.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/12/ArmyoftheWest.jpg)
The Army of the West Travels into New Mexico.

Although the Mountain Branch and the Raton Pass were dangerous, Kearny chose to head west through the mountains rather than take the Cimarron Route. The steep, narrow Raton Pass afforded better protection from invading forces and an ample water supply, unlike the dry desert along much of the Cimarron Route. Before Kearny and his men arrived, a team of workers set out along the trail to make passage more accessible, including clearing rocks and debris from the notorious Raton Pass. Despite their efforts, Kearny’s journey was still fraught with difficulty. Many wagons were destroyed, and supplies had to be left behind.

Weakened, the men emerged from the Raton Pass and expected to meet resistance from Mexican forces that the provincial governor Manuel Armijo sent. They instead found the valley abandoned. Kearny’s takeover of Santa Fe thus was swift. Without a struggle, the United States laid claim to the territory.

The Mountain Branch was again mostly abandoned after Kearny’s army used it because traders and travelers still preferred the shorter, easier route. However, the Raton Pass was used once again after the outbreak of the [Civil War](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/civil-war/) in 1860. The vulnerability of the Cimarron Branch was recognized as concerns heightened around [Confederate](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/ah-confederatestates/) raids. The Santa Fe Trail saw heavy use as a [Union](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/ah-unioncivilwar/) Army supply route west, and the narrow, protected Raton Pass was easy to guard. The pass continued to serve Union troops through 1865.

[![Image 6: Ox team in Raton Mountains between Trinidad and Raton](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Ox-team-in-Raton-Mountains-between-Trinidad-and-RatonAbt1915-300-300x204.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Ox-team-in-Raton-Mountains-between-Trinidad-and-RatonAbt1915-300.jpg)
Ox team in Raton Mountains between Trinidad and Raton.

Raton Pass became part of a toll road that entrepreneur[Richens L. Wootton](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/we-richenswootton/) built and managed for several years after the war. Beginning in 1866, the most treacherous part of the Santa Fe Trail was heavily altered by grading, blasting, bridge building, and clearing. The formerly difficult Raton Pass was made passable in all seasons for horses, wagons, and stagecoaches alike. While Wootton’s toll road was highly profitable, the advancing western railroad system soon overtook it. By the late 1870s, train traffic replaced Raton Pass and the Santa Fe Trail, which led to the abandonment of the epic trade route by 1880.

The railroad that once scaled the pass via a series of switchbacks has since been re-routed beneath the mountain through a tunnel. Much of the rest of the rail line still follows the old route of the [Santa Fe Trail](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/nm-santafetrail/) through Raton Pass and along Raton Creek. Though new highway construction has wiped out much of the trail, distinct original segments remain.

The 7,881-foot summit is accessible via I-25. A New Mexico Welcome Center allows visitors to step out of their vehicles to see the incredible view once only afforded to the Santa Fe Trail travelers. An informative historical marker for Raton Pass interprets the landmark at the center and on the [Colorado](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/colorado/) side of the State border. However, public access to the land is restricted, as the wilderness is privately owned. The nearby city of [Raton](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/raton-new-mexico/), New Mexico, celebrates its trail heritage, and the Raton Museum, located at 108 2nd Street, interprets the area’s past for curious visitors.

Today, Raton Pass is a National Historic Landmark located five miles North of Raton, New Mexico, along the Santa Fe National Historic Trail, a unit of the National Park Service.

[![Image 7: Railroad through Raton Pass](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/RatonPassRailroad-300x191.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/RatonPassRailroad.jpg)
Railroad through Raton Pass.

# Canyons of the Ancients National Monument, Colorado

[![Image 4: Canyons of the Ancients, Colorado by Bob Wick, Bureau of Land Management.](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Canyons-of-the-AncientsCOBobWickblm2013-700.jpg)](https://photos.legendsofamerica.com/southerncolorado/e9b53ee28)
Canyons of the Ancients, Colorado by Bob Wick, Bureau of Land Management.

Canyons of the Ancients National Monument protects an archaeologically significant landscape in southwest [Colorado](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/colorado/). Encompassing more than 176,000 acres of federal land, it is administered by the Bureau of Land Management.

The Monument contains the highest known archaeological site density in the United States, with rich, well-preserved evidence of [native cultures](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/native-americans/) that have been part of this landscape for at least 10,000 years. The archeological record etched into this landscape is much more than isolated islands of architecture. This cultural landscape contains more than 6,355 recorded sites that reflect all the physical components of past human life: villages, field houses, check dams, reservoirs, great kivas, cliff dwellings, shrines, sacred springs, agricultural fields, petroglyphs, and sweat lodges. Some areas have more than 100 sites per square mile. The number of sites is estimated to be up to 30,000.

[![Image 5: Paleo Indian People](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/PaleoPeople-300x200.jpg)](https://www.legendsofamerica.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/PaleoPeople.jpg)
Paleo Indian People.

People lived on this landscape as early as the late Pleistocene (or Ice Age), approximately 10,000 years ago. Small bands of Paleoindians hunted large game, such as mammoths and camels, and gathered wild plant foods in cool, moist environments.

Gradually, over several millennia, the climate warmed and became drier. During the Archaic period, beginning about 7,500 years ago, increasing numbers of hunter-gatherers roamed the landscape, expanding their diet to include a wider variety of plants and animals, facilitated by the warmer climate.

Agriculture, introduced from the south about 4,000 years ago, marked the beginnings of Pueblo culture in the Four Corners area. Basketmaker II people began supplementing their diet by growing corn and squash. At that time, people began to adopt a more settled lifestyle, and by about 2,500 years ago, they had become dependent on corn for the majority of their daily calories.
