##### ☢️ NUKE NOTICE ⚛

**NPR is [reporting](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/30/nx-s1-5983482/valar-atomic-nuclear-data-center-project-beehive-utah) that Valar Atomics is looking to build a massive data center and nuclear reactor complex — complete with fuel production and radioactive waste dump facilities — on more than 9,000 acres of public land east of Price, Utah.** The complex would be powered by 456 small modular reactors with a mind-boggling generation capacity of 9.6 gigawatts, nearly three times the capacity of Palo Verde nuclear plant near Phoenix.

Valar is one of several startups looking to advance a new generation of reactors that are smaller, portable, require less up-front capital, and supposedly not weighed down with all of the baggage of the old-school conventional reactors, which not only cost a lot to build, but also tend to evoke visions of Chernobyl, Three Mile Island, or Fukushima.

While these small modular reactors go by slick, newfangled names, they still rely on the same nuclear reaction as the old, conventional reactors. Meaning they are still expensive to build, require dangerous and damaging mining to extract uranium for fuel, produce toxic and radioactive waste, and could potentially melt down. Furthermore, none of these new reactors has been proven on a commercial scale.

To fuel a single reactor — small modular, advanced, or conventional — requires extracting hundreds of thousands of tons of ore from the earth, milling the ore to produce yellowcake (triuranium octoxide), converting the yellowcake to uranium hexafluoride gas, enriching it to concentrate the uranium-235, and fabricating the fuel pellets and rods.

Each of these steps generates [ample volumes of toxic waste products](https://www.hcn.org/issues/52-1/nuclear-energy-nuclear-power-is-emissions-free-but-at-what-cost-waste/). Mining leaves behind lightly radioactive waste rock; milling produces mill tailings containing radium, thorium, radon, lead, arsenic, and other nasty stuff; and enrichment and fabrication both produce liquid and solid waste. The reaction, itself, generates the most dangerous form of leftovers, containing radioactive fission products such as iodine, strontium, caesium, and transuranic elements, including plutonium.

If Valar is indeed looking to fabricate fuel on-site, as NPR is reporting, then it will also use that public land to store the fuel enrichment waste as well as the “spent nuclear fuel,” or radioactive waste, that is removed from the reactor during refueling. It would turn a large swath of public land not only into a high-tech industrial site and nuclear power plant, but also a radioactive waste depository.

“If we have facilities like this on public land for waste storage, for massive nuclear development, for data centers,” Lexi Tuddenham, HEAL Utah’s executive director told NPR, “that’s going to have tremendous implications for how public lands are used.”

The Bureau of Land Management told NPR that it was reviewing Valar’s application for “Project Beehive” and that as soon as the application is completed the agency would launch an environmental review that would include opportunities for public input. The project will also need Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing and permits from the state of Utah. Under a normal regime, this process for a project of this scope would take years to complete.

Under the Trump administration, almost anything could happen, even Valar’s wildly ambitious goal to bring the facility online in 2028. President Donald Trump, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, and Energy Secretary Chris Wright all are gung-ho for AI data centers and nuclear energy, as is Utah Gov. Spencer Cox. Just as the administration fast-tracked permitting for a Utah uranium mine, so could it invoke the Defense Production Act or the purported “energy emergency” to push this project through licensing and permitting — even if doing so would be illegal.

Valar, which has partnered with the Department of Energy to test its reactor, is a plaintiff in a lawsuit filed by Utah, Arizona lawmakers, and other parties seeking to weaken or remove federal licensing requirements for small reactors. The nascent firm’s CEO, Isaiah Taylor, has been [linked to](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/02/the-trump-administrations-favorite-nuclear-startup-has-ties-to-russia-and-epstein/) an Idaho Christian nationalist church, Russian oligarchs, and even Jeffrey Epstein.

##### ⛏️ MINING MONITOR ⛏️

**I briefly mentioned last dispatch that Land Survey Advisors had staked an additional 36 mining claims in areas that President Donald Trump had removed from Bears Ears National Monument. A**t first glance, these new claims didn’t seem much different than the 30-something claims located in the former national monument by Kimmerle Mining.

But as I looked more closely, I noticed some curious details that may or may not mean anything at all. Still, I figured they were worth noting.

*   The 36 claims located (that’s the agency’s term for “staked”) by Land Survey Advisors were not only filed with the San Juan County Recorder, like Kimmerle’s claims, but they **were also filed with the Bureau of Land Management** and are now in the federal agency’s [system and database](https://mlrs.blm.gov/s/). Of the 72 claims filed in the former national monument since Sept. 11, Land Survey Advisors are the only ones on file with the BLM.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZbGa!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6eb7c0af-f467-436a-a985-4809575d9110_2326x1371.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZbGa!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6eb7c0af-f467-436a-a985-4809575d9110_2326x1371.png)

Clusters of new claims staked by Land Survey Advisors. All of them are on abandoned mine sites. Source: BLM. 

*   **Land Survey Advisors is not a mining company, it is a [consulting firm](https://www.linkedin.com/company/land-survey-advisors/about/), made up of landmen, who help clients stake mineral claims, acquire mineral rights, and conduct surveys.** It is run by Michael Murphy out of Heber, Utah, and was incorporated in 2023. So even though Land Survey Advisors (LSA) is listed as the claimant, it is likely that they are acting on the behalf of a client, which could be a mining firm or an individual.

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OcC3!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe3af09f7-1448-46ba-83e9-2201a936678d_2035x1050.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OcC3!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe3af09f7-1448-46ba-83e9-2201a936678d_2035x1050.png)

Land Survey Advisors’ Ace claim is on the site of the historic and abandoned Four Aces Mine and pushing up against the boundary of Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. Source: BLM. 

*   Some news stories and advocates have [portrayed the claimants as “hobbyists,”](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/09/trump-bears-ears-national-monument-mining-uranium-claims-hobby-prospectors/) as opposed to serious mining firms. This may be the case: **It’s absurdly easy to file a mining claim**, and some folks do it just to “own” a little piece of a cherished landscape, or perhaps with thoughts of doing some gold panning when they retire. But keep in mind that it costs $200 to locate a claim and the same amount annually to keep it active. So this claimant forked out $7,200, plus the cost to hire a landman, to stake these claims. That’s an expensive hobby.

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BBMb!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F197a3092-5fff-4819-a85f-5e40cc1441d8_2224x1317.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BBMb!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F197a3092-5fff-4819-a85f-5e40cc1441d8_2224x1317.png)

*   **The 36 claims are in nine separate clusters**, spread out from lower White Canyon, to the Mormon Pasture area, with no discernible pattern except that they are all within the boundaries of the original BENM. Land Survey Advisors has not staked any claims in San Juan County outside those boundaries.

*   Curiously, most of the clusters of claims **include both placer and lode claims, usually overlapping each other**. Lode claims are for classic hard rock mining, when you’re digging into rock and following a vein. Placer claims are typically for hydraulic or slurry mining, when you’re using water and gravity to extract minerals from gravel or sand. In southeastern Utah, nearly all uranium-targeting claims are lode. Placer claims in this area are typically for lithium or potash extraction (and historically were used for placer gold mining in creeks and riverbeds).

[![Image 10](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fc83!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fca60ba47-3718-43a0-811e-32d96f1c6e1f_1451x998.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fc83!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fca60ba47-3718-43a0-811e-32d96f1c6e1f_1451x998.jpeg)

Satellite imagery showing Land Survey Advisors’ recently filed Rex claim on the old Rex mining site. Notice the light areas, made up of waste material from the abandoned mine. Source: BLM. 

*   When I zoomed in on LSA’s new claims, I noticed that they all were **located on previously mined or prospected areas,** including on once-producing mines with associated waste rock piles. In most cases, the claims are named for the former mines: The new Ace claim sits atop the old Four Aces mine; the new PVQ claim is at the old Peavine Queen Mine[1](https://www.landdesk.org/p/massive-nuclear-plantwaste-dumpdata#footnote-1); the WDW claim is at the abandoned Widowmaker Mine, and so forth. One pair of claims, the FCL lode and placer, include on the old waste/tailings pile from the long-defunct ore upgrading mill and copper heap leaching operation. While old mines might be an obvious place to seek ore reserves, staking a claim on them risks assuming any liability for the mess left by the long-gone former owners and operators.

*   **So what does it all mean? Maybe nothing.**Maybe someone was just jumping on the mining-claim-in-a-former-national-monument bandwagon. But I have another, wildly speculative, absolutely unconfirmed hypothesis: This claimant is not a hobbyist, but an emerging mining firm that is looking to use highly pressurized water to extract minerals from abandoned mine waste piles. This would explain the placer claims and the presence of waste dumps within all of the claims. I have an email into the company that I’m hypothesizing about, and will let you all know what they say or don’t say.

Regardless, one thing is clear: the people who said a national monument designation was unnecessary because no one is interested in staking mining claims in the area anymore were wrong.

Title: Flght 93, Manassas, Clara Barton, Antietam, and Fort Necessity NP Units

URL Source: https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/2019/06/11/flght-93-manassas-clara-barton-antietam-and-fort-necessity-np-units/

Published Time: 2019-06-11T14:30:56+00:00

Markdown Content:
# [The Martin's Blog](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/)

Some Life Adventures

« [Some Washington DC Area and Southeast PA NP Units](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/2019/04/29/washington-dc-area-np-units/)

[NP Unit Road Trip OH, KY, MO, NM, CO, UT, and NE](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/2019/07/05/np-unit-road-trip-oh-ky-mo-nm-co-ut-and-ne/) »

![Image 1: h1](https://s0.wp.com/wp-content/themes/pub/neat/images/h1.gif?m=1158640643i)
## Flght 93, Manassas, Clara Barton, Antietam, and Fort Necessity NP Units

June 11, 2019 

**6/5 W** – left Springfield before 6am, stopped at the **Flight 93 N Mem** in PA for an hour. Chad and I had been here in October 2011 but I wanted to introduce Helen to the site, take a few more pics, and hear the new Tower of Voices. There are to be 40 wind chimes representing the 40 men and women who tried to re-take the plane from the terrorists at the entrance to the Memorial.

[![Image 2](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4421.jpg?w=450&h=295)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4421.jpg)

[![Image 3](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4422b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4422b.jpg)

[![Image 4](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4423b.jpg?w=450&h=285)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4423b.jpg)

Unfortunately, the electronic wind chimes, one for each victim, were not working. They had only installed 8 thus far and were still testing them.

[![Image 5](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4426b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4426b.jpg)

[![Image 6](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4425b.jpg?w=450&h=675)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4425b.jpg)

We then went to the Visitor Center

[![Image 7](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4431b.jpg?w=450&h=297)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4431b.jpg)

[![Image 8](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4430b.jpg?w=450&h=273)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4430b.jpg)

[![Image 9](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4434b.jpg?w=450&h=290)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4434b.jpg)

[![Image 10](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4435b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4435b.jpg)

Then to the Overlook of the crash site and finally to the crash site itself before we left

[![Image 11](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4432b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4432b.jpg)

[![Image 12](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4433b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4433b.jpg)

We spent the night with Fred and Liz in Egg Harbor NJ, their granddaughters made the sign for us

[![Image 13](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_3741b.jpg?w=450&h=338)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_3741b.jpg)

**6/6 Th** – I dropped Helen off at Carol and Dave’s house in Mays Landing and then drove to Glen Burnie MD to visit my brother Joe. I arrived about noon. He is no longer able to drive (glioblastoma), so I took him shopping for food, clothes, an ice cream, and we ran errands. He bought pants and underwear and stated that this was the first time in 3 years he was able to shop for himself.

**6/7 F** – “Field Trip Day,” we spoke to Frankie on the phone as we were driving to **Manassas National Battlefield Park**in VA. He was on his way to the airport to fly to Taiwan for his brother Anthony’s graduation from university. The Union suffered two defeats here (Bull Run) during the first two years of the Civil War (1861 and 1962)

[![Image 14](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4439b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4439b.jpg)

[![Image 15](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4441b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4441b.jpg)

The location of the first Battle of Bull Run centered around the Henry Hill Visitor Center area

[![Image 16](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4442b.jpg?w=450&h=287)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4442b.jpg)

[![Image 17](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4454b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4454b.jpg)

I finally found a Civil War site where they had a sword like mine on display! Note the top sword – it is a non-commissioned officer’s sword. An identical sword was given to me by my father’s friend when I was 13 years old. My sword was made in Trenton NJ in 1863.

[![Image 18](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4454.2b.jpg?w=450&h=338)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4454.2b.jpg)

The hero of both battles, Confederate Gen. Thomas J. Jackson, earned his nick name here – see engraving below his statue.

[![Image 19](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4444b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4444b.jpg)

Henry House and the “Bull Run” monument constructed by Union soldiers in 1865 to honor those who died in the first battle

[![Image 20](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4446b.jpg?w=450&h=266)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4446b.jpg)

We then toured the Brawner Farm area, where the second battle of Bull Run (1862) took place

[![Image 21](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4457b.jpg?w=450&h=308)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4457b.jpg)

[![Image 22](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4458b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4458b.jpg)

[![Image 23](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4463b.jpg?w=450&h=271)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4463b.jpg)

Then drove to and hiked to the Deep Cut battlefield area and the Groveton Monument to the Union soldiers who died in the second battle of Bull Run

[![Image 24](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4464b.jpg?w=450&h=281)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4464b.jpg)

[![Image 25](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4467b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4467b.jpg)

We stopped at the Stone Bridge before departing for Glen Echo Park and the Clara Barton NHS in MD just west of DC

Bought some subs for lunch and ate them in **Glen Echo Park** MD, which is administered by the **George Washington Memorial Parkway**

[![Image 26](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4475b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4475b.jpg)

[![Image 27](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4476b.jpg?w=450&h=668)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4476b.jpg)

[![Image 28](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4477b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4477b.jpg)

Glen Echo Amusement Park was state of the art when it opened in 1891, with various attractions added through the years; roller coasters, bumper cars, Hall of Mirrors, Spanish Ballroom, the Dentzel Carousel (1921), Crystal Pool (1931), and Arcade (1939)

[![Image 29](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4478b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4478b.jpg)

[![Image 30](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4482b.jpg?w=450&h=292)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4482b.jpg)

[![Image 31](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4487b.jpg?w=450&h=298)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4487b.jpg)

From the beginning there was a strictly enforced segregation policy. In 1960 a group of students from Howard University came to Glen Echo with a message of equal access. Protestors were arrested but in 1961, with the help of Robert Kennedy, the park was open to any patron regardless of their skin color. It is now run by the Glen Echo Park Partnership for Arts and Culture.

[![Image 32](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4483b.jpg?w=450&h=315)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4483b.jpg)

**Clara Barton National Historic Site** is across the parking lot

[![Image 33](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4474b.jpg?w=450&h=289)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4474b.jpg)

[![Image 34](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4488b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4488b.jpg)

[![Image 35](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4492b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4492b.jpg)

This was her home, later becoming the administrative offices of the American Red Cross, which she established in 1881. Born in 1821 she aided wounded soldiers at Manassas, Antietam, Fredericksburg, The Wilderness, and Spotsylvania. She worked with the International Red Cross during 1870-71 and from that experience decided to work toward an American Red Cross (ARC). At that time, the International Red Cross (IRC) only provided assistance during wars. When Barton started the ARC, she expanded the concept to include natural disasters. Later, the IRC also started serving during natural disasters.

[![Image 36](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4489b.jpg?w=450&h=325)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4489b.jpg)

[![Image 37](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4493b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4493b.jpg)

The house had been closed for renovation and is now open for tours. However, we were told it will take some time before items can be placed back in rooms. For now, they offer photos in each room as to how they will look when complete.

[![Image 38](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4494b.jpg?w=450&h=333)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4494b.jpg)

[![Image 39](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4499b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4499b.jpg)

[![Image 40](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4497b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4497b.jpg)

[![Image 41](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4500b.jpg?w=450&h=333)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4500b.jpg)

[![Image 42](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4504b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4504b.jpg)

Departing after an excellent tour. Note the two Red Crosses in the upper middle windows. They are back-lit so they can be easily seen at night.

[![Image 43](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4506b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4506b.jpg)

**6/8 Sat** – I stopped at the **Old Swedes Church Historic Site** in Wilmington DE on my way to NJ. It is part of the **First State National Historical Park.** It was established as a National Monument by President Obama in 2013 and changed to a NHP in 2014. It is the first National Park Unit in the state of Delaware. The Visitor Center for the church is in the Hendrickson House.

[![Image 44](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4513b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4513b.jpg)

[![Image 45](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4514b.jpg?w=450&h=310)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/img_4514b.jpg)

Holy Trinity Church was founded by Swedish colonists in 1698; making it one of the oldest active congregations in the U.S.

# More mining claims staked at Bears Ears

### Plus: The story of Lake Powell’s 26,000-ton pile of radioactive waste

[![Image 3: Jonathan P. Thompson's avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Qzr2!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F303055ea-4e27-416f-9114-0b761dbe48c0_400x400.jpeg)](https://substack.com/@landdesk)

##### ⛏️ MINING MONITOR ⛏️

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IqhI!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa3d23295-d57f-45be-924c-fe61928ed71c_2096x1228.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IqhI!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa3d23295-d57f-45be-924c-fe61928ed71c_2096x1228.jpeg)

Several of the latest claims located within the pre-shrinkage Bears Ears National Monument are on the north side of the Tables of the Sun, seen here in the background on the right. Jonathan P. Thompson photo. 

**The mining claim game continues to heat up in the areas Trump illegally slashed from Bears Ears National Monument,** and the top player is, once again, Kimmerle Mining of Moab. Since the _Land Desk_[last wrote about this mini-land rush](https://www.landdesk.org/p/trump-guts-the-endangered-species), Kimmerle has filed seven additional claims areas that had been within the national monument, and therefore off limits to new mining claims.

The latest claims are in the White Canyon area. During the post-War uranium frenzy, the federal government, county crews, prospectors, and mining companies webbed this area with roads, poked it full of prospect holes and mine adits, and contaminated waters with radioactive materials. Part of that legacy includes a 26,000-ton pile of uranium tailings entombed within the ~~waters~~ silt of Lake Powell.

It’s important to keep in mind that the presence of active mining claims does not necessarily mean anyone is going to mine or even explore these pieces of land. And while the claims may be active, which simply means the claimant is up to date on their $200/year location and maintenance fee, they may not be valid. That requires, at least theoretically, proof that the claim contains valuable minerals.

But it does appear as if Kimmerle is targeting viable mining areas, which indicate that the firm either intends to mine the claims, or consolidate enough of them to sell them to a larger company. The newly revealed claims are located in two clusters on either side of Natural Bridges National Monument.

The notices of location have been declared with the San Juan County Recorder, but have not yet shown up on the Bureau of Land Management database. Just before publishing this, I checked the San Juan County records search and found that an entity called Land Survey Advisers — which typically stakes claims for other firms or individuals — filed location notices on more than three dozen claims in San Juan County. At least some of those claims appear to be within the pre-shrinkage BENM boundaries, but the location description on many of them included sections that don’t exist (43, 47) in the public land survey system, and the document download function isn’t working for me, so I have yet to confirm any of this. Still, it’s potentially alarming.

Subscribe

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gioz!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffd434448-7ef6-4de9-94db-d537511e6603_2298x1608.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gioz!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffd434448-7ef6-4de9-94db-d537511e6603_2298x1608.png)

Map showing the approximate location of the claims filed by Kimmerle Mining in Sept. 2026. It also shows pre-existing active claims (in pink) that were staked before Bears Ears’ 2016 establishment, or following the Trump I-shrinkage. Map: BLM and Land Desk. 

The Kimmerle claims include:

*   Six lode claims (each at 20.66 acres) on the north slope of the Tables of the Sun formations in the upper Fry Canyon drainage, just on the boundary line of the original Bears Ears National Monument. While this specific area has seen little mining activity in the past, it is in the same vicinity as the Daneros Mine, which was up for expansion as recently as 2016. And the new claims are adjacent to Kimmerle’s Lucky group of claims.

The nearest historic mining activity was at the [Fry # 4 mine](https://mrdata.usgs.gov/mrds/show-mrds.php?dep_id=10079007)[1](https://www.landdesk.org/p/more-mining-claims-staked-at-bears#footnote-1), an underground uranium mine with over 400 meters of workings. In 1977, the operator was Utah Power & Light Co., which was the main mining company of the area at the time.

*   One lode claim on the east slope of Upper Lost Parks, an appendage of Elk Ridge just north of Natural Bridges National Monument and south of the Woodenshoe formation. It’s across Deer Creek Canyon from Kimmerle’s Geitus and Cedar claims, which the firm staked just before President Barack Obama designated Bears Ears, and right after President Donald Trump shrunk the monument for the first time. It’s also in the vicinity of the Sandy claims that Kimmerle held, but that were closed in 2015.

The area was mined and prospected heavily during the Cold War. The nearest historical mines and prospects were the Big Red, the Sandy, and the Hideout. In 1977, the Big Red — operated by Utah Power & Light — was reported to have a flooded, a caved, and an open adit. While the Hideout sparked a 1950s prospecting boom in the area, none of these were ever large producers. However, a 1965 USGS report did indicate this part of Elk Ridge was favorable for uranium deposits, which is likely one reason the Trump administration stripped it of national monument protections.

The White Canyon area was known to contain rich uranium reserves back in the 1940s and 1950s, but its remoteness and the rugged landscape created challenges for mining companies looking to exploit the resources. One of the biggest hurdles was getting the ore to the Monticello processing plant, which required driving gnarly roads across the crinkled landscape and up and over Elk Ridge.

So in 1949, the Vanadium Corporation of America built a small mill at the [confluence](https://www.google.com/maps/d/u/0/edit?mid=1OOtbc2hDAVue6Tk9Oy4Cyry3EmfFWNc&usp=sharing) of White Canyon and the Colorado River, primarily to process uranium ore from the nearby Happy Jack Mine, located upstream in the White Canyon drainage (and just within the original Bears Ears National Monument boundaries). For the next four years, the mill went through about 20 tons of ore per day, crushing and grinding it up, then treating it with sulfuric acid, tributyl phosphate, and other nastiness. One ton of ore yielded about five or six pounds of uranium, meaning that each day some 39,900 pounds of tailings were piled up outside the mill on the banks of the river.

In 1953 the mill was closed, and the tailings were left where they sat, uncovered, as was the practice of the day. Ten years later, water began backing up behind the newly built Glen Canyon Dam; federal officials decided to let the reservoir’s waters inundate the tailings. There they remain today, though at current lake levels they are probably buried by and mixed in with the Dominy Formation of silt, rather than covered with water.

[Buy Me a Coffee](https://buymeacoffee.com/thelanddesk)

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4cpq!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6a4ced47-8a92-45da-b86e-9b6ba5e34614_1528x966.png)](https://www.google.com/maps/d/u/0/edit?mid=1OOtbc2hDAVue6Tk9Oy4Cyry3EmfFWNc&usp=sharing)

Satellite image showing the location of the White Canyon Mill and its silt-entombed tailings pile. 

During the uranium days of the West, more than a dozen mills — all with processing capacities at least ten times larger than the one at White Canyon — sat on the banks of the Colorado River and its tributaries. Mill locations included: Shiprock, Mexican Hat, Monument Valley, Tuba City, Monticello, Rifle, Grand Junction, Moab, Uravan, Green River, and Naturita. There was even an ore upgrading mill at Fry Canyon, followed by a copper heap leaching operation. Groundwater contamination continues to today, and was partially responsible for the Fry Canyon Lodge’s demise.

At the Durango mill the tailings were piled into a hill-sized mound just a stone’s throw from the Animas River. They weren’t covered or otherwise contained, so when it rained tailings simply washed into the river. Worse, the mill’s liquid waste stream poured directly into the river at a rate of some 340 gallons per minute, or half-a-million gallons per day. It was laced not only with highly toxic chemicals used to leach uranium from the ore and iron-aluminum sludge (a milling byproduct), but also radium-tainted ore solids.

Radium is a highly radioactive “bone-seeker.” That means that when it’s ingested it makes its way to the skeleton, where it decays into other radioactive daughter elements, including radon, and bombards the surrounding tissue with alpha, beta, and gamma radiation. According to the Toxic Substances and Diseases Registry, exposure leads to “anemia, cataracts, fractured teeth, cancer (especially bone cancer), and death.”

It wasn’t any better at any of the other mills. In the early 1950s, researchers from the U.S. Public Health Service sampled Western rivers and found that “the dissolved radium content of river water below uranium mills was increased considerably by waste discharges from the milling operations” and that “radium content of river muds below the uranium mills was 1,000 to 2,000 times natural background concentrations.”

That was just from daily operations. In 1960, one of the evaporation ponds at the Shiprock mill broke, sending at least 250,000 gallons of highly acidic raffinate, containing high levels of radium and thorium, into the river. None of the relevant officials were notified and individual users continued to drink the water, put it on their crops, and give it to their sheep and cattle. It wasn’t until five days later, after hundreds of dead fish had washed up on the river’s shores for 60 miles downstream, that the public was alerted to the disaster.

Of course, what’s dumped into the river at any of these places doesn’t stay there, but makes its way downstream. In the early 1960s, while Glen Canyon Dam was still being constructed, the Public Health Service folks did extensive sediment sampling in the Colorado River Basin, with a special focus on Lake Mead’s growing bed of silt, which had been piling up at a rate of 175 million tons per year after Hoover Dam started impounding water in 1935. The Lake Mead samples had higher-than-background levels of radium-226. The report concludes:

> _“The data have shown, among other things, that Lake Mead has been essentially the final resting place for the radium contaminated sediments of the Basin. With the closure of Glen Canyon Dam upstream, Lake Powell will then become the final resting place for future radium contaminated sediments. The data also show that a small fraction of the contaminated sediment has passed through Lake Mead to be trapped by Lakes Mohave and Havasu.”_

And so, the billions of tons of silt that has accumulated in Lake Mead and Lake Powell serve as archives of sorts. They hold the sedimental records of an era during which people, health, land, and water were all sacrificed in order to obtain the raw material for weapons that are capable of destroying all of humanity. If the new mining claim mini-rush is any indication, some more records may be added to the archive before long.

##### ☢️ NUKE NOTICE ⚛

**NPR is [reporting](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/30/nx-s1-5983482/valar-atomic-nuclear-data-center-project-beehive-utah) that Valar Atomics is looking to build a massive data center and nuclear reactor complex — complete with fuel production and radioactive waste dump facilities — on more than 9,000 acres of public land east of Price, Utah.** The complex would be powered by 456 small modular reactors with a mind-boggling generation capacity of 9.6 gigawatts, nearly three times the capacity of Palo Verde nuclear plant near Phoenix.

Valar is one of several startups looking to advance a new generation of reactors that are smaller, portable, require less up-front capital, and supposedly not weighed down with all of the baggage of the old-school conventional reactors, which not only cost a lot to build, but also tend to evoke visions of Chernobyl, Three Mile Island, or Fukushima.

While these small modular reactors go by slick, newfangled names, they still rely on the same nuclear reaction as the old, conventional reactors. Meaning they are still expensive to build, require dangerous and damaging mining to extract uranium for fuel, produce toxic and radioactive waste, and could potentially melt down. Furthermore, none of these new reactors has been proven on a commercial scale.

To fuel a single reactor — small modular, advanced, or conventional — requires extracting hundreds of thousands of tons of ore from the earth, milling the ore to produce yellowcake (triuranium octoxide), converting the yellowcake to uranium hexafluoride gas, enriching it to concentrate the uranium-235, and fabricating the fuel pellets and rods.

Each of these steps generates [ample volumes of toxic waste products](https://www.hcn.org/issues/52-1/nuclear-energy-nuclear-power-is-emissions-free-but-at-what-cost-waste/). Mining leaves behind lightly radioactive waste rock; milling produces mill tailings containing radium, thorium, radon, lead, arsenic, and other nasty stuff; and enrichment and fabrication both produce liquid and solid waste. The reaction, itself, generates the most dangerous form of leftovers, containing radioactive fission products such as iodine, strontium, caesium, and transuranic elements, including plutonium.

If Valar is indeed looking to fabricate fuel on-site, as NPR is reporting, then it will also use that public land to store the fuel enrichment waste as well as the “spent nuclear fuel,” or radioactive waste, that is removed from the reactor during refueling. It would turn a large swath of public land not only into a high-tech industrial site and nuclear power plant, but also a radioactive waste depository.

“If we have facilities like this on public land for waste storage, for massive nuclear development, for data centers,” Lexi Tuddenham, HEAL Utah’s executive director told NPR, “that’s going to have tremendous implications for how public lands are used.”

The Bureau of Land Management told NPR that it was reviewing Valar’s application for “Project Beehive” and that as soon as the application is completed the agency would launch an environmental review that would include opportunities for public input. The project will also need Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing and permits from the state of Utah. Under a normal regime, this process for a project of this scope would take years to complete.

Under the Trump administration, almost anything could happen, even Valar’s wildly ambitious goal to bring the facility online in 2028. President Donald Trump, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, and Energy Secretary Chris Wright all are gung-ho for AI data centers and nuclear energy, as is Utah Gov. Spencer Cox. Just as the administration fast-tracked permitting for a Utah uranium mine, so could it invoke the Defense Production Act or the purported “energy emergency” to push this project through licensing and permitting — even if doing so would be illegal.

Valar, which has partnered with the Department of Energy to test its reactor, is a plaintiff in a lawsuit filed by Utah, Arizona lawmakers, and other parties seeking to weaken or remove federal licensing requirements for small reactors. The nascent firm’s CEO, Isaiah Taylor, has been [linked to](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/02/the-trump-administrations-favorite-nuclear-startup-has-ties-to-russia-and-epstein/) an Idaho Christian nationalist church, Russian oligarchs, and even Jeffrey Epstein.

##### ⛏️ MINING MONITOR ⛏️

**I briefly mentioned last dispatch that Land Survey Advisors had staked an additional 36 mining claims in areas that President Donald Trump had removed from Bears Ears National Monument. A**t first glance, these new claims didn’t seem much different than the 30-something claims located in the former national monument by Kimmerle Mining.

But as I looked more closely, I noticed some curious details that may or may not mean anything at all. Still, I figured they were worth noting.

*   The 36 claims located (that’s the agency’s term for “staked”) by Land Survey Advisors were not only filed with the San Juan County Recorder, like Kimmerle’s claims, but they **were also filed with the Bureau of Land Management** and are now in the federal agency’s [system and database](https://mlrs.blm.gov/s/). Of the 72 claims filed in the former national monument since Sept. 11, Land Survey Advisors are the only ones on file with the BLM.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZbGa!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6eb7c0af-f467-436a-a985-4809575d9110_2326x1371.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZbGa!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6eb7c0af-f467-436a-a985-4809575d9110_2326x1371.png)

Clusters of new claims staked by Land Survey Advisors. All of them are on abandoned mine sites. Source: BLM. 

*   **Land Survey Advisors is not a mining company, it is a [consulting firm](https://www.linkedin.com/company/land-survey-advisors/about/), made up of landmen, who help clients stake mineral claims, acquire mineral rights, and conduct surveys.** It is run by Michael Murphy out of Heber, Utah, and was incorporated in 2023. So even though Land Survey Advisors (LSA) is listed as the claimant, it is likely that they are acting on the behalf of a client, which could be a mining firm or an individual.

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OcC3!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe3af09f7-1448-46ba-83e9-2201a936678d_2035x1050.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OcC3!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe3af09f7-1448-46ba-83e9-2201a936678d_2035x1050.png)

Land Survey Advisors’ Ace claim is on the site of the historic and abandoned Four Aces Mine and pushing up against the boundary of Glen Canyon National Recreation Area. Source: BLM. 

*   Some news stories and advocates have [portrayed the claimants as “hobbyists,”](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/09/trump-bears-ears-national-monument-mining-uranium-claims-hobby-prospectors/) as opposed to serious mining firms. This may be the case: **It’s absurdly easy to file a mining claim**, and some folks do it just to “own” a little piece of a cherished landscape, or perhaps with thoughts of doing some gold panning when they retire. But keep in mind that it costs $200 to locate a claim and the same amount annually to keep it active. So this claimant forked out $7,200, plus the cost to hire a landman, to stake these claims. That’s an expensive hobby.

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BBMb!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F197a3092-5fff-4819-a85f-5e40cc1441d8_2224x1317.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BBMb!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F197a3092-5fff-4819-a85f-5e40cc1441d8_2224x1317.png)

*   **The 36 claims are in nine separate clusters**, spread out from lower White Canyon, to the Mormon Pasture area, with no discernible pattern except that they are all within the boundaries of the original BENM. Land Survey Advisors has not staked any claims in San Juan County outside those boundaries.

*   Curiously, most of the clusters of claims **include both placer and lode claims, usually overlapping each other**. Lode claims are for classic hard rock mining, when you’re digging into rock and following a vein. Placer claims are typically for hydraulic or slurry mining, when you’re using water and gravity to extract minerals from gravel or sand. In southeastern Utah, nearly all uranium-targeting claims are lode. Placer claims in this area are typically for lithium or potash extraction (and historically were used for placer gold mining in creeks and riverbeds).

[![Image 10](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fc83!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fca60ba47-3718-43a0-811e-32d96f1c6e1f_1451x998.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fc83!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fca60ba47-3718-43a0-811e-32d96f1c6e1f_1451x998.jpeg)

Satellite imagery showing Land Survey Advisors’ recently filed Rex claim on the old Rex mining site. Notice the light areas, made up of waste material from the abandoned mine. Source: BLM. 

*   When I zoomed in on LSA’s new claims, I noticed that they all were **located on previously mined or prospected areas,** including on once-producing mines with associated waste rock piles. In most cases, the claims are named for the former mines: The new Ace claim sits atop the old Four Aces mine; the new PVQ claim is at the old Peavine Queen Mine[1](https://landdesk.substack.com/p/massive-nuclear-plantwaste-dumpdata?r=ek6sp#footnote-1); the WDW claim is at the abandoned Widowmaker Mine, and so forth. One pair of claims, the FCL lode and placer, include on the old waste/tailings pile from the long-defunct ore upgrading mill and copper heap leaching operation. While old mines might be an obvious place to seek ore reserves, staking a claim on them risks assuming any liability for the mess left by the long-gone former owners and operators.

*   **So what does it all mean? Maybe nothing.**Maybe someone was just jumping on the mining-claim-in-a-former-national-monument bandwagon. But I have another, wildly speculative, absolutely unconfirmed hypothesis: This claimant is not a hobbyist, but an emerging mining firm that is looking to use highly pressurized water to extract minerals from abandoned mine waste piles. This would explain the placer claims and the presence of waste dumps within all of the claims. I have an email into the company that I’m hypothesizing about, and will let you all know what they say or don’t say.

Regardless, one thing is clear: the people who said a national monument designation was unnecessary because no one is interested in staking mining claims in the area anymore were wrong.

## Reagan Boyhood Home NHS in IL, Keweenaw NHP and Father Marquette NMEM in the UP of MI

August 22, 2019 

**7/24 W** – 6hrs to **Ronald Reagan Boyhood Home National Historic Site,** Dixon IL (Authorized) $8 adult, CST. Statue of Reagan has kernels of corn in his hand – signifying that he was a product of IL. Reagan was our 40 th President and served two terms (1981-1989).

[![Image 2](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5921b.jpg?w=450&h=310)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5921b.jpg)

[![Image 3](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5922b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5922b.jpg)

This modest 1891 Queen Anne style house was rented by the Reagan family from 1920 to 1923 (when Reagan was roughly 9 to 12 years old). Though the family moved from the house they remained in Dixon throughout the former president’s formative years; Visitor Center on left.

[![Image 4](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5945b.jpg?w=450&h=297)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5945b.jpg)

[![Image 5](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5949b.jpg?w=450&h=301)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5949b.jpg)

[![Image 6](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5925b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5925b.jpg)

[![Image 7](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5926b.jpg?w=450&h=316)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5926b.jpg)

[![Image 8](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5927b.jpg?w=450&h=290)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5927b.jpg)

Born in Tampico, Illinois, on February 6, 1911, Ronald Reagan and his family moved many times during his childhood. This is the site of his earliest childhood memories, and a place he recalled with great fondness. The gable roofed, two-­story white frame house is a typical late 19th­century small ­town American home.

[![Image 9](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5934b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5934b.jpg)

[![Image 10](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5946b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5946b.jpg)

Our tour guide explained that Reagan hid his pennies under a tile in front of the fireplace

[![Image 11](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5938b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5938b.jpg)

[![Image 12](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5937b.jpg?w=450&h=286)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5937b.jpg)

[![Image 13](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5939b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5939b.jpg)

[![Image 14](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5940b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5940b.jpg)

[![Image 15](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5936b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5936b.jpg)

Downtown Dixon IL, monument on the Rock River

[![Image 16](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5950b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5950b.jpg)

[![Image 17](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5954b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5954b.jpg)

[![Image 18](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5955b.jpg?w=450&h=493)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5955b.jpg)

The Lincoln Highway – The nation’s first coast-to-coast Highway! U.S. 40 and now Interstate 70 carry Americans from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean.

[![Image 19](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5960b.jpg?w=450&h=269)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5960b.jpg)

[![Image 20](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5959b.jpg?w=450&h=256)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5959b.jpg)

[![Image 21](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5958b.jpg?w=450&h=261)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/img_5958b.jpg)

Towed a U-Haul trailer with cast iron patio furniture, a bed for Lena, etc. to the Martins in Milwaukee WI and spent the night

**7/25 Th** – 5hrs to Baraga Lakeside Inn, in Baraga, MI for the Highpointers Club annual convention

**7/26 F** – Convention activities

**7/27 Sat** – 8am breakfast and then 0.75hr to **Keweenaw National Historical Park,**Quincy Unit. From 7,000 years ago to the 1900s people mined Keweenaw copper. Native peoples made copper into tools and trade items. Investors and immigrants arrived in the 1800s in a great mineral rush, developing thriving industries and cosmopolitan communities. Though the mines have since closed, their mark is still visible on the land and people.

[![Image 22](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5967b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5967b.jpg)

Quincy Mine from the Quincy Dry House Ruins

[![Image 23](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5956b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5956b.jpg)

[![Image 24](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5957b.jpg?w=450&h=274)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5957b.jpg)

[![Image 25](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5962b.jpg?w=450&h=294)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5962b.jpg)

Arrived 15 minutes before the Information Desk opened in order to be on the first mine tour, $22 Sr for 2hr tour

[![Image 26](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5964b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5964b.jpg)

[![Image 27](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5966b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5966b.jpg)

[![Image 28](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5968.1b.jpg?w=450&h=675)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5968.1b.jpg)

Walked around the grounds before the tour. The tall building is the No2. Shaft-Rock House (1908), the stone building in the foreground is the Old No.2 Hoist House that operated from 1882 until 1894

[![Image 29](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5969b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5969b.jpg)

Railroads were extremely important in order to bring in supplies and ship out the ore

[![Image 30](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5973b.jpg?w=450&h=290)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5973b.jpg)

The Old No. 2 Hoist House that operated between 1894 and 1920 is on the left and the Old No. 2 Hoist House (Nordberg) that operated from 1920 to 1931 is on the right

[![Image 31](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5972b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5972b.jpg)

The tour started in the Old No. 2 Hoist House (1894) Museum

[![Image 32](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5978b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5978b.jpg)

[![Image 33](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5984b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5984b.jpg)

Had some time to go through a few displays in the museum before the tour

[![Image 34](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5979.1b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5979.1b.jpg)

Ready to start the tour

[![Image 35](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5982b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5982b.jpg)

Cog Rail Tram (built for tours in 1996) descending to early mine opening. Our guide was excellent – knowledgeable and articulate

[![Image 36](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5987b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5987b.jpg)

Entering mine

[![Image 37](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5989b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5989b.jpg)

Copper ore

[![Image 38](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5991b.jpg?w=450&h=344)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5991b.jpg)

Sledgehammers and handheld chisels gave way to two-man drills, and then one-man drills that used air compressors. Each time technology advanced, fewer miners were needed. Strikes were called because of job cuts and low wages.

[![Image 39](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5992b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5992b.jpg)

We returned to the Nordberg Hoist House to get an explanation of its operation. See the gigantic spool on the right. It connected by steel cables to Shaft-Rock House elevators

[![Image 40](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6003b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6003b.jpg)

[![Image 41](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6004b.jpg?w=450&h=305)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6004b.jpg)

When the mine opened in 1840, miners used hand tools and primitive dynamite

[![Image 42](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5997b.jpg?w=450&h=675)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5997b.jpg)

This was **Manual Labor**

[![Image 43](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5998b.jpg?w=450&h=675)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5998b.jpg)

Products

[![Image 44](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5996b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_5996b.jpg)

Nice schematic of Shaft-Rock House on left and the Nordberg Mine Hoist on the right

[![Image 45](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6000b.jpg?w=450&h=274)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6000b.jpg)

Shaft-Rock House – Ore cars on left, man-cars on right

[![Image 46](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6007b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6007b.jpg)

[![Image 47](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6009b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6009b.jpg)

Men were moved up and down by man-cars, while water was pumped out of the mine, and ore was brought up to start processing

[![Image 48](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6010b.jpg?w=450&h=434)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6010b.jpg)

Final shaft length was 9,260ft. Final shaft depth was 6,225ft, over a mile underground!

[![Image 49](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6011b.jpg?w=450&h=328)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6011b.jpg)

From the mine, I drove 15min NE to Calumet MI, this is the entrance to downtown off Rt41. The Park Headquarters is across the street.

[![Image 50](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6014b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6014b.jpg)

That is almost 5 tons of copper! The building in the background is the Keweenaw History Center

[![Image 51](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6015b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6015b.jpg)

The former St Anne’s (Roman Catholic-French Canadian) church is now the Keweenaw Heritage Center. The **Keweenaw NHP** Visitor Center is located in the Union Building on the right, a former lodge hall for various fraternal organizations.

[![Image 52](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6017b.jpg?w=450&h=278)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6017b.jpg)

It contains many interesting exhibits

[![Image 53](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6048b.jpg?w=450&h=561)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6048b.jpg)

[![Image 54](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6021b.jpg?w=450&h=675)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6021b.jpg)

Copper Timeline (see the bottom of the photos) up to 1917; copper production on the peninsula ceased in 1968 with the closing of the Calumet & Hecla Mining Company

[![Image 55](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6023b.jpg?w=450&h=257)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6023b.jpg)

[![Image 56](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6024b.jpg?w=450&h=234)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6024b.jpg)

[![Image 57](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6025b.jpg?w=450&h=255)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_6025b.jpg)

MI copper in the Statue of Liberty

## [OH to OR – Devils Tower NM, Yellowstone NP, Grand Teton NP, Craters of the Moon NM, Lewis and Clark NHP](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/2024/07/31/trip-to-portland-or/)

July 31, 2024

**7/18/24**– 12hr drive to Fairmont MN. We were pulling a 5 x 8 U-Haul trailer with items for Kate’s house in Portland OR. We were surprised to see a herd of Texas Longhorns as we took an after-dinner stroll from our motel.

[![Image 2](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/3b-tx-longhorns-in-fairmont-mn.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/3b-tx-longhorns-in-fairmont-mn.jpg)

**7/19**– stopped in Mitchell SD to tour **The World’s Only****Corn Palace**. The first one was built in Sioux City in 1887, and then each year until 1891 when the city flooded. In 1892 Mitchel SD built it’s first Corn Palace and the tradition has continued every year. Each year the “palace” is stripped and redecorated with new corn and grains.

[![Image 3](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/7b-mitchell-sd.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/7b-mitchell-sd.jpg)

Of course, we had to have some popcorn before we left –

[![Image 4](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/21b.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/21b.jpg)

Made it to Rapid City SD in time to attend my first meeting at the Highpointers Club Convention

**7/20**– we took advantage of the Convention bus trip to the Gordon Stockade in Custer State Park for the traditional watermelon feast and pizza.

[![Image 5](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/6b.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/6b.jpg)

1868 – Fort Laramie Treaty establishing the Great Sioux Reservation

[![Image 6](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/8b.jpg?w=1024)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/8b.jpg)
Story of the Gordon Stockade

[![Image 7](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/12b.jpg?w=1024)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/12b.jpg)
Black Hills of SD

[![Image 8](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/14b.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/14b.jpg)

[![Image 9](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/18b.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/18b.jpg)

In the evening, gave a slide presentation at the Annual Club Banquet, reviewed club history and encouraged members to participate in the Buy-A-Brick program to support the HPC Display at Campbell Hill, the highpoint of OH.

[![Image 10](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/24b-2023-11-21-3c.jpg?w=1024)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/24b-2023-11-21-3c.jpg)
**7/21** – 2hr drive to **Devils Tower NM**

[![Image 11](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/5b.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/5b.jpg)

We visited here in 1969 when we were moving from Seattle back to the U of MD to continue our graduate work. I then visited with Stacy in 1993.

[![Image 12](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/14b-stacy-1993.jpg?w=901)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/14b-stacy-1993.jpg)
2024

[![Image 13](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/15b-2024.jpg?w=900)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/15b-2024.jpg)
1,000ft across at base

[![Image 14](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/20b-1000ft-across-at-base-1969.jpg?w=900)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/20b-1000ft-across-at-base-1969.jpg)
How Devils Tower was created –

[![Image 15](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/21b-1.jpg?w=378)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/21b-1.jpg)

[![Image 16](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/22b.jpg?w=1024)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/22b.jpg)

[![Image 17](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/19b.jpg?w=525)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/19b.jpg)

Again, did the 1.5-mile loop trail around the 867ft monolith.

[![Image 18](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/39b.jpg?w=702)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/39b.jpg)

[![Image 19](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/31b.jpg?w=900)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/31b.jpg)
The top is 180ft x 300ft and was featured in the 1977 movie classic “Close Encounters of the Third Kind” by Steven Spielberg.

[![Image 20](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/91b-top-180x300ft.jpg?w=378)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/91b-top-180x300ft.jpg)

[![Image 21](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/93b.jpg?w=1024)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/93b.jpg)
I wanted to climb Devils Tower but could never fit it into our schedule. Climbers and standard routes –

[![Image 22](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/95b-climbers.jpg?w=560)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/95b-climbers.jpg)

[![Image 23](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/97b.jpg?w=1004)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/97b.jpg)
Climbing history and some climbers on route –

[![Image 24](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/99b.jpg?w=1024)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/99b.jpg)

[![Image 25](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/107b.jpg?w=378)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/107b.jpg)

A sacred place for Native Americans –

[![Image 26](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/170b.jpg?w=1024)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/170b.jpg)
Prairie Dog Town – 1969

[![Image 27](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/181b-prairie-dog-town-1969.jpg?w=675)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/181b-prairie-dog-town-1969.jpg)

[![Image 28](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/185b-1969-prairie-dog-town.jpg?w=900)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/185b-1969-prairie-dog-town.jpg)
Continued West on I-90 until we blew a tire on the U-Haul trailer by Crazy Woman Creek in the “middle of nowhere.”

[![Image 29](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/blown-u-haul-trailer-tireb.jpg?w=440)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/blown-u-haul-trailer-tireb.jpg)

Fortunately, we had cell phone service and were able to call the U-Haul emergency number. A new tire was pre-mounted on a rim and brought to us from over 40-miles away. BUT, that made us late driving through **Yellowstone NP**.

[![Image 30](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/131b-e-entrance.jpg?w=900)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/131b-e-entrance.jpg)
West Thumb Geyser Basin and Yellowstone Lake

[![Image 31](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/137b-west-thumb-geyser-basin.jpg?w=900)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/137b-west-thumb-geyser-basin.jpg)[![Image 32](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/141b.jpg?w=900)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/141b.jpg)
Crossing the Continental Divide

[![Image 33](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/144b-continental-divide.jpg?w=900)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/144b-continental-divide.jpg)
South Entrance

[![Image 34](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/145b-s-entrance.jpg?w=900)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/145b-s-entrance.jpg)
This was my sixth visit and Helen’s second, but this is my first entry on **Yellowstone NP** in this Blog. So, here is an overview of our first National Park (1872). According to Ken Burns, National Parks are “America’s Best Idea.” I have included some pics from each visit.

[![Image 35](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/1b.jpg?w=608)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/1b.jpg)

**Yellowstone NP**is in the Northwest corner of WY but also includes areas in the bordering states of MT and ID. It is a large NP and has four major areas: the #1 Geyser Basin,#2 Yellowstone Lake, #3 Mammoth Hot Springs, and #4 Grand Canyon and Falls of the Yellowstone River.

[![Image 36](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/9b.jpg?w=502)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/9b.jpg)

**#1**– the**Geyser Basin**is roughly a 30- by 45-mile oval that is the result of a collapsed volcano. Someday I would like to stay at the famous Old Faithful Lodge (1991).

[![Image 37](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/20b-old-faithful-lodge-1991.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/20b-old-faithful-lodge-1991.jpg)

Lunch in Old Faithful Lodge 2007

[![Image 38](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/41b-old-faithful-lodge-2007.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/41b-old-faithful-lodge-2007.jpg)

[![Image 39](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/40b-old-faithful-lodge-2007.jpg?w=280)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/40b-old-faithful-lodge-2007.jpg)

There are more geysers in this basin than anywhere else in the world. Geyser Hill 2007

[![Image 40](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/36b-geyser-hill-2007.jpg?w=635)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/36b-geyser-hill-2007.jpg)

Heat from deep underground magma powers the geysers, hot springs, fumaroles, and mudpots.

[![Image 41](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/12b-1.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/12b-1.jpg)

Old Faithful is the world’s best-known geyser with regular eruptions varying between 40 and 126 minutes (1967).

[![Image 42](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/17b-old-faithful-1967.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/17b-old-faithful-1967.jpg)

[![Image 43](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/18.1b-old-faithful-teapot.jpg?w=286)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/18.1b-old-faithful-teapot.jpg)

[![Image 44](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/18.2b-geyser-works.jpg?w=241)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/18.2b-geyser-works.jpg)

It is great fun to walk through the geyser fields and see, hear, smell, and feel the activity. Grotto Geyser 2007

[![Image 45](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/22b-grotto-geyser-2007-grotto-geyser.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/22b-grotto-geyser-2007-grotto-geyser.jpg)

1991

[![Image 46](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/23b-1991.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/23b-1991.jpg)

Grand Prismatic Spring 1967

[![Image 47](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/21b-1967.jpg?w=452)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/21b-1967.jpg)

Morning Glory Pool 1991

[![Image 48](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/33b-morning-glory-pool-1991.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/33b-morning-glory-pool-1991.jpg)

Firehole River 1991

[![Image 49](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/30b-firehole-river-1991.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/30b-firehole-river-1991.jpg)

Riverside Geyser 1991

**#2 – Yellowstone Lake**is noted for fishing, underwater hydrothermal vents, and a great variety of birds. It is America’s largest high-altitude lake (7,733ft).

[![Image 50](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/111b-yellowstone-lake-1967.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/111b-yellowstone-lake-1967.jpg)

The forested slopes provide habitat for many large animals – Elk 1991 –

[![Image 51](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/106b-elk-1991.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/106b-elk-1991.jpg)

Note the buffalo eyeing the trout fisherman (1991).

[![Image 52](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/108b-buffalo-fishing-friend-1991.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/108b-buffalo-fishing-friend-1991.jpg)

There have been large forest fires in the NP, but the land has made a surprisingly swift recovery.

[![Image 53](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/107b-fire-recovery-2007.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/107b-fire-recovery-2007.jpg)

In the 1960s we saw bears all over the place, on the roads, and even in our camp – one knocked over our cooler, opened it, and ran off with a pound of bacon! In 2007, we did not see any. 1967 –

[![Image 54](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/100b-bear-1967.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/100b-bear-1967.jpg)

Twin Cubs

[![Image 55](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/102b-twin-cubs-1967.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/102b-twin-cubs-1967.jpg)

Feed Me!

[![Image 56](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/104b-feed-me-1967.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/104b-feed-me-1967.jpg)

Times and conservation practices have changed. Now, buffalo are more dangerous for tourists than bears! Buffalo Herd – I did not see any buffalo here in the 1960s.

[![Image 57](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/117b-buffalo-herd-2007.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/117b-buffalo-herd-2007.jpg)

Do Not Approach Buffalo (1993)!

[![Image 58](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/123b-buffalo-2007.jpg?w=595)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/123b-buffalo-2007.jpg)

Bison = Buffalo 2007

[![Image 59](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/127b-bison-2007.jpg?w=648)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/127b-bison-2007.jpg)

Elk 2007
