# East Rock Creek Trail

Publié le 22/12/2021 par [Marie-Catherine](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/author/mcdotta/). Modifié le 14/05/2024

Contrairement à hier, la randonnée du jour se fait en mode exploration. Quelques pétroglyphes trouvés sur la falaise nous mettent en appétit. Puis, nous visitons deux alcôves abritant chacune un joli site. La découverte d’une anse de pot vient compléter cette belle journée.

Parce qu’il est rare que nous refassions deux fois les mêmes erreurs, je n’ai pas droit à ma virée champêtre autour de _Cortez_. Nous allons droit au but. Efficacité à la _Suisse_. Sur la _G road_, devant l’entrée de l’allée qui mène à une maison, un panneau jaune attire mon œil. J’y lis : _government is the virus._ Je n’ai pas le temps de déchiffrer un autre panneau, également jaune, un peu plus bas. Ce soir, en rentrant, je serai très attentive car quelque chose me dit que ça va être rigolo. Consternant, désespérant, mais drôle. Mieux vaut rire de l’idiotie et de la stupidité d’autrui.

A part le ciel un peu plus voilé qu’hier, rien n’a changé._Castle Rock_ est toujours là et, sur le sol, près d’une pierre, gît un petit tas de sable rouge, celui-là même que nous avons patiemment décollé de nos chaussures hier.

Je demande à Stefano retourner près de _Castle Rock_. J’ai de la peine à croire qu’il n’y ait pas la moindre trace visible du _pueblo_. Nous avons beau ouvrir grands nos yeux, nous ne voyons rien de rien… Et pourtant… En 1874, une expédition – _Hayden Survey_ – guidée par _John Moss_, photographia et décrivit le site. _John Moss_, qui parlait la langue Hopi, narra une légende qui fut ensuite publiée dans le [_New York Tribune_](https://crowcanyon.org/ResearchReports/CastleRock/Text/crpw_oralhistory) du 3 novembre 1874. Cette légende décrit comment le peuple qui vivait ici, paisiblement, fut petit à petit chassé de ses terres. Ni par les espagnols ou les européens, mais par les ancêtres des _Ute_.

Au printemps, lors de la floraison des fleurs des _prickly pears_, l’endroit doit être magique.

[![Image 3](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/17/SON06729-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/17/SON06729.jpg)

Nous avons deux options pour rejoindre le départ du sentier : une interdite aux chevaux, l’autre aux vélos. Aucune n’est défendue aux piétons. Ouf ! Nous choisissons celle où les vélos peuvent circuler. La trajectoire n’est pas optimale et nous soupçonnons les créateurs du tracé de s’être amusé à l’allonger au maximum, pour le plus grand bonheur de ses usagers. Une bonne partie du parcours se fait sur du _slick rock_ et, tandis que nous marchons, nous nous remémorons quelques sorties à VTT que nous avons faites à _Moab_ ou _Grand Junction_. Des sensations extraordinaires dont les souvenirs sont encore vibrants, presque 10 ans après.

[![Image 4](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/17/SON06730-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/17/SON06730.jpg)

Par endroit, quelques points blancs dessinés au sol, pour dissiper les doutes et confirmer l’itinéraire.

[![Image 5](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/17/SON06732-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/17/SON06732.jpg)

Après un peu plus de 2 kilomètres, nous arrivons à la jonction où commence le sentier vert. Il suit de façon assez rectiligne le _rim_ ouest d’un canyon. Cheminant du sud vers le nord, nous observons avec attention les parois proches sur notre gauche et celles un peu plus éloignées sur notre droite. Nous repérons très rapidement, sur le _rim_ opposé, une alcôve dans laquelle il nous semble discerner des ruines. Non loin d’un relief qui nous fait penser à la silhouette d’un château fort. Côté gauche, les falaises sont arrondies, n’offrant ni de belles surfaces où les talents artistiques des _natives_ auraient pu s’exprimer, ni belles alcôves propices à la construction d’un _pueblo_.

Nous sommes à l’entrée d’un canyon plus court que _Sand Canyon_ mais également plus large.

[![Image 6](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/17/SON06736-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/17/SON06736.jpg)

Ce caillou nous fait penser à un dessin animé ou un film d’animation dont nous n’arrivons pas à resituer le contexte. Mais il nous fait rire.

[![Image 7](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/17/SON06734-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/17/SON06734.jpg)

Même si le _slick rock_ s’est fait plus rare, le terrain est varié. Aucune ruine ou aucun dessin ne sont venus nous surprendre avant que nous arrivions au point de retour, au fond du canyon, ravis de cette première partie de randonnée. Après le passage du _wash_, le sentier reprend, cette fois direction nord vers le sud, sur le côté est du canyon.

[![Image 8](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06737-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06737.jpg)

Parvenus à la hauteur d’une voûte aperçue à l’aller, nous décidons de faire un écart pour aller la contempler de plus près. Nous suivons le lit de petits cours d’eau asséchés et éphémères, sautant d’une pierre à l’autre lorsque ceux-ci ne vont pas dans la bonne direction, afin d’épargner le _microbiotic crust_. Nous espérons y découvrir quelques dessins gravés dans la roche. Au moins un, quand même !

Plus qu’une voûte, on dirait l’entrée vers la nef d’une église. En nous approchant, nous réalisons qu’il s’agit d’une arche, puisque la partie supérieure s’est détachée de la falaise.

[![Image 9](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06738-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06738.jpg)

A cet endroit, la falaise prend un air de cathédrale. En prêtant l’oreille, il me semble entendre résonner les grandes orgues. A moins que ce ne soit le vent…

[![Image 10](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14174-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14174.jpg)

Le socle de l’ouvrage, envahi par la végétation – _juniper_, _sage brush_, sans parler des _yuccas_ aux feuilles bien pointues et des cactus aux harpons acérés – n’est pas très propice à une quelconque construction. Sans parler de l’orientation au soleil qui la place à l’ombre le matin.

[![Image 11](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06745-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06745.jpg)

Nous restons à proximité de la paroi et partons en exploration.

[![Image 12](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06746-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06746.jpg)

Dans la mesure où aucune des falaises n’est recouverte de ce beau vernis brun-rouge foncé, nous n’avons pas trop d’espoir.

[![Image 13](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06748-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06748.jpg)

Nous sommes d’autant plus contents lorsque nous dénichons quelques pétroglyphes, profondément gravés dans la roche. Pour avoir contemplés des dessins similaires, quoique beaucoup plus élaborés, notamment vers _Crow Canyon_, nous les assimilons à des épis de maïs. Ou peut-être des roseaux. Ou peut-être était-ce le symbole du clan. Qui sait ?

[![Image 14](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06749-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06749.jpg)

On ne peut pas parler ici de piquetage (_pecking_) mais plutôt d’abrasion ou d’incision (_scratching_ – _carving_). Un morceau de pierre dure, taillé en pointe, passé et repassé sur une même ligne. A chaque passage, des grains de sable qui s’égrainent, détachés du rocher par la friction. Patience et huile de coude sont les second et troisième ingrédients.

[![Image 15](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14179-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14179.jpg)

Sur un rocher, une collection de morceaux de poterie. Que nous nous empressons d’éparpiller dans le sable et dans les buissons environnants.

[![Image 16](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06753-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06753.jpg)

Guère surprenant car à quelques pas, quelques pierres encore alignées témoignent de l’existence presque oblitérée d’une construction.

[![Image 17](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06754-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06754.jpg)

Sur la droite, à environ deux mètres au-dessus du sol, des cavités creusées dans la roche, rondes et carrées, nous interpellent. Il est peu probable qu’elles aient été réalisées juste pour de l’esthétique. A quoi pouvaient-elles donc servir ? D’autant que, au fond de la niche circulaire, trois perforations de quelques centimètres de diamètre sont alignées à la verticale.

[![Image 18](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14181-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14181.jpg)

Une autre «exposition», que nous nous hâtons à nouveau de «ranger».

[![Image 19](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06760-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06760.jpg)

Quelques mètres plus loin, un autre pétroglyphes, tout près du sol.

[![Image 20](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06764-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06764.jpg)

Les lieux étaient fréquentés, c’est certain.

[![Image 21](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14187-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14187.jpg)

Peut-être que ces amas de rocher recouvrent-ils un monde perdu…

[![Image 22](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06766-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06766.jpg)

Nous errons aux alentours, à la recherche de quelques bouts de poterie affleurant au sol. Nous en trouvons quelques-uns qui nous permettent de compléter une nouvelle « exposition » à ciel ouvert laissée par nos prédécesseurs. Dont deux beaux morceaux de _corrugated_ et quelques jolis fragments de poteries peintes.

[![Image 23](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14186-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14186.jpg)

Une fois remis à leur place originelle, nous nous préparons à quitter le site. Lorsque je repère, sous une roche, une petite surface sablonneuse plane d’où émerge une pierre fine dont je ne vois que la tranche. Mon cerveau enregistre la disposition. Je fais un pas, puis deux et reviens en arrière. La courbe est trop parfaite pour être naturelle. Bien que Dame nature sache faire des choses que nous, pauvres êtres à deux pattes, soient bien loin de savoir reproduire. Néanmoins… Je m’approche et regarde de plus près. Délicatement, je passe un doigt autour et caresse la surface qui s’avère être lisse. Je réalise que je suis en présence d’un morceau de poterie. Mais certainement pas d’un objet entier car, d’après la section visible, la niche dans laquelle il se trouve n’est pas suffisamment large. Et d’autre part car après avoir délicatement tâtonné et effleuré le sable alentours, la section se termine et ne se prolonge pas. J’extrais donc précautionneusement les 2 ou 3 cm enfouis dans le sable. A quelques centimètres, un caillou, rond et gris, affleure. Qui s’avère être une anse. Entière. Ce n’est certes pas le plus gros morceau que nous ayons trouvé mais la découverte est de taille et je suis tout émue.

Une photo plus tard, je replace les objets dans leur cachette, efface mes traces de pas avec une branche de _juniper_ tombée au sol. Seul le sable déplacé est encore humide et plus foncé. D’ici une heure ou deux, rien n’indiquera la présence de ces deux « trésors ».

[![Image 24](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14191-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14191.jpg)

Remis en route, suivant toujours le flanc de la falaise, nous trouvons encore quelques dessins de plantes et des mains gravées. J’ai un faible pour les mains, peintes ou gravées : elles m’attendrissent. Car, pour chaque main représentée, une «vraie» main a été posée afin de servir de chablon (un pochoir en français de France, pour nos amis français).

[![Image 25](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14194-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14194.jpg)

Puis, encore, un reste de mur.

[![Image 26](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06770-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06770.jpg)

L’heure tourne. Nous rejoignons le sentier puis arrivons à une jonction qui permet de rejoindre le _Sand Canyon trail_ emprunté hier.

[![Image 27](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06777-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06777.jpg)

Curieux, nous le suivons un moment, afin de voir ce que nous réserve la vue après un petit promontoire. Rien qui en vaille la peine nous semble t-il. Nous revenons sur nos pas, non sans s’être approchés de l’entrée d’une ancienne mine d’uranium, creusée dans de la roche ocre. Au vu de la longueur réduite du tunnel, les prospecteurs ont vite renoncé, à moins que la galerie ne se soit effondrée. Néanmoins cette prospection se révéla suffisamment prometteuse pour qu’une route y soit construite.

[![Image 28](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06775-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06775.jpg)

De la route il n’en reste que deux vagues ornières que le sentier officiel met à profit.

[![Image 29](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06778-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06778.jpg)

Nous sommes à nouveau sur le bord est du canyon et devinons le sentier suivi ce matin. De loin, nous pouvons étudier les falaises que nous avons longées et confirmer qu’elles sont «stériles».

Par contre, de notre côté, nous repérons deux petites alcôves.

[![Image 30](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06805-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06805.jpg)

La première, à gauche, abrite une pièce carrée dont le toit est effondré. A droite, quelques restes de mur.

[![Image 31](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC06184-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC06184.jpg)

Nous renonçons à aller les voir de plus près car nous avons du plus gros gibier.

[![Image 32](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14199-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14199.jpg)

Nous nous attendons à voir une flèche indiquant _Spur trail_, comme hier. Rien. Néanmoins des traces de pas partent, déviant du sentier. Traces qui invitent, bien sûr, à une exploration. Nous perdons les traces sur un bout de _slick rock_ mais avons néanmoins une bonne idée de la direction générale.

[![Image 33](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06780-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06780.jpg)

Il nous faut néanmoins négocier le passage au _ledge_ inférieur, qui se fait somme toute assez facilement, malgré la neige, en fine couche, qui rend la pierre glissante.

[![Image 34](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06789-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06789.jpg)

Nous sommes sur un site composé de deux parties. A droite, sous un piton rocheux, un mur de pierre sèche, à la géométrie parfaite. Tellement parfaite qu’il nous fait penser à un décor de parc d’attraction.

[![Image 35](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14206-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14206.jpg)

A gauche, dans une large alcôve, un long mur rectiligne percé de petites ouvertures et d’une porte. Les petites ouvertures ont été aménagées simplement en omettant une à deux pierres. Elles devaient amener la lumière du jour et permettre à l’air de circuler. La porte, par contre, a été pensée et construite et s’ouvre dans le vide.

[![Image 36](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14202-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14202.jpg)

Nous nous approchons par le côté, afin de préserver le _miden_ et éviter l’usure de la roche. Le mur s’avère être double. Derrière, une ouverture qui a été consolidée avec du contreplaquée. Nous n’essaierons pas d’entrer ni d’aller plus loin. La maçonnerie est soignée et nous retrouvons le ciment de boue rouge consolidé de petites pierres plates.

[![Image 37](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14208-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14208.jpg)

Nous rejoignons le fond du canyon et continuons notre progression vers la seconde alcôve. En période hivernale, la végétation n’est pas trop dense et l’avancée est facile.

Le second site se concentre dans une alcôve. Son état est moins préservé que le précédent. Du mur longitudinal protégeant l’ensemble, il ne reste que quelques portions encore debout.

[![Image 38](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06794-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06794.jpg)

En retrait, plus au fond, deux pièces, l’une à l’extrême gauche et l’autre à l’extrême droite semblent avoir leurs murs plus ou moins intacts. Entre, c’est un peu l’hécatombe, avec des pierres éparpillées au sol, indiquant que d’autres structures étaient là, aujourd’hui écroulées.

[![Image 39](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14221-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/DSC14221.jpg)

Nous nous remettons en route.

[![Image 40](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06792-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/22/SON06792.jpg)

Nous voudrions aller voir de plus près les ruines près du « château fort » entraperçues ce matin. Cependant, nous n’arrivons pas à les localiser. Il nous semble reconnaître un profil familier mais l’alcôve à proximité est vide. Avons-nous rêvé ? L’endroit repéré n’est-il pas le bon ? Mystère que nous gardons entier pour notre prochaine visite. Il y a encore des choses à explorer et c’est tant mieux.

Roulant sur la _G road_ en direction de _Cortez_, je me dévisse le cou, guettant le petit panneau jaune aperçu ce matin. Mes efforts sont récompensés. Le text _Government is the virus_ est complété fort à propos par _Freedom is the vaccine._ Sans surprise, nous sommes dans le même registre. A quelques mètres, un mat et un drapeau qui flotte au vent sur lequel est écrit :_pray to end abortion_. Sans commentaire.

Pour fêter nos découvertes et notre belle journée, nous dînons à la Fiesta Mexicana. A 18h30, nous sommes repus et douchés. A 20h30 et des poussières, les feux s’éteignent.

#### À voir aussi ...

[![Image 44: Le long des falaises d'Indian Creek](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/23/le-long-des-falaise-dindian-creek-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/le-long-des-falaise-dindian-creek/ "Le long des falaise d’Indian Creek")
#### [Le long des falaise d’Indian Creek](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/le-long-des-falaise-dindian-creek/ "Le long des falaise d’Indian Creek")

Nous nous déplaçons de Cortez vers Monticello qui sera notre camp de base pour les 4 nuits à venir. Au programme de la journée, une re-visite de Shay Canyon et l'exploration d'une portion des falaises qui longent la route, le long de Indian Creek. Nos trouvailles dépassent nos espérances.

[![Image 45: Barrage d'Agaro - Corte Verde](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/08/barrage-dagaro-corte-verde-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/barrage-dagaro-corte-verde/ "Barrage d’Agaro – Corte Verde")
#### [Barrage d’Agaro – Corte Verde](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/barrage-dagaro-corte-verde/ "Barrage d’Agaro – Corte Verde")

Partis de Goglio, nous montons vers Ausone et le Lago di Agaro. Nous le trouvons partiellement gelé et une coulée de neige traversant le sentier qui mène à sa pointe nord nous stoppe très rapidement. S'ensuit un petit détour vers Corte Verde avant de redescendre à la voiture par Costa.

[![Image 46: Lago Tomeo](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/30/lago-tomeo-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/lago-tomeo/ "Lago Tomeo")
#### [Lago Tomeo](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/lago-tomeo/ "Lago Tomeo")

Parce qu'il ne faut pas tirer sur la corde, la balade du jour est choisie en fonction de son faible dénivelé. Le lago di Tomé est petit et encaissé mais la vue depuis Corte Piatto, au pied du Monte Zucchero est exceptionnelle. Néanmoins, à part une ou deux sections, le…

[![Image 47: Salmon Ruins](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/19/salmon-ruins-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/salmon-ruins/ "Salmon Ruins")
#### [Salmon Ruins](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/salmon-ruins/ "Salmon Ruins")

En transit entre Alamosa et Cortez, nous faisons une première halte à Conejos pour admirer l'église la plus ancienne du Colorado encore en activité et le Veterans Boulevard. Puis, un second arrêt à Bloomfield, au Nouveau Mexique, pour visiter Salmon Ruins, un site composé d'un musée et d'un village chacoan…

[![Image 48: Mesa Verde](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2012/12/mesa-verde-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/mesa-verde/ "Mesa Verde")
#### [Mesa Verde](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/mesa-verde/ "Mesa Verde")

Première visite du parc national de Mesa Verde, et de ses incroyables ruines Anasazi. À l'époque, en 2008, nous nous intéressions peu à la culture des Ancestral Puebloans.

[![Image 49: Rifugio Fiorasca](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/29/rifugio-fiorasca-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/rifugio-fiorasca/ "Rifugio Fiorasca")
#### [Rifugio Fiorasca](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/rifugio-fiorasca/ "Rifugio Fiorasca")

Une montée de 1'800 mètres et des poussières qui restera gravée dans notre mémoire, tout comme le passage de la Bochetta di Fiorasca, où, parait-il on faisait passer les vaches pour rejoindre le taureau qui attendait à Alpe di Brünesc. Nous avons de la peine à imaginer un bovidé sur ces…

# Canyons of the Ancients National Monument

Le**Canyons of the Ancients National Monument** est un monument national américain situé au sud-ouest de l’État du Colorado, dans la région des Four Corners.

Il a été désigné le 9 juin 2000 par proclamation présidentielle afin de protéger les ressources culturelles et archéologiques locales.

‎Le Monument est géré par le Bureau of Land Management (BLM). Il englobe une surface de 663 km2 tout en entourant trois des quatre sections du monument [Hovenweep National Monument](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/destinations/hovenweep-national-monument/), qui est administré par le National Park Service.

La ville la plus proche est Cortez, située à environ 16 km.

Site web de référence : _[Canyons of the Ancients | Bureau of Land Management](https://www.blm.gov/programs/national-conservation-lands/colorado/canyons-of-the-ancients)_

## NP Unit Road Trip OH, KY, MO, NM, CO, UT, and NE

July 5, 2019 

The following describes a 6,400 mile National Park Unit road trip to sites in OH, KY, MO, NM, CO, UT, and NE

**6/11 Tu** – **William Howard Taft National Historic Site**. Helen and I did the house tour on one of our trips to Cincy, however, I did not have any photos. So, I felt I had to return.

[![Image 2](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/1b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/1b.jpg)

27 th U.S. President, 1909-1913

[![Image 3](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/2b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/2b.jpg)

He was the only President to have also served as chief justice of the Supreme Court (1921-1930)

[![Image 4](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/9b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/9b.jpg)

3hrs to **Mill Spring Battlefield National Monument**KY. This was the site of the Union’s first decisive Civil War victory on January 19,1862; 4,400 Union troops turned back about 5,900 Confederates. It became a National Monument in 2019.

[![Image 5](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4669b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4669b.jpg)

I began my tour by walking through the adjacent National Cemetery. Union casualties amounted to 40 killed, 207 wounded, and 15 missing; Confederate losses were 125 killed, 309 wounded, and 95 missing.

[![Image 6](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4670b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4670b.jpg)

Overview

[![Image 7](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4671b.jpg?w=450)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4671b.jpg)

I did auto tour stops 1-8 (15mi) driving from the Visitors Center south to the Cumberland River

[![Image 8](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4682b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4682b.jpg)

[![Image 9](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4684b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4684b.jpg)

There was an interesting 0.5mi trail at Zollicoffer Park where the fiercest fighting took place

[![Image 10](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4689b.jpg?w=450&h=310)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4689b.jpg)

Confederate Cemetery

[![Image 11](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4686b.jpg?w=450&h=316)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4686b.jpg)

Zollicoffer monument

[![Image 12](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4688b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4688b.jpg)

Ferry Landing on Cumberland River

[![Image 13](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4709b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4709b.jpg)

[![Image 14](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4710b.jpg?w=450&h=337)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4710b.jpg)

4.5hrs to **Parker’s Cross Roads National Battlefield Park** TN (Affiliated Park Unit).

[![Image 15](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4718b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4718b.jpg)

[![Image 16](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4712b.jpg?w=450&h=292)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4712b.jpg)

In late 1862, Confederate Brig. Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest’s cavalry campaign (1800 men) in Western TN had been successful in harassing Union forces, destroying railroads, and disrupting communications. When Forest reached Parker’s Cross Roads on December 31 st, a part of Brig. Gen Jeremiah C. Sullivan’s (3000 men) Union forces under Col. Cyrus Dunham tried to cut Forest off from retreating back across the Tennessee River. Forest successfully attacked Dunham and demanded an unconditional surrender, Dunham refused.

[![Image 17](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4741b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4741b.jpg)

[![Image 18](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4740b.jpg?w=450&h=315)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4740b.jpg)

Forest was then attacked from the north by the other part of Sullivan’s forces under Col. John Fuller. Forest ordered attacks on both fronts and then retreated across the Tennessee River to Lexington TN.

[![Image 19](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4734b.jpg?w=450&h=610)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4734b.jpg)

[![Image 20](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4735b.jpg?w=450&h=592)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4735b.jpg)

The Confederates had about 500 casualties and the Union 237. Because Forest had been successful in his Western TN campaign up to this point, and was able to escape, Confederates called this a victory. However, Union forcess claimed victory as well. A Confederate bias can be noted in this description.

[![Image 21](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4721b.jpg?w=450&h=675)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/img_4721b.jpg)

[![Image 22](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4719b.jpg?w=450&h=322)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4719b.jpg)

In April 1864, troops under Forrest’s command massacred Union troops who had surrendered, most of them black soldiers along with some white fighting for the Union, at the Battle of Fort Pillow. Forest joined the Ku Klux Klan in 1867 and was elected its first Grand Wizard.

**6/17 M** – After a 1.5hr drive, I arrived at **Chimney Rock National Monument**(USFS) in southwest CO at 8am. It opened at nine, so I took a few pictures and had my standard breakfast of Honey-Nut Cheerios and an orange.

[![Image 132](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4982b.jpg?w=450&h=300)](https://tomhelenmartinblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/img_4982b.jpg)

There were two nice displays at the entrance gate. Designated in 2012 by President Barack Obama, making it the seventh national monument managed by the USDA Forest Service. The Chimney Rock National Monument encompasses 4,726 acres of the San Juan National Forest between Durango and Pagosa Springs, Colorado. Chimney Rock represents one of the largest Pueblo II (900-1150 AD) communities in southwestern Colorado and is considered a Chacoan cultural “outlier.” The Chaco phenomenon was a complex system of dispersed communities bound by economic, political and religious interdependence centered in Chaco Canyon, New Mexico. The pinnacles that give Chimney Rock its name frame multiple astronomical alignments. The Ancestral Puebloans incorporated their knowledge of astronomy into the design of their community. Today Chimney Rock is one of the best recognized archaeo-astronomical resources in North America, with alignments with the northern lunar standstill, summer solstice, equinoxes and Crab Nebula. Chimney Rock preserves 200 ancient homes and ceremonial buildings, some of which have been excavated for viewing and exploration: a Great Kiva, a Pit House, a Multi-Family Dwelling, and a Chacoan-style Great House Pueblo. Chimney Rock is the highest in elevation of all the Chacoan sites, at about 7,400 feet above sea level.

As it turned dark, it started to storm and continued for over two hours as I drove south through the San Juan Mountains of SW CO.

1.   There is a 2000ft gain in elevation from Montrose (5,807ft) to Ouray (7,792ft)
2.   From Ouray to Silverton (9,320) you cross Red Mountain Pass (11,075ft)
3.   From Silverton to Durango (6,512ft) you cross Molas Pass (10,910ft) and then Coal Bank Hill Pass (10,640ft)

The section from Ouray to Silverton is called the “Million Dollar Highway.” It is said that it cost one million dollars per mile to build in the 1920s. This is a difficult drive during the day in good weather. I drove it at night during a storm – torrential rain, snow/sleet, wind, fog, etc.! I encountered deer, rocks, standing water, and trees on the road. Water was crashing off the cliffs and running across the road. It was horrible driving necessitating 5-10mph on numerous blind hairpin turns. According to Wikipedia, “. . . the route is characterized by steep cliffs, narrow lanes, and a lack of guardrails; the ascent of Red Mountain Pass is marked with a number of hairpin curves used to gain elevation, and again, narrow lanes for traffic—many cut directly into the sides of mountains. Travel north from Silverton to Ouray allows drivers to hug the inside of curves; travel south from Ouray to Silverton perches drivers on the vertiginous outside edge of the highway.”

It cleared by the time I got to Durango and then it was a straight shot to Cortez on Rt160. I arrived at my Super 8 Motel after midnight for a two-night stay.

# Railroad Panel au Grand Gulch

Publié le 10/11/2019 par [Marie-Catherine](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/author/mcdotta/). Modifié le 19/01/2026

Avant-hier soir, à notre retour du _Grand Gulch_, Stefano s’est rendu compte que, entre _Fortress Ruin_ et _Round House Ruin_, il y avait _Railroad Panel_, un magnifique panneau de pétroglyphes dont une des formes dessinées ressemble à une locomotive sur une voie ferrée. Lorsqu’il m’a montré les photos, je me suis écriée : il faut que nous y retournions !

Nous renonçons donc à l’activité prévue par Stefano, pour retourner au _Grand Gulch_ via le _Government Trail_.

Voilà pourquoi, ce matin, cette photo a un air de déjà-vu.

[![Image 3](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04055-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04055.jpg)

Nous en profiterons pour faire d’une pierre deux coups. Retourner voir _Round House Ruin_, en espérant que les ruines soient moins à l’ombre, puis chercher et, espérons, trouver le _Railroad Panel_.

Tiens, mais il y a quelques nuages dans le ciel ce matin…

La marche jusqu’au départ du sentier officiel se fait d’un pas rapide. Chacun a son ornière et nous pouvons marcher de front, conversant de choses et d’autres. L’air est frais et la lumière différente d’il y a deux jours.

[![Image 4](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04061-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04061.jpg)

Le réservoir sans son eau, comme il y a deux jours…

[![Image 5](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04062-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04062.jpg)

Stefano, en train de faire ses devoirs du matin. Il remarque qu’un groupe de 9 personnes est passé ce matin.

[![Image 6](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04063-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04063.jpg)

Arrivés au bord du _rim_, nous dégustons la premième _Clif Bar_ du jour, et nous arrêtons un moment à contempler _Polly’s Island_ et la portion du _Grand Gulch_ qui s’offre à nos yeux. Soudain, j’entends le raclement d’une chaussure sur le _slick rock_. Je me retourne et vois deux randonneurs, assis. Nous ne les avions tout simplement pas vus. Ils viennent vers nous : ce sont les accompagnateurs du groupe de 9 personnes.

Les pièces du puzzle se mettent en place. Il y a deux jours, en quittant la _UT-261_ pour la piste, nous avions aperçu un groupe de _hikers_, sur une plateforme de _slick rock_, en train de préparer leurs sacs. Nous en avions conclu qu’ils avaient passé la nuit sur place, ce qui nous avait semblé un peu étrange compte tenu de la proximité de la route.

Le soir, en rentrant, nous les avions retrouvés, au même endroit. Encore plus étrange. Mais maintenant tout s’explique. Ils font partie d’un cours organisé par _[NOLS](https://www.nols.edu/)_. Nous apercevons le groupe en bas qui se dirige _upstream_. Tant mieux. Nous serons seuls puisque allant dans la direction opposée.

La descente dans le _Grand Gulch_ est expéditive. Nous ne voulons pas perdre de temps et arriver le plus tôt possible à _Round House Ruin_. Nous laissons derrière nous _Polly’s Island._

[![Image 7](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04066-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04066.jpg)

La magie du _Grand Gulch_ s’opère. Tous nos sens sont en éveil. Nos mollets aussi d’ailleurs, à cause de la marche dans le sable.

[![Image 8](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04071-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04071.jpg)

_Cottonwood trees_.

[![Image 9](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04070-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04070.jpg)

Une heure et demi plus tard, nous arrivons en vue de _Round House Ruin_.

[![Image 10](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04073-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04073.jpg)

Même s’il y a deux jours nous avions trouvé un moyen de monter sur le _ledge_, nous avons pris la décision de ne pas essayer.

[![Image 11](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11868-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11868.jpg)

Nous les contemplerons du bas. C’est ce passage qui nous semble un peu problématique. Nul besoin de se casser le cou, même pour de belles ruines.

[![Image 12](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11863-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11863.jpg)

Et belles, elles le sont !

[![Image 13](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01630-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01630.jpg)

_Round House_ est si… ronde.

[![Image 14](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01631-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01631.jpg)

Nous faisons demi-tour et nous mettons en mode exploration. Nous n’avons aucune idée de l’endroit où se trouve _Railroad Panel_ mais nous avons la journée pour le découvrir, si ce n’est qu’il est situé quelques part entre _Fortress Ruin_ et _Round House Ruin_. Ce qui devrait suffire.

Nous trouvons d’autres mains rouges…

[![Image 15](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11869-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11869.jpg)

et tout près, quelques pictogrammes blancs et délavés.

[![Image 16](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01632-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01632.jpg)

Toujours pas de _Railroad Panel_ en vue.

[![Image 17](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04081-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04081.jpg)

Nous retournons voir le replat où nous avions trouvé quelques pétroglyphes. Nous explorons plus minutieusement l’endroit. Rien. C’est en revenant vers le _wash_ que nous l’apercevons, de l’autre côté. _Yes!_

[![Image 18](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01634-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01634.jpg)

Il est bien là, même si nous ne discernons pas très bien les motifs.

[![Image 19: Nous sommes arrivés au Railroad Panel, enorme panneau de pétroglyphes au Grand Gulch.](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11896-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11896.jpg)

Le contraste entre le vernis et la pierre mise à nue est tel que les dessins paraissent avoir été gravés hier.

[![Image 20: Vue d'ensemble du Railroad Panel, un panneau exceptionnel situé dans le Grand Gulch.](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11895-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11895.jpg)

Nous restons bouche bée.

[![Image 21: Vue d'ensemble de l'extraordinaire Railroad Panel, au Grand Gulch.](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11891-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11891.jpg)

Peut-être plus marquant que la «locomotive», le dessin qui ressemble à un paquebot, avec ses trois cheminées.

[![Image 22: Quelques détails choisis de l'incroyable Railroad Panel, au Grand Gulch.](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/Aggregation01_20191110-1040x585.png)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/Aggregation01_20191110.png)

La partie droite du panneau est beaucoup plus ancienne : les pétroglyphes sont moins nets et différentes époques se sont enchaînées, où des dessins plus récents se superposant à ceux plus anciens.

[![Image 23: Le côté droit du Railroad Panel, comprenant des pétroglyphes plus anciens.](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04089-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04089.jpg)

Deux belles spirales terminent le panneau.

[![Image 24](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04090-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04090.jpg)

Il est midi lorsque nous nous décidons à bouger. Nous optons pour la remontée par _Polly’s Canyon_, histoire de varier l’itinéraire. En plus, nous n’avons fait que le descendre.

Nous revenons sur nos pas et laissons à droite le départ du _Government Trail_.

[![Image 25](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04092-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04092.jpg)

_Polly’s Canyon_ étant bien moins fréquenté que le _Grand Gulch_, le sentier est moins net et la végétation ne s’est pas gênée pour remplir les espaces. La Nature a horreur du vide, avons-nous coutume de dire.

[![Image 26](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01645-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01645.jpg)

_Polly’s Canyon Arch_, moins de 500 mètres après l’entrée du canyon.

[![Image 27](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11899-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC11899.jpg)

Jeux d’ombre et de lumière.

[![Image 28](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04095-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04095.jpg)

A quelques reprises, le sentier devient difficile et nous devons contourner des obstacles.

[![Image 29](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04096-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04096.jpg)

Stefano marchant sur du _slick rock_, durant un court moment de répit.

[![Image 30](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04097-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04097.jpg)

Le répit est effectivement de courte durée.

[![Image 31](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04099-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04099.jpg)

Nous rencontrons deux randonneurs, marchant dans le même sens que nous. Ils ont fait un détour par les ruines, ruines que nous avions explorées en 2016 lors notre descente par _[Polly’s Canyon](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/pollys-canyon/)_. Aujourd’hui, nous sommes un peu trop à court en temps pour pouvoir y monter.

Le passage d’un _pour-off_ nous oblige le contourner en montant sur le _ledge_. Bon, c’est aussi parce que Stefano n’a pas eu assez confiance en mes capacités de chamois.

[![Image 32](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04102-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04102.jpg)

Les parois du canyon deviennent moins hautes signalant que la sortie est proche.

[![Image 33](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04105-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04105.jpg)

La remontée sur le _rim_ est beaucoup moins technique que dans nos souvenirs. Nous n’avons même pas besoin d’utiliser les mains pour nous accrocher aux rochers.

[![Image 34](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04107-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04107.jpg)

À partir de là, il nous faudra presque une heure pour rejoindre la voiture. La faute au _microbiotic crust_.

[![Image 35](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04109-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/SON04109.jpg)

Nous zigzaguons au gré des _social trails_ jusqu’à arriver au réservoir. Sitôt que nous retrouvons la piste, nous reprenons notre marche d’un bon pas et arrivons à la voiture à 17h15, alors que le soleil vient de disparaître derrière l’horizon.

[![Image 36](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01652-1040x585.jpg)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/10/DSC01652.jpg)

C’est notre dernière nuit à _Blanding_. Nous apprécions d’autant plus le retour : les longues lignes droites avant d’arriver à la _Kane Gulch Ranger Station_, le passage de _Salvation Knoll_, la vision du _Comb Ridge_, sa traversée entre les deux murailles et les derniers virages avant de rejoindre la _UT-191_.

#### À voir aussi ...

[![Image 38: Fortress Ruin au Grand Gulch](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/08/fortress-ruin-au-grand-gulch-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/fortress-ruin-au-grand-gulch/ "Fortress Ruin au Grand Gulch")
#### [Fortress Ruin au Grand Gulch](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/fortress-ruin-au-grand-gulch/ "Fortress Ruin au Grand Gulch")

Retour dans le Grand Gulch pour notre plus grand plaisir. Après une petit visite à Polly's Island Ruins, nous descendons le wash avec un objectif certain : Fortress Ruin. Un bel ensemble de ruines dont un mur, percé de plusieurs ouvertures qui ressemblent à des meurtrières.

[![Image 39: Grand Gulch par Kane Gulch](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2014/04/05/grand-gulch-par-kane-gulch-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/grand-gulch-par-kane-gulch/ "Grand Gulch par Kane Gulch")
#### [Grand Gulch par Kane Gulch](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/grand-gulch-par-kane-gulch/ "Grand Gulch par Kane Gulch")

Kane Gulch est un canyon qui se termine dans le Grand Gulch. Longtemps peuplée par les Native Americans, la région recèle de nombreux témoignages de cette occupation.

[![Image 40: Polly's Canyon, près du Grand Gulch, dans l'Utah.](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/01/polly-canyon-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/pollys-canyon/ "Polly’s Canyon")
#### [Polly’s Canyon](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/pollys-canyon/ "Polly’s Canyon")

Nous allons revoir Big Man Panel. Nous allons rejoindre le Grand Gulch via Polly Canyon. Le beau temps est revenu. Pas de sentier mais des surprises à chaque méandre du wash. Que du bonheur !

[![Image 41: Big Man Panel - Grand Gulch - Utah](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/01/big-man-panel-2016-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/big-man-panel-2016/ "Big Man Panel en 2016")
#### [Big Man Panel en 2016](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/big-man-panel-2016/ "Big Man Panel en 2016")

Nous remontons le Grand Gulch en direction du Big Man Panel. Nous nous réjouissons de cette seconde visite car, depuis 2011, nous avons beaucoup approfondi nos connaissances sur les Ancestral Puebloans.

[![Image 42: Big Man Panel - Grand Gulch - Utah](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2011/09/20/big-man-panel-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/big-man-panel/ "Big Man Panel")
#### [Big Man Panel](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/big-man-panel/ "Big Man Panel")

Première visite Big de Man Panel, un panneau représentant deux anthropomorphes (homme et femme ?), situé dans le Grand Gulch. A proximité de Blanding, Utah.

[![Image 43: Bannister House Ruin](https://i0.wp.com/www.twoswisshikers.net/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/26/bannister-ruins-featured.jpg?resize=600%2C240&ssl=1)](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/collins-canyon/ "Collins Canyon")
#### [Collins Canyon](https://www.twoswisshikers.net/articles/collins-canyon/ "Collins Canyon")

Nous descendons une nouvelle fois dans le Grand Gulch mais cette fois par Collins Canyon. Notre objectif du jour est d'aller voir Bannister Ruins. Mais avant, nous suivons les conseils de randonneurs et faisons un détour par les Narrows où se trouvent deux panneaux de pictogrammes.

# Day 59-60: Canyons of the Ancients National Monument

April 15, 2025

It was midmorning by the time we left our campsite for the last two nights (thanks, Boggy Draw Trails!), heading to the [Canyons of the Ancients Visitor Center & Museum](link_5). Canyons of the Ancients contains the highest known archaeological site density in the United States, although you’re more likely to see various objects, dwellings, and human remains of Indigenous people who have lived here in a museum rather than on a hike. It costs $7 to check out the museum at the Canyons of the Ancients Visitor Center, but we decided to spend our time hiking the various pueblo sites that make up the Canyons. Similar to when we visited the Petroglyph National Monument in Albuquerque, the pueblos are a significant drive away – we planned a curved drive from the Visitor Center, stopping by Lowry Pueblo (24 miles away), then to Painted Hand Pueblo and Hovenweep National Monument Visitor Center (the furthest west), before looping back west to the Sand Canyon Trail System.

## Lowry Pueblo: The Great House & Great Kiva

On the decent drive to Lowry Pueblo, we saw a lot of prairie dogs scurrying across the road in front of us along the way. When we first saw prairie dogs in New Mexico, we thought they looked like meerkats, and their name is indeed a misnomer – they’re a type of burrowing ground squirrel native to the grasslands of North America. It was a fairly quiet drive where we could take in the fertile scenery around us – not many cars, and the noisiest it got was when we drove onto unpaved road as we got closer to Lowry, making our RV jolt around with each hurdle.

![Image 3: Only one parked at Lowry Pueblo](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Only-one-parked-at-Lowry-Pueblo.jpg)

Only one parked at Lowry Pueblo

![Image 4: Amazing brickwork](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Amazing-brickwork.jpg)

Amazing brickwork

![Image 5: The Great Kiva](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/The-Great-Kiva.jpg)

The Great Kiva

We were the only visitors at Lowry Pueblo, which has a short trail where we saw two attractions – the first was the Great House, a 40+ room pueblo. The second was the impressive and well-named Great Kiva, a meeting place over 15 meters (nearly 50 feet) in diameter, where dances and religious ceremonies and other rituals were held. The sunken remains of this Ancestral Puebloan site were probably constructed around 1090 AD.

## Painted Hand Pueblo

Our next stop was over 20 kilometers (13 miles) away, at the Painted Hand Pueblo, 13 miles away. This is where we trusted the signs and ignored Google Maps, which informed us to turn left (instead of straight at an intersection, which had a sign), which would take an hour and 5 minutes! It may have been because Google didn’t recognize the unpaved road to get there.

![Image 6: Google maps telling us to drive an hour when the trail was 4 mins away](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Google-maps-telling-us-to-drive-an-hour-when-the-trail-was-4-mins-away-473x1024.jpg)

Google maps telling us to drive an hour when the trail was 4 mins away

![Image 7: Only people parked yet again at Painted Hand Pueblo](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Only-people-parked-yet-again-at-Painted-Hand-Pueblo.jpg)

Only people parked yet again at Painted Hand Pueblo

![Image 8: Looking over the edge](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Looking-over-the-edge.jpg)

Looking over the edge

![Image 9: Some ruins](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Some-ruins.jpg)

Some ruins

At this site, we saw a small pueblo that once had about 20 rooms, which was built around 1200 AD. It started to get hot as we hiked, but we saw more pueblos, and we were lucky to have the place all to ourselves again!

## Hovenweep Visitor Center: Filled with Pueblos, Cliff Dwellings & Castles

At Hovenweep Visitor Center, we finally encountered other visitors, and more people along the trail. Hovenweep means “deserted valley” in the Ute/Paiute language, and in 1923 President Warren G. Harding proclaimed Hovenweep a national monument.

![Image 10: Hovenweep National Monument](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Hovenweep-National-Monument.jpg)

Hovenweep National Monument

![Image 11: Ruins along the ridge](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Ruins-along-the-ridge-768x1024.jpg)

Ruins along the ridge

![Image 12: Hovenweep Castle](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Hovenweep-Castle.jpg)

Hovenweep Castle

While the Visitor Center was closed, the hike was awesome – we saw tall towers, outlines of multiroom pueblos, tumbled stone piles, and small cliff dwellings scattered across the canyon landscape. It’s incredible to try and imagine what it was like hundreds of years ago. Along the trail, we saw that researchers are conducting an interesting experiment on Hovenweep Castle from February 2025 to February 2026. The castle has been chosen for a vibration study, which will assess how the structures in the area respond to vibration energy inputs – including from wind, earthquakes, explosions, and passive vehicles – and how this affects the deterioration of the buildings. There was cabling, solar panels and a data collection box, so visitors need to be careful that they don’t disturb the items to affect the study!

## A Bumpy Ride Toward Sand Canyon

What was significantly less entertaining, however, was the undulating roads, which made our RV bounce violently up and down at some points, making us nervous about the impact it could have on our pipes immediately below. At one point, we jumped when we heard a loud crash below us, anxiously worrying that something had been damaged, but fortunately it seemed to have hit our (currently not functional) self-leveling system.

We finally arrived at Sand Canyon and Rock Creek Trail System, which entails a much longer hike to see a spate of pueblos. At the entrance, we had a brief chat with a man who’d been living the nomadic lifestyle for a while, and had ridden his motorbike all the way up to Alaska, the Arctic Circle, and many other places, although he’s been in Colorado for the last year. He gave a glowing endorsement of Sand Canyon, and while it was already late afternoon and the sun was starting to set, we decided to hike a little bit of the trail, taking Sheila with us, who at one point sidled right up to a cactus to pee!

![Image 13: Almost the only ones parked again at Sand Canyon](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Almost-the-only-ones-parked-again-at-Sand-Canyon.jpg)

Almost the only ones parked again at Sand Canyon

![Image 14: Sand Canyon hike in the afternoon](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Sand-Canyon-hike-in-the-afternoon.jpg)

Sand Canyon hike in the afternoon

As there were no signs saying we couldn’t stick around, we stayed at Sand Canyon for the night, enjoying a quiet and peaceful evening ahead of tackling the trail the following morning.

The last stop on Canyons of the Ancients National Monument was looping back toward San Canyon Rock Creek Trail System. Again, it’s a decent drive, but we were entertained by the fascinating views of the green-dotted, fertile western Colorado landscape, which was also at times in stark contrast to the other side of the road, which was more barren, with rich brown dirt.

## Hiking the Sand Canyon Trail

When we woke up, there were already several empty cars parked, indicating that quite a few other folks had beat us to hike Sand Canyon Trail. Our plan was to hike just over 9.6 kilometers (6 miles) in and out, as the attractions were all within 3 miles into the trail – namely, Saddlehorn Pueblo (mile 1), Corncob House, Double Cliff House (mile 2), and Sunny Alcove, Tucked Award Two Story House, Wall Curves with Bedrock House, House with Standing Curved Wall (mile 3). After that, there are no more pueblos, and there are some steep switchbacks after mile 4 at a 213 meters (700 feet) elevation gain.

![Image 15: Crazy looking rock formations](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Crazy-looking-rock-formations.jpg)

Crazy looking rock formations

![Image 16: You can get up close to the ruins at Sand Canyon](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/You-can-get-up-close-to-the-ruins-at-Sand-Canyon.jpg)

You can get up close to the ruins at Sand Canyon

![Image 17: One of the larger buildings in a cave](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/One-of-the-larger-buildings-in-a-cave.jpg)

One of the larger buildings in a cave

![Image 18: Imagine living here hundreds of years ago](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Imagine-living-here-hundreds-of-years-ago.jpg)

Imagine living here hundreds of years ago

The pueblos were incredible, because they’re all quite high up above where we were standing, and are impressively compacted within the caves! There’s also a ton of Mormon/Brigham tea plants, Utah juniper (often right next to each other), and cacti to keep the trail interesting. It seems that this area is also popular to explore on horseback, as there are other trails dedicated to horses (and we saw lots of evidence of this with their poop too)!

In the afternoon it was all about errands – filling up on petrol, emptying our grey/black water tanks for free at a spot in Cortez (water refills were about 25c for 12 gallons, so we spent $1), laundry, and more groceries (again! We go through yogurt and drinks at an outrageous pace).

Next stop: Mesa Verde National Park!

## Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difficulty level of the Sand Canyon Pueblo Trail?
The Sand Canyon Pueblo Trail is generally rated as **moderate to difficult**. While some sections involve moderate canyon walking on uneven rock, the upper portion of the trail is notably steep and rugged, including a challenging stretch with 30 switchbacks that gain approximately 700 feet in elevation over about half a mile. Hikers should plan their turnaround point based on their fitness level and available time.

What kind of terrain can I expect on the trail?
You'll encounter diverse terrain, including slickrock, sandy washes, and areas with loose rock. The trail winds through quiet red-rock country, past dramatic sandstone bluffs, and through pinyon and juniper forests. As you ascend, you'll get wide-open views across branching canyons.

What archaeological sites can I see along the Sand Canyon Pueblo Trail?
The trail offers access to numerous Ancestral Puebloan archaeological sites. Key sites visible include **Castle Rock Pueblo** near the southern trailhead, **Saddlehorn Pueblo**, and the significant **Sand Canyon Pueblo**. You can also spot smaller habitation sites like Wall Curves with Bedrock House, Corncob House, and Double Cliff House. Interpretive signs provide historical context, and binoculars are recommended for viewing distant structures.

Where is the trailhead for the Sand Canyon Pueblo Trail located?
The Sand Canyon Pueblo Trail is located within the Canyons of the Ancients National Monument near Cortez, Colorado. The southern trailhead is situated near Castle Rock Pueblo.

Do I need a permit or is there an entrance fee for the Canyons of the Ancients National Monument?
There is no entrance fee for Canyons of the Ancients National Monument itself. However, visitors should always check the official Bureau of Land Management (BLM) website for any specific regulations or permits that might be required for certain activities or areas within the monument. You can find more information on the [BLM website](link_12).

Is the Sand Canyon Pueblo Trail dog-friendly?
Information regarding dog policies for this specific trail within Canyons of the Ancients National Monument is not explicitly provided in the research. Generally, national monuments have specific rules for pets, often requiring them to be on a leash and restricting access to certain archaeological sites. It's best to check the official Canyons of the Ancients National Monument website or contact the BLM directly for current pet regulations before your visit.

What is the best time of year to hike the Sand Canyon Pueblo Trail?
Given the trail has little to no shade, spring and fall are generally the best times to hike to avoid the extreme heat of summer and potential snow or ice in winter. During these seasons, temperatures are more moderate, making for a more enjoyable experience. Always check weather conditions before heading out.

What should I bring for a hike on this trail?
Due to the lack of shade, ample water and sun protection (hat, sunscreen, sunglasses) are essential. Sturdy hiking shoes are recommended for the varied and sometimes rugged terrain. Binoculars will enhance your experience by allowing you to spot distant archaeological structures. Always carry a map and be prepared for changing weather conditions.

Is the Sand Canyon Pueblo Trail a loop or an out-and-back?
The Sand Canyon Pueblo Trail is primarily an out-and-back trail, with a considerable length of 6.5 miles one-way. Hikers often plan their turnaround point based on their fitness and time constraints.

Are there any specific regulations for visiting the archaeological sites?
Yes, it is crucial to stay on designated trails and **never disturb or touch the fragile archaeological sites**. These sites are protected by law. Visitors are encouraged to observe them from a distance and use binoculars for closer views. Respecting these rules helps preserve these invaluable historical resources for future generations.

Is the Sand Canyon Pueblo Trail suitable for families with young children?
Due to its rating as moderate to difficult, with steep and rugged sections and a considerable length (6.5 miles one-way), the full Sand Canyon Pueblo Trail may not be suitable for very young children or those unaccustomed to strenuous hiking. However, families might enjoy shorter, easier sections near the trailheads, but should be prepared for uneven terrain and lack of shade.

# Our Ultimate North American Route

Michael and Lisette (mostly Michael), spent almost 3 months researching to come up with a route tat would allow them to take in all 48 of the lower US states along with a few Canadian provinces. This route is specific to us as we had already roadtripped extensively throughout the west coast while living in San Francisco and didn't need to revisit many of those places, even though they were some of the most amazing destinations in the country. That's why you won't see Yosemite or anything really along the HWY 1 coastline from San Diego to northern Oregon.  
  
We'll do our best to keep updating the route from red to green as we make our way along. Please note that there will likely be a delay of at least a few days while we're on the road.

![Image 2: Route-1](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Route-1-1.jpg)
## Update 1:

Due to the challenges of living on the road, it is significantly more difficult to perform some tasks. One of those is renewing Michael's Australian passport. While it is not due to expire until the end of September, that means he will not have 6 months remaining when we re-enter the US from Canada and that could cause issues.  
  
Given this fact we have decided not to cross the border into Canada on this trip. This gives us an extra 24 days to re-jig the itinerary and make adjustments to the route.  
  
Below is a work-in-progress of those changes but we are always open to suggestions on what might be good to see that isn't a huge diversion from the original plan.  
  
In the map below you will see some different colors now. Green is still where we have been, red is the original route, orange markers have been added to reflect potential new stops and the orange lines indicate potentially new routes. The blue lines indicate where we have removed sections of the old route and finally the purple markers reflect the stops we were going to make in Canada (that we are missing now).

![Image 3: Route-2](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Route-2.jpg)
## Update 2:

We have started to narrow our plans down but still leaving a lot of room for flexibility as we are now pretty sure we don't want to spend so many nights in big cities and prefer to camp out in nature. Below is the most recent updated map.

![Image 4: Route 3](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Route-3.jpg)
## Update 3:

Things first got slowed down in Salt Lake City where we spent almost 2 weeks. We then spent a lot longer in Washington, seeing more of the state than planned and with Michael flying back to San Francisco for a dermatologist appointment.

![Image 5: Route 4](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Route-4-1.jpg)
## Update 4:

We are now just under the halfway mark of our trip and have moved over to the eastern half of the country where we will zigzag up and down, taking in the so called "flyover states". This section will see a lot of long driving days through vast farmlands.

![Image 6: Route 5](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Route-5.jpg)
## Update 5:

Having surpassed the 6-month mark we are really starting to feel like the trip is moving faster and faster. As you can see from the latest map, we extended the route in a few places, even making it back over to Iowa to visit the Field of Dreams. The heat has really been a big factor over the last few weeks which has forced us into RV parks, thus increasing the budget.  
  
We also had our first ride-along visitor with Martynas coming to join us from Cincinnati to Nashville.

![Image 7: Route 6](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Route-6.jpg)
## Update 6:

WE DID IT! We completed the trip through all 48 lower states of the United States.

![Image 8: Complete USA Roadtrip Map](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Complete-USA-Roadtrip-Map.jpg)
## Final Update:

As you can see, we decided not to finish our trip in Florida and to instead, continue our journey through Central America to Nicaragua. We entered Mexico and traveled through Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras before finally ending the trip in Granada, Nicaragua.

![Image 9: Route 8](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Route-8.jpg)

Hiking in Canyons Of The Ancients National Monument offers exploration across a high desert landscape characterized by mesas, deeply incised canyons, and sandstone cliffs. The region is home to an extensive network of archaeological sites, including ancient cliff dwellings and pueblos, often integrated into the trails. Pinyon-juniper forests and sagebrush cover the terrain, providing a diverse ecosystem for outdoor activities. The monument's elevation, often above 5,000 feet, contributes to its rugged environment.

# About Us

Hi! We’re Michael, Lisette and Sheila Glass, 3 Aussies (2 expats and 1 Aussie cattle dog) who lived in San Francisco for over 13 incredible years.   
  
We’ve always been keen travelers and adventure seekers. We’ve both traveled to 40+ countries, and have enjoyed strolling down the cobblestone streets and eating fried bread in Vilnius, ziplining and diving in Boracay, taking traditional dancing and drumming classes in Conakry, to everything else in between. We both believe that life is what you make of it, and it’s meant to be lived to the fullest.   
  
This website–Glassies on the Road–will focus on our travels around North America in a 30-foot RV, which will take us to every state in the continental USA and Canada for about 10 months. We’ll share a recap of the places we visit, the challenges we’ll inevitably face, and any other tips and observations along the way. Let’s go!

![Image 2: Michael, Lisette and Sheila](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Michael-Lisette-and-Sheila.jpg)

# Day 65: Glen Canyon Dam, Horseshoe Bend and Navajo Bridge

April 21, 2025

## Page, Arizona

After two convenient nights sleeping in a Walmart parking lot, we were ready to move on. The city of Page is the gateway to popular attractions including Antelope Canyon, Lake Powell, Glen Canyon Dam and Horseshoe Bend so we weren’t expecting to do much in Page itself.

We checked out a couple of quirky places – the first was the [Street of Little Motels](https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/street-of-the-little-motels), filled with motels built in the 1950s to house workers constructing the Glen Canyon Dam. We drove through this street and saw that the majority are now private homes, although there are at least a couple that are still functioning as motels. We also checked out the [Boiler Tube Slot Canyon](https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/boiler-tube-slot-canyon-arizona), a funky art installation made out of boiler tubes made to resemble Antelope Canyon.

![Image 3: Boiler Tube Slot Canyon](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Boiler-Tube-Slot-Canyon-769x1024.jpg)

Boiler Tube Slot Canyon

Our last stop was a free grey/black water dump at the Maverik gas station in Page, where we met a friendly Swiss family – father, mother and 3 kids traveling for a year around the world, including about a month in the US. Michael exchanged phone info should we bump into them again on our travels.

## Glen Canyon Dam and a Wahweap Overlook

Did you know that Glen Canyon Dam is bigger than its more famous cousin, the Hoover Dam? While Hoover Dam is slightly taller, Glen Canyon Dam is considered larger due to its greater volume and width. Hoover Dam is 221 meters (726 feet) tall and 379 meters (1,244 feet) long, while Glen Canyon Dam is 216 meters (710 feet) tall and 475 meters (1,560 feet) long. Since we were high up on a bridge looking down at only a small part of the canyon, it was hard for us to put in perspective that Glen Canyon was indeed bigger, particularly as we’d seen the Hoover Dam in more of its entirety when we visited.

![Image 4: Glen Canyon Dam](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Glen-Canyon-Dam.jpg)

Glen Canyon Dam

![Image 5: Close up](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Close-up.jpg)

Close up

To see the Dam, we parked on the side of the road just before the bridge. We crossed over to see it from both sides of the bridge, feeling small looking at the tiny specks of rocks (probably boulders) below us. There’s also a section of the bridge that has a rectangular opening to take a photo or video through, uninterrupted by the wire fence. Michael was brave enough to stick his hand through, potentially sacrificing his phone to a long, sheer drop below had it fallen from his grip!

![Image 6: Sitting watching the view at Wahweap Overlook](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Sitting-watching-the-view-at-Wahweap-Overlook.jpg)

Sitting watching the view at Wahweap Overlook

![Image 7: Sheila had some freedom](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Lisette-had-some-freedom.jpg)

Sheila had some freedom

Not far from Glen Canyon Dam we drove up to Wahweap Overlook, a beautiful vista point where we could absorb the views of the terrain and lake below us, with the occasional sight of a boat sailing through the water, or a jet soaring above us. It’s a popular spot for people to drive up and take photos, but when we arrived there weren’t many vehicles parked around, which gave us the opportunity to set up our camping chairs facing the lake, and enjoy a relaxing, long lunch overlooking this glorious view.

## Horseshoe Bend: An Incredible Rock Castle

Just like Antelope Canyon which we’d visited the day before, [Horseshoe Bend](https://www.nps.gov/glca/planyourvisit/horseshoe-bend.htm) has exploded in popularity, thanks largely to the litany of social media posts showcasing its beauty. It’s a craggy, rock formation surrounded by the Colorado River, positioned like a formidable rock castle sitting within its moat.

![Image 8: Walking to Horseshoe Bend](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Walking-to-Horseshoe-Bend.jpg)

Walking to Horseshoe Bend

It costs $10 per vehicle ($5 per motorcycle) to park at the trailhead (National Park passes don’t apply). From here, it’s a short, gravelly, 2.4 kilometers (1.5 miles) to get to this incredible natural wonder. We took Sheila with us, although we had to be conscious of the furry little squirrel that would occasionally pop out in along the trail!

![Image 9: Lots of people](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Lots-of-people.jpg)

Lots of people

There’s a viewing area directly facing Horseshoe Bend, where the majority of visitors were congregated around to take their numerous photos. But all the perimeter, there are many other viewpoints that _don’t_ have barriers in front of them. Sure, they can make for more impressive photos – although the overlook is 1,300 meters (4,200 feet) above sea level, and the Colorado River is at 1,000 meters (3,200 feet) above sea level, so the drop would be a long 300 meter (1,000 feet down)!

![Image 10: Lisette on the edge at Horseshoe Bend](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Lisette-on-the-edge-at-Horseshoe-Bend.jpg)

Lisette on the edge at Horseshoe Bend

![Image 11: Michael sitting on the edge](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Michael-sitting-on-the-edge.jpg)

Michael sitting on the edge

![Image 12: Michael must have told a funny joke](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Michael-must-have-told-a-funny-joke.jpg)

Michael must have told a funny joke

![Image 13: Last view of Horseshoe Bend](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Last-view-of-Horseshoe-Bend.jpg)

Last view of Horseshoe Bend

Of course, we were one of the many people who decided to sit close (but still safely!) to the edge, mesmerized by the view in front of us. Lisette (and quite a few other visitors) was a bit put off by the several ladies, faces thick with makeup, who hogged a particular section of unexposed views, taking a billion photos of themselves in every angle imaginable. We get it, everyone wants to take a great photo, but keep it moving for others to also have the opportunity!

## Navajo Bridge: Twin Steel Bridges

Navajo Bridge are actually twin steel arch bridges that cross the Colorado River, in Grand Canyon National Park, in northern Arizona. The bridges were initially called Grand Canyon Bridge, but renamed five years later. The dual spans of the Navajo Bridge are tied in ninth place among the highest bridges in the US, at 142.3 meters (467 feet) and 143.3 meters (470 feet) tall respectively. We could walk from the start of the bridge to the other side, where there’s a Visitor Center and some signposts along the way detailing the history and cultural significance of the bridge and the area.

![Image 14: Navajo Bridge parking](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Antelope-Trails-parking.jpg)

Navajo Bridge parking

![Image 15: Selfie at Navajo Bridge](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Selfie-at-Navajo-Bridge.jpg)

Selfie at Navajo Bridge

![Image 16: Lisette and Sheila checking out the bridges](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Lisette-and-Sheila-checking-out-the-bridges.jpg)

Lisette and Sheila checking out the bridges

![Image 17: Looking up the river](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Looking-up-the-river.jpg)

Looking up the river

We drove across the bridge and found an incredible open space, parked alongside rising red rock formations. It was a huge space, and we were amazed that only one other car with two people were our only neighbors! Making the most of the beautiful weather, gorgeous scenery and golden sunset, we put out our camping chairs and sat outside for dinner, until the sun disappeared from the horizon on this wonderful day.

![Image 18: Lisette stoked at our campsite watching sunset](https://glassiesontheroad.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Lisette-stoked-at-our-campsite-watching-sunset.jpg)

Lisette stoked at our campsite watching sunset
